🅰️ How ATI words it (she likes ATI style questions)

Her exam questions look like ATI: a one-line client scenario, a "which of the following" question, and four short, plain options with no explanation inside them. The bank now has 86 questions written exactly this way, including the two from your ATI screenshots. The Cram Sheet has ATI style: 20 and ATI style: 50 buttons.

ATI stem wordingWhat it is really askingHow to attack it
Which of the following actions should the nurse take?Pick the one safe, correct nursing actionRule out anything unsafe or outside nursing scope first
...should the nurse take first? / ...is the priority?Order of actionsAirway, safety, stop the cause, then drugs, then notify
Which of the following findings should the nurse expect?The classic sign of the named conditionMatch the condition to its textbook picture
Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider?The abnormal or dangerous valueThree options are normal. Find the one outside the range
Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as a risk factor?Cause, not symptomThink what came before the condition
...indicates an understanding of the teaching?The one TRUE statementThree are myths. Pick the one that matches the rule
...indicates a need for further teaching?The one FALSE statementReverse of the last one. Pick the wrong statement
Which of the following medications should the nurse anticipate?Drug of choice for the conditionGeneric names. Know the one first-line drug
For which of the following medications is the client's condition a contraindication?The drug that would hurt THIS clientMatch each drug to its one big contraindication
Which of the following should the nurse include in the teaching?The correct client instructionShort rule statements. Look for absolutes that are wrong
Select all that applyEach option is its own true or falseJudge every line alone. Do not count how many you picked
ATI habits to noticeWhy it matters
"Client" not "patient"Same person
"Provider" not "doctor"OB, midwife, or nurse practitioner
"Weeks of gestation"The number decides preterm, term, or post-term and which drugs are allowed
Generic drug names onlyOxytocin, methylergonovine, carboprost, misoprostol, betamethasone, nifedipine, terbutaline, indomethacin, labetalol, hydralazine, magnesium sulfate
"0.9% sodium chloride"Normal saline
Vital signs with units38.2 C (100.8 F), 160/110 mm Hg, 10/min. Know the cutoffs
One correct answer is usually the plain safe oneThe flashy or fastest-sounding option is often the trap

Her two ATI screenshots: a postpartum client with heavy lochia and a distended bladder she cannot empty (catheterize, because a full bladder causes atony) and a client at 35 weeks in preterm labor (indomethacin is contraindicated after 32 weeks). Both are in the bank with full rationales.

🍼 Baby safety rules, always

Never move a baby before placing a matching band on the baby, the mom, and the dad.

  • Security bands are removed only by the discharge nurse.
  • Keep babies in the rolling bassinet. No carrying babies down the hall.

🗣️ Her in-class questions (answers)

Her questionAnswer
A woman who develops diabetes during pregnancy has type 2 diabetes. True or false?
  • False
  • It is gestational diabetes
A woman with class II heart disease has symptoms with increased activity. True or false?True.
Iron-deficiency anemia: pink membranes, increased appetite, fatigue, or bradycardia?Fatigue.
A pregnant woman who is HIV positive must have a cesarean. True or false?
  • False
  • It depends on viral load and clinical factors
Oligohydramnios in labor: early, variable, or late deceleration?Variable (B).
PPROM teaching (SATA): temperature daily, nipple stimulation, baths, perineal care, kick counts, signs of labor?
  • A, D, E, F
  • Not B (oxytocin) and not C (bacteria)
Risk factors for hypertensive disorders (SATA): advanced age, obesity, Hispanic ethnicity, family history of CVD, preterm birth history?
  • 🎤 A, B, D, E
  • The only choice that is NOT a risk factor is Hispanic ethnicity (C)

🎤 What she stressed in lecture

TopicKnow
Spontaneous abortion
  • = miscarriage = early pregnancy loss
  • Before 20 weeks
  • Misoprostol (Cytotec) bleeding is heavier than a period
  • Return for 2 pads an hour for 2 hours, severe pain, foul discharge, fever
Mole
  • Complete: no fetal parts
  • Partial: abnormal tissue plus a non-viable fetus
  • Avoid pregnancy 1 year
  • Watch hCG, choriocarcinoma (lungs, brain)
Accreta spectrum
  • Accreta 80%, increta 15%, percreta 5%
  • Prior cesarean is a risk
  • Expect 3 to 5 L blood loss and possible hysterectomy
Pelvic rest
  • Nothing in the vagina, no sex, no tampons, no heavy lifting
  • Cerclage for cervical insufficiency
Hypertension
  • Only Hispanic ethnicity is NOT a risk factor
  • About 25% progress to preeclampsia
  • Gestational should resolve by 12 weeks postpartum
Severe features
  • BP 160/110, platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 or doubled, liver enzymes twice normal, brain or vision changes, epigastric pain.
  • 24-hour urine over 300 mg
Magnesium
  • Seizure prevention, not BP control
  • Flushing and sweating are normal
  • Toxicity: lethargy, slow breathing, absent reflexes, dysrhythmias
  • Antidote: calcium gluconate
GDM
  • Two-step diagnosis (abnormal 2-hour, then abnormal 3-hour)
  • Management fasting under 92
  • Insulin first
  • A1C at the first visit if high risk
  • Urine ketones for DKA, protein for preeclampsia
Twins and ABO
  • Monozygotic: identical, shared placenta, higher risk
  • Dizygotic: fraternal
  • ABO: type O mother, A or B baby, jaundice, phototherapy
Preterm
  • 20 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks
  • Under 20 weeks is a miscarriage
  • Confirm fluid with nitrazine (blue) or fern
GBS
  • Not an STI
  • Not reportable
  • Fewer than 2 antibiotic doses before birth: notify the physician
TORCH
  • Toxoplasmosis (raw meat, cat feces), Other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus, hepatitis), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes
  • Herpes with active lesions at birth: cesarean
HIV
  • Medicine starts at 14 weeks
  • Low viral load may allow vaginal birth
  • Avoid operative procedures
  • Newborn syrup for 6 weeks
Drugs
  • Retinoids: absolutely contraindicated (iPLEDGE, two birth controls)
  • NSAIDs: avoid from 30 weeks (ductus arteriosus)
  • Warfarin: only with a mechanical valve
  • ACE inhibitors and ARBs: teratogenic
Substances
  • Caffeine under 200 mg a day
  • No safe amount of alcohol (FASD)
  • Positive screens are reported to CPS
  • Nonjudgmental care
Iron and meds
  • Ferrous sulfate: dark stools, take with vitamin C
  • Hemabate: avoid in asthma
  • Methergine: avoid in hypertension

⭐ Know these cold: Ch 19

  1. High-risk pregnancy puts the mother, the fetus, or both in jeopardy. Assess at the first visit and keep assessing.
  2. Spontaneous abortion is loss before 20 weeks. Most common cause is fetal genetic abnormality. RhoGAM within 72 hours if she is Rh-negative.
  3. Ectopic pregnancy: classic triad is pain, amenorrhea, bleeding. Shoulder pain, dizziness, and hypotension mean rupture and shock.
  4. Methotrexate for ectopic: no folic acid, no alcohol, no sun, antiemetic, avoid pregnancy for 3 months. It is hepatotoxic.
  5. Previa is PAINLESS, BRIGHT red, soft uterus: no vaginal exams. Abruption is PAINFUL, DARK, rigid uterus, linked to hypertension.
  6. Abruption: oxygen, strict bedrest left lateral, labs (CBC, fibrinogen, PT/aPTT, type and crossmatch), NST and BPP.
  7. 📝 Bleeding by trimester (classmate notes): first = spontaneous abortion and ectopic. Second = molar pregnancy. Third = previa, abruption, vasa previa.
  8. Hyperemesis: weight loss over 5%, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance. Gut rest is the priority, then IV fluids and antiemetics, TPN if needed.
  9. Intrahepatic cholestasis: bile acids build up, severe itching. Drug: ursodeoxycholic acid.
  10. Gestational HTN: new BP over 140/90 after 20 weeks (about 25% progress to preeclampsia). Chronic HTN: before pregnancy or before 20 weeks (25% develop preeclampsia).
  11. Preeclampsia: new hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria. Severe features: liver, brain, kidney involvement.
  12. Eclampsia: seizure. Client safety first, turn left, suction after, continuous fetal monitoring, magnesium sulfate.

⭐ Know these cold: Ch 20

  1. Diabetes that starts in pregnancy is gestational diabetes, not type 2.
  2. GTT at 24 to 28 weeks: 75 g glucose, level at 2 hours. Abnormal leads to a 3-hour test.
  3. Insulin is first line. Glyburide and metformin are second line.
  4. First-trimester hyperglycemia causes congenital anomalies. Later hyperglycemia causes macrosomia and birth trauma.
  5. Neonate: polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia, birth trauma, and risk of hypoglycemia.
  6. Labor: glucose every 1 to 2 hours, insulin drip, 50% dextrose at the bedside, monitor FHR and urine output.
  7. Class II heart disease: slight limitation, symptoms when she increases her activity.
  8. Cardiac nursing: vitals, apical rate, heart sounds, daily weights, edema, rest, prevent fluid overload, anticipate epidural.
  9. Chronic hypertension: before pregnancy or before 20 weeks, or lasting over 12 weeks after birth.
  10. Asthma: pregnancy worsens it for many women. Teach triggers and keep the medications.
  11. Iron-deficiency anemia: fatigue, pallor, tachycardia, more infections. Not pink membranes, not bradycardia.
  12. Sickle cell: preeclampsia, preterm labor, abruption, IUGR. Fluid overload can cause heart failure.

⭐ Know these cold: Ch 21

  1. Dystocia (difficult labor, "failure to progress") is the leading cause of cesarean birth.
  2. Uterine dystocia: hypertonic or hypotonic dysfunction, uncoordinated activity. Hypertonic contractions are painful with little dilation and little relaxation. Rest and hydration usually fix it.
  3. Active phase disorder (cervix at 6 cm or more): 4 hours of adequate contractions with no cervical change, or more than 6 hours on oxytocin with no change.
  4. Second stage disorder (10 cm): no progress after at least 2 to 4 hours of active pushing. Precipitous labor: under 3 hours start to finish.
  5. Tachysystole is more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes.
  6. Oxytocin is a high-alert medication, titrated IV up and down by response. Cervidil (dinoprostone) and Cytotec (misoprostol) ripen the cervix.
  7. Induction criteria: 41 weeks or maternal or fetal distress. Contraindications: placenta previa, cord prolapse, transverse or breech presentation.
  8. 📝 Your notes: dystocia is the leading cause of cesarean birth. Hypertonic = painful contractions with no dilation. High stress can lead to dystocia. Precipitous labor = birth in under 3 hours.
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: hypertonic uterus contracts too much and does not relax (rupture and fetal distress risk). Do NOT give oxytocin for it. Oxytocin is for hypotonic.
  10. 🎤 Active phase disorder: cervix over 6 cm with adequate contractions and no change, or inadequate contractions with no change after oxytocin for over 6 hours. Pushing 2 to 4 hours counts as lack of progress.
  11. 🎤 Induction starts labor. Augmentation moves along labor that already started. She said expect NCLEX style questions on this.
  12. 🎤 AROM (amniotomy) is provider only, only in L&D, not ruptured over 24 hours. Cervidil has a string (pull it out for hyperstimulation). Cytotec has no string.
  13. 🎤 Stress can contribute to dystocia (true).
  14. Vacuum risks to the baby: cephalhematoma, intracranial and retinal hemorrhage, asphyxia, jaundice. Mother: tears, cervix detachment, traumatic PPH.
  15. Forceps risks to the baby: facial injury, facial muscle paralysis, eye trauma, skull fracture, seizures. Mother: tears, incontinence, hemorrhage, bladder or urethra damage.
  16. VBAC: about 90% of women with a prior cesarean are eligible, with a 69 to 80% success rate. TOLAC is the trial. VBAC is the success.

⭐ Know these cold: Ch 22

  1. PPH is blood loss over 1,000 mL regardless of type of delivery.
  2. Most common cause: uterine atony. Lacerations are second. Treatment of choice for primary PPH: oxytocin.
  3. Four Ts: Tone, Tissue, Trauma, Thrombin. Atony is a boggy uterus. Trauma is a firm uterus with steady bright red bleeding.
  4. Two-pronged approach: resuscitate and treat shock, and find and treat the cause.
  5. Resuscitation: fluids, blood transfusion, bimanual compression, fundal massage, iron, uterotonics.
  6. Uterotonics: oxytocin, methylergonovine (Methergine), misoprostol (Cytotec), carboprost (Hemabate).
  7. Shock: mild about 20% loss, moderate 20 to 40%, severe over 40%. Signs: tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, oxygen under 95%, oliguria, pallor, dizziness, altered mental status.
  8. 🎤 Oct 21: oxytocin is FIRST line. Methergine, Hemabate, and misoprostol are all SECOND line. Methergine: avoid with uncontrolled hypertension. Hemabate: avoid with asthma. Misoprostol: option when Methergine cannot be used.
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: firm fundus with a steady trickle of bright red blood means laceration. Boggy fundus: massage until firm like a baseball.
  10. 🎤 Oct 21: she said PPH is likely on the exam and the med quiz covers PPH drugs and their contraindications.
  11. ➕ Methergine avoided in hypertension, so use oxytocin, Hemabate, or Cytotec. Hemabate avoided in asthma, so use oxytocin, Methergine, or Cytotec.
  12. Coagulation disorders on her slide: DIC, anaphylactoid syndrome (AFE), and VTE.
  13. AFE: rare but fatal, during pregnancy, labor, or up to 24 hours postpartum. Hypoxia, lung injury, pulmonary hypertension, hypotension, cardiac arrest, coagulopathy.
  14. Thrombosis causes: venous stasis, injury to the vessel lining, hypercoagulation. Types: superficial (saphenous vein), deep vein thrombosis (can cause PE).
  15. Postpartum DVT: the drug is heparin (not ibuprofen, amoxicillin, or acetaminophen).
  16. Endometritis: cesarean is the primary cause. Temp over 100.4 F, uterine tenderness, subinvolution, foul lochia. Treat with antibiotics.

⭐ Know these cold: FHR

  1. Baseline 110 to 160 bpm over 10 minutes. Tachycardia above 160 and bradycardia below 110 for 10 minutes or more.
  2. Moderate variability (6 to 25 bpm) is reassuring. Minimal, absent, and marked are concerning.
  3. VEAL CHOP: Variable = Cord, Early = Head, Acceleration = OK, Late = Placental insufficiency.
  4. Early needs no action. Late and variable: reposition, stop oxytocin, fluids, oxygen, notify.
  5. Category I normal. Category II indeterminate. Category III abnormal: absent variability with recurrent lates, variables, or bradycardia, or sinusoidal.
  6. Intrauterine resuscitation: reposition, stop oxytocin, IV bolus, oxygen, check for prolapse, check vitals, notify, prepare for birth.
  7. Check her pulse: a rate of 70 to 90 may be the mother.
  8. Magnesium, opioids, fetal sleep, and acidemia lower variability.

⚡ Quick-fire recall: FHR patterns

Say each pattern, cause, and action out loud.

QuestionAnswer
Normal baseline?
  • 110 to 160 bpm
  • Tachycardia above 160 and bradycardia below 110 for 10 minutes or more
Variability levels?Absent undetectable, minimal 5 or less, moderate 6 to 25, marked over 25.
Acceleration?15 bpm for 15 seconds (10 and 10 under 32 weeks).
Early deceleration?
  • Mirrors the contraction
  • Head compression
  • Watch
Variable deceleration?
  • Abrupt, 15 bpm or more, 15 seconds to under 2 minutes
  • Cord compression
  • Reposition
Late deceleration?
  • Starts after the contraction, low point after the peak
  • Placental insufficiency
  • Turn left, fluids, oxygen, stop oxytocin, call
Prolonged deceleration?
  • 2 minutes or more but under 10
  • Fix the cause
Sinusoidal?
  • Smooth sine wave
  • Category III
  • Severe anemia or hypoxia
Category I?Baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations.
Category II?
  • Everything else
  • Evaluate and act on the cause
Category III?
  • Absent variability with recurrent lates, variables, or bradycardia, or sinusoidal
  • Act now
Recurrent?With at least half of contractions in 20 minutes.
Resuscitation steps?Reposition, stop oxytocin, LR bolus (250 mL for low BP), oxygen only if SpO2 under 95%, check prolapse, check vitals, notify.
What lowers variability?Fetal sleep, opioids, magnesium, acidemia.
Reading order?DR C BRAVADO: Determine Risk, Contractions, Baseline Rate, Variability, Accelerations, Decelerations, Overall.

🅰️ How ATI words it (she likes ATI style questions)

Her exam questions look like ATI: a one-line client scenario, a "which of the following" question, and four short, plain options with no explanation inside them. The bank now has 86 questions written exactly this way, including the two from your ATI screenshots. The Cram Sheet has ATI style: 20 and ATI style: 50 buttons.

ATI stem wordingWhat it is really askingHow to attack it
Which of the following actions should the nurse take?Pick the one safe, correct nursing actionRule out anything unsafe or outside nursing scope first
...should the nurse take first? / ...is the priority?Order of actionsAirway, safety, stop the cause, then drugs, then notify
Which of the following findings should the nurse expect?The classic sign of the named conditionMatch the condition to its textbook picture
Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider?The abnormal or dangerous valueThree options are normal. Find the one outside the range
Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as a risk factor?Cause, not symptomThink what came before the condition
...indicates an understanding of the teaching?The one TRUE statementThree are myths. Pick the one that matches the rule
...indicates a need for further teaching?The one FALSE statementReverse of the last one. Pick the wrong statement
Which of the following medications should the nurse anticipate?Drug of choice for the conditionGeneric names. Know the one first-line drug
For which of the following medications is the client's condition a contraindication?The drug that would hurt THIS clientMatch each drug to its one big contraindication
Which of the following should the nurse include in the teaching?The correct client instructionShort rule statements. Look for absolutes that are wrong
Select all that applyEach option is its own true or falseJudge every line alone. Do not count how many you picked
ATI habits to noticeWhy it matters
"Client" not "patient"Same person
"Provider" not "doctor"OB, midwife, or nurse practitioner
"Weeks of gestation"The number decides preterm, term, or post-term and which drugs are allowed
Generic drug names onlyOxytocin, methylergonovine, carboprost, misoprostol, betamethasone, nifedipine, terbutaline, indomethacin, labetalol, hydralazine, magnesium sulfate
"0.9% sodium chloride"Normal saline
Vital signs with units
  • 38.2 C (100.8 F), 160/110 mm Hg, 10/min.
  • Know the cutoffs
One correct answer is usually the plain safe oneThe flashy or fastest-sounding option is often the trap

  • Her two ATI screenshots: a postpartum client with heavy lochia and a distended bladder she cannot empty (catheterize, because a full bladder causes atony) and a client at 35 weeks in preterm labor (indomethacin is contraindicated after 32 weeks)
  • Both are in the bank with full rationales

🪤 How she could trap you

  • Painless vs painful: Painless bright red bleeding is previa. Painful dark bleeding with a hard uterus is abruption. Questions swap them.
  • Vaginal exam: Do not do a vaginal exam on a bleeding client until previa is ruled out.
  • Gestational vs chronic: Over 20 weeks new = gestational. Before pregnancy or before 20 weeks = chronic. The number is 140/90 for both.
  • Proteinuria: Gestational hypertension has no proteinuria. Add proteinuria and it is preeclampsia.
  • ABO vs Rh: Rh is the more severe one. ABO is a type O mother with an A or B baby.
  • Who gets RhoGAM: Only an Rh-negative mother. An Rh-positive mother never needs it.
  • Preterm cut-off: Preterm is under 37 weeks. Very preterm is under 32. Late preterm is 34 to 36.
  • PROM vs PPROM: PPROM adds the word preterm: before 37 weeks.
  • Gestational vs type 2: Diabetes that develops in pregnancy is gestational diabetes. It is not type 2.
  • First trimester: Anomalies come from high glucose in the first trimester. Macrosomia comes later.
  • Class II: Class II is symptoms with increased activity. Class IV is symptoms at rest.
  • Iron-deficiency findings: Pale membranes and tachycardia, not pink and not bradycardia.
  • Cesarean for HIV: Not automatic. Viral load, rupture time, and labor progress decide the method.
  • Instrumentation: With HIV avoid episiotomy and fetal scalp electrodes.
  • Advanced age cut-off: Advanced maternal age is over 35.
  • Obesity cut-off: Obesity is a BMI over 30.
  • Induction vs augmentation: Induction STARTS labor. Augmentation STRENGTHENS labor that has already started.
  • Oxytocin and ripening: Her slide lists oxytocin under both ripening and augmentation.
    • The prostaglandins Cervidil and Cytotec are the ripening drugs.
  • TOLAC vs VBAC: TOLAC is the planned trial. VBAC is a trial that ends in a vaginal birth. A failed trial is still a TOLAC.
  • Vacuum vs forceps injuries: Facial paralysis and facial injury are forceps. Cephalhematoma and retinal hemorrhage are vacuum.
  • Emergent vs urgent: Emergent is immediate (cord prolapse, rupture, abnormal FHR).
    • Urgent is rapid but not immediate (malpresentation, previa with mild bleeding and Category I).
  • Non-urgent: Failure to progress or descend with a Category I tracing. The FHR category is what keeps it non-urgent.
  • Most common cause: Uterine atony. Lacerations are second. Hematomas are painful and the uterus is firm.
  • Treatment of choice: Oxytocin for primary PPH, not terbutaline (that relaxes the uterus), not misoprostol, and not heparin.
  • DVT drug: Heparin. The other choices treat pain or infection.
  • AFE timing: During pregnancy, labor, or up to 24 hours postpartum.
  • Blues vs depression timing: Blues: first 2 weeks. Depression: within 12 months. Psychosis: as early as 2 to 3 days.
  • Most severe form: Postpartum psychosis (true on her slide).

🩸 Bleeding in Pregnancy

Definitions first: high risk, abortion types, ectopic, mole, cervical insufficiency, previa, abruption, and accreta.

🧠 The big idea

Every bleeding problem is solved by asking: when, what color, and is it painful?
Early pregnancy: abortion, ectopic, mole → Mid to late pregnancy: previa (painless, bright red) vs abruption (painful, dark, rigid) → Priority: tissue perfusion for mom and baby, no vaginal exams until previa is ruled out

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 Molar pregnancy: prune juice (dark brown) bleeding, very high hCG, no fetal heart rate. Avoid pregnancy for 1 year. RhoGAM if Rh-negative.
  2. 🎤 Ectopic is the leading cause of death in the first trimester. Shoulder pain means blood is irritating the diaphragm.
  3. 🎤 After a loss, call the provider for 2 maxi pads an hour for 2 hours, severe belly or back pain, foul discharge, or fever.
  4. 🎤 Previa always ends in cesarean. Abruption: fetal mortality 40%, maternal mortality 5%.
  5. 🎤 Accreta spectrum: accreta 80%, increta 15%, percreta 5%. Blood loss 3 to 5 L (usual is 500 mL).
  6. High-risk pregnancy puts the mother, the fetus, or both in jeopardy. Assess at the first visit and keep assessing.
  7. Spontaneous abortion is loss before 20 weeks. Most common cause is fetal genetic abnormality. RhoGAM within 72 hours if she is Rh-negative.
  8. Ectopic pregnancy: classic triad is pain, amenorrhea, bleeding. Shoulder pain, dizziness, and hypotension mean rupture and shock.
  9. Methotrexate for ectopic: no folic acid, no alcohol, no sun, antiemetic, avoid pregnancy for 3 months. It is hepatotoxic.
  10. Previa is PAINLESS, BRIGHT red, soft uterus: no vaginal exams. Abruption is PAINFUL, DARK, rigid uterus, linked to hypertension.
  11. Abruption: oxygen, strict bedrest left lateral, labs (CBC, fibrinogen, PT/aPTT, type and crossmatch), NST and BPP.
  12. 📝 Bleeding by trimester (classmate notes): first = spontaneous abortion and ectopic. Second = molar pregnancy. Third = previa, abruption, vasa previa.

📖 Bleeding in pregnancy (34 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
High-risk pregnancy
  • A pregnancy that puts the mother, the fetus, or both in jeopardy
  • It comes from the pregnancy itself or from a condition that was there before it, and it carries higher morbidity and mortality
Risk assessmentDone at the first prenatal visit and repeated through the pregnancy to find high-risk factors early.
Spontaneous abortion
  • Loss of the fetus before 20 weeks
  • It is the most common complication of early pregnancy
  • Also called: miscarriage
Induced abortionTermination caused by a procedure or a medication.
Elective abortionTermination before viability at the request of the woman.
Therapeutic abortionTermination for serious maternal medical indications or fetal anomalies.
D&C (dilation and curettage)
  • Procedure that empties the uterus
  • Used when products of conception are not all expelled on their own
Threatened abortion
  • Bleeding with a closed cervix
  • The pregnancy may continue
  • (added)
Inevitable abortion
  • Bleeding and cramping with a dilated cervix
  • The loss cannot be stopped
  • (added)
Incomplete abortionSome products of conception are passed and some are retained. (added)
Complete abortionAll products of conception are passed. (added)
Missed abortionThe embryo or fetus has died but nothing has been expelled. (added)
Ectopic pregnancy
  • The ovum implants outside the uterus: fallopian tube, cervix, ovary, or abdominal cavity
  • It happens in about 1 in 50 pregnancies and is the leading cause of death in the first trimester
Classic triad of ectopic pregnancy
  • Abdominal pain, amenorrhea, and vaginal bleeding
  • Most women do not have all three
Hallmark sign of ectopic pregnancyAbdominal pain and spotting within 6 to 8 weeks after a missed period.
SalpingostomySurgery that opens the fallopian tube to remove an ectopic pregnancy.
Methotrexate
  • Single-dose IM drug for ectopic pregnancy
  • Teach: no folic acid, it is hepatotoxic, take an antiemetic, no alcohol, avoid pregnancy for at least 3 months, and it causes photosensitivity
Gestational trophoblastic disease
  • Abnormal growth of placental tissue
  • The two types are hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma
  • The pregnancy is not viable
Hydatidiform mole
  • A benign neoplasm of the placenta
  • It can be complete or partial
  • Also called: molar pregnancy
Choriocarcinoma
  • A cancer that can follow a complete molar pregnancy
  • It can occur during pregnancy, after childbirth, or years later
  • Remission rate is about 90%
Cervical insufficiency
  • Painless premature dilation of the cervix without contractions
  • Cause is unknown
  • Possible causes are cervical damage, less elastin or collagen, and more relaxin
  • Also called: incompetent cervix
CerclageA stitch placed around the cervix to hold it closed in cervical insufficiency.
Placenta previa
  • The placenta is inserted in the lower uterine segment and partly or completely covers the internal os
  • Painless bright red bleeding in the last two trimesters
Placental abruption
  • Early separation of the placenta, which compromises the fetal blood supply
  • Dark red bleeding, knifelike pain, and a firm to rigid uterus
Placenta accreta
  • The placenta attaches too deeply into the uterine wall
  • Postpartum hemorrhage is likely and a hysterectomy may be needed
Concealed hemorrhage
  • Bleeding that stays trapped behind the placenta
  • It can happen with abruption, so the outside blood loss can understate how much she has lost
Maternal-fetal medicine (MFM)Specialists a high-risk client may be referred to after risk assessment at the first prenatal visit.
Early pregnancy lossAnother name for spontaneous abortion or miscarriage: loss before 20 weeks.
Misoprostol (Cytotec)
  • Medication that can end an early pregnancy
  • Bleeding is heavier than a normal period
Uterine aspirationProcedure that removes the products of conception after an early pregnancy loss.
Vasa previa
  • Fetal vessels cross the cervical opening
  • Third trimester bleeding cause with risk to the baby
Placenta increta
  • About 15% of accreta cases
  • The placenta invades the uterine muscle
Placenta percreta
  • About 5% of accreta cases
  • The placenta goes through the uterus into other organs such as the bladder
Placenta accreta spectrum
  • Accreta (about 80%), increta (15%), percreta (5%)
  • Ranked by depth of invasion
  • Prior cesarean is a risk

🏥 High-risk pregnancy basics

TopicKnow
What it is
  • A condition from the pregnancy or present before it that jeopardizes the mother, fetus, or both
  • Higher morbidity and mortality
When to assessAt the first antepartal visit and on an ongoing basis.
ExamplesGestational diabetes, hypertensive disorders, PCOS, obesity, HIV/AIDS, advanced maternal age, substance, tobacco, or alcohol use, previous preterm birth, multiple gestation.
Biophysical factors
  • Genetics (cystic fibrosis)
  • Nutrition (anorexia, obesity)
  • Chronic illness (diabetes and hypertension lead to macrosomia and preeclampsia)
  • Obstetric history (repeated loss, fibroids, prior cesarean, multiples)
Impact on the familySelf-esteem, home and work life, and finances can all suffer.
General nursing actions
  • Give time to express concerns and feelings
  • Give information repeatedly
  • Facilitate referrals

🧸 Abortion: classification and care

TypeMeaning
InducedBy a procedure or medication.
ElectiveTermination before viability at her request.
TherapeuticSerious maternal medical reasons or fetal anomalies.
Spontaneous
  • Loss before 20 weeks
  • 80% happen in the first trimester
  • Most common cause is fetal genetic abnormality
Spontaneous abortion careKnow
Risk factorsAge, endocrine disorders, drug use or toxins, infections, genetic factors.
Assess
  • Bleeding color, amount, clots or tissue
  • Lower back or abdominal cramping
  • Vital signs
  • Look for fetal parts
Medical management
  • Make sure all products of conception are expelled (D&C if not resolved at home)
  • RhoGAM
Nursing management
  • Physical and emotional support, grief support, referral to a community support group
  • RhoGAM within 72 hours if Rh-negative

➕ Types of spontaneous abortion

TypeCervix and tissue
Threatened
  • Bleeding, cervix closed
  • Pregnancy may continue
Inevitable
  • Cervix dilated, cramping
  • Cannot be stopped
IncompleteSome tissue passed, some retained.
CompleteAll tissue passed.
MissedFetus has died, nothing expelled.
RecurrentThree or more losses in a row.

📍 Ectopic pregnancy

TopicKnow
What it is
  • Implantation outside the uterus: tube, cervix, ovary, abdominal cavity
  • About 1 in 50 pregnancies
Why it matters
  • Primary cause of death in the first trimester
  • A ruptured ectopic is a medical emergency
Classic triad
  • Abdominal pain, amenorrhea, vaginal bleeding
  • Most women do not have all three
Hallmark signAbdominal pain and spotting within 6 to 8 weeks after a missed period.
Rupture signsSudden severe sharp lower abdominal pain, dizziness, pain referred to the shoulder, hypotension, hypovolemic shock.
AssessmentUrine pregnancy test, pregnancy and sexual history, and watch hCG levels fall.
Management
  • Methotrexate single IM dose
  • Prostaglandins, misoprostol, actinomycin
  • Surgery: salpingostomy
  • Follow hCG, pain control, emotional support, teach risk reduction
➕ Risk factorsPrior ectopic, tubal damage or surgery, pelvic infection, IUD, smoking.

💉 Methotrexate teaching (her list)

  • No folic acid (it blocks the drug)
  • Hepatotoxic, so no alcohol
  • Give an antiemetic
  • Avoid pregnancy for at least 3 months
  • Causes photosensitivity, so protect from the sun
  • Single dose IM

🍇 Gestational trophoblastic disease

TopicKnow
Two types
  • Hydatidiform mole (benign neoplasm, complete or partial)
  • Choriocarcinoma (can follow a complete mole)
Choriocarcinoma
  • Can occur during pregnancy, after childbirth, or years later
  • 90% remission rate
Cause and viability
  • Exact cause unknown
  • The pregnancy is not viable
Signs
  • Looks like a spontaneous abortion at about 12 weeks
  • Brownish bleeding
  • Early pregnancy signs
  • No fetal heart rate
  • Severe persistent nausea and vomiting
  • Very high hCG
Nursing management
  • Prepare for evacuation (D&C)
  • Emotional support
  • Teach treatment, serial hCG monitoring, prophylactic chemotherapy, and cancer risk
➕ Also expectUterus larger than dates and passage of grapelike clusters.

🧵 Cervical insufficiency

TopicKnow
What it isPremature dilation of the cervix without contractions.
Cause
  • Unknown
  • Possibly cervical damage, less elastin or collagen, more relaxin
Assess
  • Risk factors
  • Pink-tinged discharge, pelvic pressure, loss of amniotic fluid
  • Transvaginal ultrasound
  • Watch for preterm labor
ManageBed rest, pelvic rest, no heavy lifting, cerclage, emotional support, education.

FindingPlacenta previaPlacental abruption
OnsetInsidiousSudden
BleedingAlways visible, slight then heavierConcealed or visible
Blood colorBright redDark
PainNone (painless)Constant, knifelike, uterine tenderness
Uterine toneSoft and relaxedFirm to rigid
Fetal heart rateUsually normalDistress or absent
PresentationMay be breech or transverse. Engagement absentNo relationship

🅿️ Placenta previa care

TopicKnow
What it is
  • Placenta in the lower uterine segment, partly or fully covering the internal os
  • Bleeding in the last two trimesters
Assess
  • Risk factors
  • Bright red painless bleeding
  • Soft nontender uterus
Monitor
  • Bleeding with a pad count
  • AVOID vaginal exams
  • FHR surveillance
ManageBed rest, prepare for possible cesarean birth, fetal movement counts, teach signs to report, support.

⚡ Placental abruption care

TopicKnow
What it is
  • Separation of the placenta that compromises fetal blood supply
  • Her slide: fetal mortality 40%, maternal mortality 5%
CauseMost cases come from gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.
Assess
  • Dark red bleeding
  • Knifelike pain, tenderness, contractions
  • Decreased fetal movement
  • Fetal distress
  • Maternal vitals
  • Rigid uterus

  • Oxygen
  • Strict bedrest left lateral

  • Cocaine use and trauma raise the risk

What it isThe placenta attaches too deeply into the uterus.
Danger

📝 Bleeding by trimester, shock signs, and accreta (classmate notes)

TopicKnow
First trimesterSpontaneous abortion (miscarriage) and ectopic pregnancy
Second trimesterMolar pregnancy
Third trimesterPlacenta previa, abruptio placentae, vasa previa (lecture also named preterm labor)
Signs of hypovolemic shockHypotension, tachycardia, thready pulse
Placenta accreta
  • Placenta attaches too deeply into the uterus
  • About 3 to 5 L of blood can be lost
  • Life threatening
  • Most commonly tied to an emergent cesarean
  • May need a hysterectomy
Why previa needs a cesareanThe placenta cannot be moved out of the way, so it blocks the baby from coming out of the cervix
Previa nursingBright red painless bleeding, soft uterus, NO vaginal exams, monitor the FHR closely and teach kick counts
Molar pregnancy

🎤 High-risk pregnancy: what she added

  • High risk is an umbrella term. There is no one-size-fits-all.
  • It can disrupt home and work life and hurt self-esteem. Some clients get home bedrest. Some stay in the hospital for a long time.
  • Assess at the first prenatal visit. She may be referred to Maternal-Fetal Medicine (MFM).
  • Chronic disease (lupus, RA, MS, any chronic condition): be stable or in remission for 6 months before getting pregnant.
  • Also high risk: age over 35 or under 18, PCOS, thyroid disease, multiple cesareans, repeated losses, twins or triplets, prior preterm birth.

🎤 Bleeding by trimester

TrimesterThink
FirstMiscarriage (spontaneous abortion), ectopic pregnancy
SecondMolar pregnancy
ThirdPlacenta previa, placental abruption, vasa previa, preterm labor

🎤 Miscarriage: terms, causes, and teaching

TopicKnow
Interchangeable termsEarly pregnancy loss, miscarriage, and spontaneous abortion all mean the same thing.
Definition
  • Loss of a pregnancy that reached the uterus but ended before viability (before 20 weeks)
  • It was not a viable pregnancy
TherapeuticTermination for a serious maternal medical reason or fetal anomalies.
Procedure and drug
  • Procedure: uterine aspiration
  • Medication: usually misoprostol (Cytotec)
Risk factorsPrior pregnancy loss (a big one), advanced maternal age, endocrine problems (diabetes, menstrual or hormonal disorders), drug use, environmental toxins, infections, uterine or cervical abnormality.
Assess
  • Amount of bleeding
  • Clots mean tissue is present
  • Low back pain or abnormal cramping
  • Look for fetal parts
Warn her
  • Bleeding is heavier than a normal period
  • That can be alarming
Call the providerSevere abdominal or back pain, heavy bleeding (soaking 2 maxi pads an hour for 2 consecutive hours), foul-smelling discharge, or fever.
Make sure
  • All products of conception are expelled
  • Ultrasound can check
  • D&C if they are not
Support
  • Physical and emotional support, grief support, community groups
  • It is often a very sad situation
RhoGAMRh-negative clients need RhoGAM to protect future pregnancies.

🎤 Ectopic pregnancy: what she added

TopicKnow
Why anywhere
  • The tubes, uterus, and abdomen form an open system, so the ovum can implant anywhere
  • Most common place is the fallopian tube
  • Also ovary, cervix, abdomen
How common
  • About 1 in 50 pregnancies
  • Leading cause of death in the first trimester
Risk factorsPelvic inflammatory disease (scarring), previous ectopic, pelvic or abdominal surgery, endometriosis, tubal ligation, smoking.
Presents
  • First trimester
  • Unilateral stabbing pain in the lower abdomen
  • She may not know she is pregnant
  • Spotting may or may not happen
Classic triad
  • Missed period, abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding
  • Most women have 1 or 2 of the 3, not always all 3
Rupture
  • Sudden sharp lower abdominal pain, dizziness, referred shoulder pain (blood irritates the diaphragm), then shock: hypotension and tachycardia
  • Bright red bleeding fits rupture
  • Watch hematocrit
Treatment
  • Surgery (she loses the tube if it ruptured)
  • If small and not ruptured: methotrexate, which may save the tube
Methotrexate
  • Single dose
  • No folic acid
  • Hepatotoxic
  • Causes nausea, so give an antiemetic
  • No alcohol
  • Avoid pregnancy at least 3 months
Support
  • She has lost a pregnancy
  • Expect grief
  • This can come through the ER

🎤 Molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease)

TopicKnow
What it is
  • Rare
  • Non-viable placental-related tumors that look like a pregnancy
  • Can turn into cancer
Complete mole
  • Benign
  • Grapelike clusters
  • No fetal parts at all
Partial moleA fetus is present but the pregnancy is not viable.
NeedsPaternal DNA must be involved, so it does require fertilization.
Cause
  • Unknown
  • Can occur during pregnancy, after childbirth, or years later
Signs
  • Prune juice (dark brown) bleeding
  • Early pregnancy signs (breast tenderness)
  • No fetal heart rate
  • Severe persistent nausea and vomiting from very high hCG
Treatment
  • Immediate removal with D&C
  • RhoGAM if Rh-negative
Follow-up
  • Watch hCG levels
  • Choriocarcinoma can follow a complete mole that was not cleared
  • It can spread to the lungs and brain
  • Some cases need chemotherapy
TeachingCannot get pregnant for 1 year, so a rise in hCG from a new pregnancy is not mistaken for cancer.
Support
  • It is a perceived loss
  • She felt pregnant and had the symptoms

🎤 Cervical insufficiency: what she added

  • Premature cervical dilation with no contractions. It happens too early.
  • Causes: hormonal changes, less elastin, cervical damage, multiple deliveries. It can happen to anyone.
  • Treatment: cerclage (a stitch around the cervix). Management is a risk-benefit talk with the OB.
  • Pelvic rest: nothing in the vagina, no sex, no tampons. Avoid heavy lifting. Activity restriction or bedrest, sometimes in the hospital.
  • She may have pink-tinged discharge or lose some amniotic fluid. Watch for infection and preterm labor.
  • Emotional support. Many have other children and responsibilities at home.

🎤 Previa, abruption, and accreta: what she added

ConditionKnow
Past 20 weeksBoth previa and abruption bleed in the second or third trimester, past 20 weeks.
Previa
  • Placenta implanted over or near the os
  • Bright red, painless, soft uterus
  • No trauma
  • Monitor the baby (fetal heart rate), no vaginal exams
  • Bedrest
  • Teach kick counts
  • Always a cesarean (the placenta cannot be moved)
  • If found by ultrasound without symptoms: manage as an outpatient and schedule the cesarean
Abruption
  • Placenta separates from the uterine wall and cuts off the baby's blood supply
  • Fetal mortality 40%, maternal mortality 5%.
Abruption causesGestational hypertension or preeclampsia (most), prior abruption, abdominal trauma (car accident), cocaine or meth, nicotine, clotting disorders.
Abruption signsDark red bleeding (or a concealed hemorrhage trapped behind the placenta), pain, uterine tenderness and rigidity, fetal distress, decreased fetal movement, shock signs (hypotension, tachycardia, pallor).
Abruption care
  • Oxygen for mom and baby, bedrest, CBC, coagulation studies, type and crossmatch
  • NST only if there is time
  • Usually an emergency cesarean
Accreta
  • Placenta attaches too deeply, often into the scar of a past cesarean
  • Loses about 3 to 5 L (500 mL is usual, under 1,000 mL is normal)
  • Emergency cesarean, possible hysterectomy
Accreta spectrum
  • Accreta 80%: invades the normal boundary (decidua)
  • Increta 15%: into the myometrium (muscle)
  • Percreta 5%: through the uterus into the bladder, intestines, and other organs

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Pregnancy after a mole vs methotrexateAfter a molar pregnancy: avoid pregnancy for 1 year. After methotrexate: at least 3 months. Do not swap them.
⚠️ Before 20 weeksLoss before 20 weeks is spontaneous abortion (miscarriage). From 20 weeks on it is preterm birth, not a miscarriage.
⚠️ Shoulder painShoulder pain in early pregnancy means a ruptured ectopic irritating the diaphragm. It is not a previa sign.
⚠️ The pad ruleCall for soaking 2 maxi pads an hour for 2 consecutive hours. Not 1 pad.
⚠️ Accreta numbersAccreta is the most common (80%) and percreta is the most severe (5%). Blood loss 3 to 5 L, not 500 mL.
⚠️ Painless vs painfulPainless bright red bleeding is previa. Painful dark bleeding with a hard uterus is abruption. Questions swap them.
⚠️ Vaginal examDo not do a vaginal exam on a bleeding client until previa is ruled out.
⚠️ Abruption can hideAbruption bleeding can be concealed, so the outside blood does not match how sick she is.
⚠️ Abruption causeHer slide: most abruptions start with gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.
⚠️ Methotrexate and folic acidNo folic acid with methotrexate. It also means no alcohol and no sun.
⚠️ Ectopic triadMost women do NOT have all three signs of the classic triad.
⚠️ Shoulder painPain referred to the shoulder in a woman with early pregnancy bleeding means a ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.
⚠️ Which trimester for a molar pregnancy?Second trimester per her notes. First is miscarriage and ectopic. Third is previa, abruption, vasa previa.

🧪 Hyperemesis, Liver, and Hypertensive Disorders

Definitions first: hyperemesis, cholestasis, the five hypertensive disorders, HELLP, lab values, and magnesium sulfate.

🧠 The big idea

  • Preeclampsia is hypertension after 20 weeks plus organ trouble
  • Protect the brain, then the baby.
    New high BP after 20 weeks + protein → Severe features hit the liver, brain, and kidneys → Seizure = eclampsia, turn left and give magnesium → Watch reflexes, breathing, and urine so magnesium does not poison her

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures. It does not lower the BP. Flushing and sweating are expected. Lethargy, respiratory depression, absent reflexes, and dysrhythmias mean toxicity: calcium gluconate.
  2. 🎤 Severe features = preeclampsia plus one: BP 160/110 or higher, platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 or doubled, liver enzymes twice normal, new headache or vision change, persistent epigastric pain.
  3. 🎤 Hispanic ethnicity is the only choice that is NOT a hypertension risk. Black women are at higher risk.
  4. 🎤 Eclampsia: protect, no restraint, nothing in the mouth, left side, suction, oxygen, continuous fetal monitoring. Seizures can happen postpartum.
  5. 🎤 HELLP: RUQ pain, malaise, unexplained bruising, bleeding at IV sites. Found by labs, so catch it early.
  6. 🎤 Hyperemesis is the most common reason for admission in the first trimester. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.
  7. 🧪 SIM: Mag Watch every 4 hours and PRN. DTRs 2+ with no clonus, RR 12 or more, urine 30 mL/hr or more, alert and oriented (GCS 15). Absent DTRs is the first warning sign.
  8. 🧪 SIM: Mag toxicity = STOP the infusion first (do not wait for an order), call for help and the provider, give calcium gluconate IV, support breathing (O2, ambu bag).
  9. 🧪 SIM: Severe-range BP is SBP 160 or higher or DBP 110 or higher, sustained 15 minutes. IV labetalol 20, 40, 80 mg, each over 2 minutes, recheck BP 10 minutes after each. Max 220 mg.
  10. Hyperemesis: weight loss over 5%, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance. Gut rest is the priority, then IV fluids and antiemetics, TPN if needed.
  11. Intrahepatic cholestasis: bile acids build up, severe itching. Drug: ursodeoxycholic acid.
  12. Gestational HTN: new BP over 140/90 after 20 weeks (about 25% progress to preeclampsia). Chronic HTN: before pregnancy or before 20 weeks (25% develop preeclampsia).
  13. Preeclampsia: new hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria. Severe features: liver, brain, kidney involvement.
  14. Eclampsia: seizure. Client safety first, turn left, suction after, continuous fetal monitoring, magnesium sulfate.
  15. HELLP: Hemolysis, Elevated liver enzymes, Low platelets. Risks: cerebral hemorrhage, DIC, abruption, liver rupture, maternal death.
  16. Labs of concern: 24-hour urine 300 mg or more, protein to creatinine 0.3 or more, platelets 100,000 or less.
  17. 📝 Your ATI notes: PEP (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, also called PUPPP) is the itchy RASH of late pregnancy, usually starting in the stretch marks. ICP is itching with NO rash and high bile acids. ICP is the dangerous one.
  18. 📝 Hypertensive disorders are the 2nd leading cause of maternal mortality (classmate notes). Hypertension is over 140 and/or over 90: either number or both.

📖 Hyperemesis, liver, and hypertension (25 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
Hyperemesis gravidarum
  • Severe nausea and vomiting of pregnancy with weight loss over 5% of pre-pregnancy weight, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance
  • It usually resolves by about week 20
Gut rest
  • NPO to rest the GI tract
  • It is the priority for hyperemesis, along with IV fluids and antiemetics
TPN
  • Total parenteral nutrition
  • IV nutrition used when a client with hyperemesis cannot take anything by mouth
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
  • Pregnancy-specific liver disease where bile acids build up
  • Main finding is severe itching (pruritus)
  • Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)The drug used to treat intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
Gestational hypertension
  • New-onset BP above 140/90 after 20 weeks of gestation, without proteinuria
  • It raises the risk of preeclampsia
Chronic hypertension
  • BP above 140/90 before pregnancy or before 20 weeks
  • About 25% of these women develop preeclampsia
PreeclampsiaNew-onset hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria.
Preeclampsia with severe featuresPreeclampsia plus signs of organ involvement: liver (epigastric pain, high liver enzymes), brain (headache, blurred vision), kidneys (oliguria, abnormal kidney tests).
Eclampsia
  • New-onset seizure activity in a woman with preeclampsia
  • Client safety is the primary concern
HELLP syndrome
  • Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
  • A severe form of preeclampsia
Superimposed preeclampsiaPreeclampsia that develops in a woman who already has chronic hypertension.
Proteinuria
  • Protein in the urine
  • 24-hour urine of 300 mg or more, or a protein to creatinine ratio of 0.3 or more, is a lab value of concern.
Oliguria
  • Low urine output
  • A sign of kidney involvement in severe preeclampsia
Magnesium sulfate
  • The drug that prevents and treats seizures in preeclampsia and eclampsia
  • Antidote: calcium gluconate
  • (added)
Calcium gluconate
  • The antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity
  • Keep it at the bedside
  • (added)
Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs)
  • Checked before and during magnesium sulfate
  • Losing the patellar reflex is the first sign of magnesium toxicity
  • (added)
UrsodiolMedication used for itching and bile acid buildup in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
Severe feature cutoffsBP 160/110, platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 or doubled, liver enzymes twice normal, brain or vision change, epigastric pain.
Mag WatchSim name for the magnesium sulfate check every 4 hours and PRN: DTRs 2+ with no clonus, RR 12 or more, urine 30 mL/hr or more, alert and oriented (GCS 15).
Clonus
  • Rhythmic muscle jerks after a reflex test
  • It is absent in the safe Mag Watch finding and can signal hyperreflexia
Hypermagnesemia
  • Magnesium toxicity
  • Cascade: absent DTRs, lethargy and slurred speech, respiratory depression, cardiac arrest
  • Stop the infusion, call for help, give calcium gluconate
Protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR)
  • Urine test for proteinuria
  • 0.3 or more is abnormal in preeclampsia.
  • Sim client had 0.38.
Labetalol IV ladder
  • Severe BP (160/110 sustained 15 min): 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg IV, each over 2 minutes, recheck BP 10 minutes after each
  • Max 220 mg
  • Notify the provider if severe BP persists after 80 mg
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP)
  • Also called PUPPP
  • Itchy red bumps and plaques that start in the stretch marks in late pregnancy
  • Normal labs, no risk to the baby
  • Topical steroids and antihistamines
  • (added)

📝 Hypertensive disorders: classmate additions

📝 From your classmate's Oct 19 notes, which win over the slides. Anything with ➕ is added from standard sources.

🎤 Hyperemesis: what she added

  • Most common reason for admission in the first trimester. Diagnosis of exclusion: there is no test for it.
  • Resolves by about week 20. Weight loss over 5% of pre-pregnancy weight. Dehydration, metabolic acidosis or alkalosis, hypokalemia.
  • Ask: how long, triggers, what helps or worsens, diet (fatty or fried foods?), hydration. Dehydration can cause preterm labor.
  • Care: bedrest, gut rest, IV fluids, TPN if severe, antiemetics (not all are safe in pregnancy, so it is a risk-benefit talk with the OB).
  • Good candidates for home health care. Give reassurance: it is not just vomiting, and you will help.

🎤 Cholestasis of pregnancy: what she added

  • Also called obstetric cholestasis. The most common pregnancy-specific liver disease.
  • Reversible, hormonally influenced. Bile acids back up in the gallbladder and cause severe itching.
  • Treat with ursodiol (UDCA). Menthol creams can help the itch.
  • Check serum bile acids. Check liver function about 6 weeks postpartum. If it has not normalized, think something else.

🎤 Hypertension rules she stressed

  • Hypertension is any BP over 140/90, confirmed with 2 readings at separate visits.
  • It is the most common complication of pregnancy and a leading cause of maternal death.
  • Gestational: first time after 20 weeks, no other signs.
    • It should return to normal by 12 weeks postpartum
    • If not, it becomes chronic hypertension
    • About 25% go on to preeclampsia
  • Chronic: before conception or before 20 weeks. It stays beyond 12 weeks postpartum. The 20 week mark is just the cutoff they chose.
  • Superimposed preeclampsia: chronic hypertension that develops proteinuria, kidney changes, or other signs.
  • Risk factors: advanced maternal age, obesity, family history of cardiovascular disease, history of preterm birth.
    • Hispanic ethnicity is not one. Black women are at higher risk.

🎤 Preeclampsia: causes and care

TopicKnow
Why it happens
  • Not fully known
  • Theories: abnormal implantation with trophoblasts that invade vessels abnormally, maternal and paternal tissue intolerance, and mom not adapting to cardiovascular and inflammatory changes
Conservative careBedrest on the left side, antihypertensives (lower the BP, because the longer it stays high the worse it gets), more prenatal visits, daily kick counts, balanced diet, plenty of water.
Home BPIf she can check reliably at home, visits may be fewer.
Why waterDehydration raises the risk and causes other problems.
DangersIt can snowball fast, even after birth.

🎤 Severe features: she listed all of these

FeatureCutoff
Blood pressureSystolic 160 or higher, or diastolic 110 or higher
CreatinineOver 1.1, or doubled, without renal disease
PlateletsUnder 100,000
Liver enzymesTwice normal
Brain and eyesNew cerebral or visual disturbance (headache, blurred vision)
PainPersistent epigastric pain

Preeclampsia plus at least one of these.

🎤 Magnesium sulfate: what she said

TopicKnow
Purpose
  • Seizure prevention
  • It is a CNS depressant
  • It does not lower the BP (maybe slightly), so another drug is needed for BP
Normal effectsFlushing, sweating, feeling uncomfortable.
ToxicityLethargy, respiratory depression, absent deep tendon reflexes, cardiac dysrhythmias.
BabyMinimal variability and respiratory depression, especially close to birth.
Antidote
  • Calcium gluconate
  • Keep it available at the bedside

🎤 Eclampsia: seizure care

  • Seizure precautions: padded side rails up, suction, oxygen, calcium gluconate available, good IV access.
  • During the seizure: do not restrain, put nothing in the mouth, turn her to the left side.
  • After: suction if needed, open the airway, oxygen, reassure her. She will be groggy.
  • Continuous fetal monitoring even during the seizure (it will be noisy).
  • Seizures and preeclampsia can happen even postpartum.

🎤 HELLP: why each letter happens

PartWhy
HemolysisRed cells squeeze through constricted vessels and break
Elevated liver enzymesLess blood flow and damage to the liver
Low plateletsPlatelets are used up at sites of vascular damage
FindingsRUQ pain, malaise, unexplained bruising, bleeding from IV or injection sites
Diagnosis
  • By labs
  • Catch labs and symptoms early
RisksCerebral hemorrhage, retinal detachment, liver rupture, DIC, abruption, maternal death

🎤 24-hour urine and UTIs

  • 24-hour urine protein over 300 mg. Double normal creatinine. Platelets.
  • Watch closely for UTIs: even a simple infection can trigger a systemic response and tip her into preeclampsia or HELLP. Treat early.
  • She posted a preeclampsia video in Canvas under today's lecture.

🧪 Sim: magnesium sulfate protocol

TopicKnow
Goal
  • Stop progression from preeclampsia to eclamptic seizures
  • It raises the seizure threshold
Class
  • CNS depressant and smooth muscle relaxant
  • A neuroprotectant, NOT primarily an antihypertensive
  • BP needs a separate drug
SafetyHigh-alert drug. Always an IV pump and an independent double-check by a second RN before starting
Loading dose4 to 6 g IV over 20 to 30 minutes
Maintenance1 to 2 g per hour by steady IV infusion
TeachSudden flushing, intense heat, and nausea during the bolus are a normal response, not an adverse reaction

🧪 Sim: the Mag Watch (every 4 hours and PRN)

CheckSafeDanger
Neuro: DTRs and clonus2+, no clonusAbsent DTRs (first warning sign)
Respirations and lungsRR 12 or more, lungs clearRR under 12
Renal: urine output30 mL/hr or more, I&O every shiftLow output: magnesium builds up
Level of consciousnessAlert and oriented, GCS 15Increasing lethargy, then obtunded

Why renal: magnesium leaves through the kidneys. 🧪 The sim says every 4 hours and PRN, with I&O every shift. ➕ Many hospital protocols check urine hourly, so if a question says hourly, that is also correct nursing care.

🧪 Sim: toxicity cascade and emergency override

StageWhat you see
1. Loss of reflexesAbsent DTRs. Primary warning sign
2. Loss of consciousnessSomnolence, profound lethargy, slurred speech
3. Loss of respirationsRR under 12, respiratory depression, arrest
4. Loss of cardiac outputSevere oliguria, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest
  1. STOP the magnesium infusion now (do not wait for an order)
  2. Call for emergency help and notify the provider
  3. Give the antidote: calcium gluconate IV (kept at the bedside)
  4. Respiratory support: oxygen, ambu bag if needed, until the antidote works

🧪 Sim: the defensive perimeter (seizure precautions)

Padded side rails up, bed in lowest positionPrevents injury during a seizure
Suction and oxygen tested and ready at the bedsideAirway rescue within seconds
Call bell within reachShe can call before she declines
Dim overhead lights, limit noise, restrict visitorsStimulation can trigger a seizure

🧪 Sim: blood pressure drugs

SituationDrug and rule
Baseline controlLabetalol 200 mg PO every 12 hours to prevent escalation
Before every oral doseCheck BP and HR. Hold for HR under 60 or SBP under 100
Rescue triggerSBP 160 or higher or DBP 110 or higher, sustained 15 minutes (recheck within 15 minutes of the first high reading)
IV ruleEvery dose slowly over 2 minutes, then wait 10 minutes and recheck BP
Step 1Labetalol 20 mg IV
Step 2If still severe: 40 mg IV
Step 3If still severe: 80 mg IV
Limit
  • Maximum cumulative dose 220 mg IV
  • If severe BP persists after the 80 mg dose, notify the provider immediately

⚠️ Conflict note: standard OB references list 20, 40, 80, 80 and a 300 mg limit, and list hydralazine and nifedipine as other first-line options. The sim says 220 mg, so use 220 if the question is about this protocol. 🎤 Lecture: the longer BP stays high, the worse it gets, so treat it.

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Magnesium and BPMagnesium does not treat the blood pressure. It prevents seizures.
⚠️ Flushing vs toxicityFlushing and sweating are normal. Lethargy, slow breathing, and absent reflexes are toxicity.
⚠️ CreatinineThe severe-feature cutoff is over 1.1 or doubled, not 0.5.
⚠️ Risk factor trickHispanic ethnicity is NOT a hypertension risk. Black women are.
⚠️ 20 week and 12 week20 weeks decides gestational vs chronic. 12 weeks postpartum decides whether it was gestational.
⚠️ Sim: Mag Watch frequencySim says every 4 hours and PRN with I&O every shift. Do not answer "only when she complains".
⚠️ Sim: flushingFlushing, heat, and nausea during the loading dose are expected. Absent DTRs are not.
⚠️ Sim: stop firstIn toxicity, STOP the infusion before anything else. Do not wait for an order, and do not give calcium first while the drug still runs.
⚠️ Sim: BP 156/96Over 140/90 but not severe range. Severe range is 160 or higher systolic or 110 or higher diastolic, sustained 15 minutes.
⚠️ Sim: magnesium and BPMag is a neuroprotectant. When BP is in severe range, you still need labetalol.
⚠️ Sim: labetalol holdHold oral labetalol for HR under 60 or SBP under 100.
⚠️ Gestational vs chronicOver 20 weeks new = gestational. Before pregnancy or before 20 weeks = chronic. The number is 140/90 for both.
⚠️ ProteinuriaGestational hypertension has no proteinuria. Add proteinuria and it is preeclampsia.
⚠️ Eclampsia is a seizureEclampsia is defined by new seizure activity. The first move is safety and turning her left, not a drug.
⚠️ HELLP lettersHemolysis, Elevated liver enzymes, Low platelets. Epigastric pain is the liver.
⚠️ WaterHer preeclampsia list says 6 to 8 glasses of water a day, not fluid restriction.
⚠️ Magnesium toxicityCheck reflexes, breathing, and urine output. The antidote is calcium gluconate.
⚠️ Abruption linkHypertension and preeclampsia are the leading cause of abruption on her slide.
⚠️ ICP vs PEPBoth itch. ICP has no rash and abnormal bile acids. PEP has a rash in the stretch marks and normal labs. Only ICP threatens the baby.
⚠️ Rank of hypertensive disorders as a cause of maternal death?Second leading cause (her notes).

💧 Blood Incompatibility, Fluid, and Multiples

Definitions first: ABO, Rh, RhoGAM, polyhydramnios, oligohydramnios, and multiple gestation.

🧠 The big idea

Too much fluid, too little fluid, too many babies, or the wrong blood type: each one has a signature risk.
Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive baby → antibodies → RhoGAM stops it → Polyhydramnios is fetal anomalies, oligohydramnios is cord compression, multiples is size and preterm birth

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 ABO incompatibility causes newborn jaundice (phototherapy lights). Less severe and less common than Rh.
  2. 🎤 RhoGAM protects FUTURE pregnancies: 28 weeks, 72 hours after birth, and after any blood mixing.
  3. 🎤 Oligohydramnios in labor: variable decelerations (cord compression). Her answer was B.
  4. 🎤 Dizygotic (fraternal) twins: own placenta. Monozygotic (identical) twins share placenta and chorion: higher risk.
  5. ABO incompatibility: type O mother with type A or B fetus. Less severe than Rh incompatibility.
  6. Rh incompatibility: Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive fetal blood, sensitization. Risk rises with each Rh-positive pregnancy.
  7. RhoGAM at 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth, and after ectopic, trauma, abortion, amniocentesis, or fetal demise.
  8. Polyhydramnios is over 2,000 mL (weeks 32 to 36). Treat with therapeutic amniocentesis or indomethacin.
  9. Oligohydramnios is under 500 mL. Expect variable decelerations from cord compression. Treat with amnioinfusion.
  10. Multiple gestation: uterus larger than dates, anemia, hypertension, preterm birth, hemorrhage after birth.
  11. ➕ RhoGAM both sides: Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive (or unknown) baby gets it. Rh-negative baby or Rh-positive mother: not needed.

📖 Blood, fluid, and multiples (14 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
ABO incompatibility
  • Type O mother with a fetus who has type A or B blood
  • Less severe than Rh incompatibility
Rh incompatibility
  • An Rh-negative mother is exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood, which makes her form antibodies (sensitization)
  • The risk rises with each later Rh-positive fetus
SensitizationThe mother makes antibodies against Rh-positive blood after exposure to it.
RhoGAM
  • Rh immune globulin
  • Given to an Rh-negative mother at 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth, and after events such as ectopic pregnancy, abortion, trauma, amniocentesis, or fetal demise
  • Also called: Rh immune globulin, RhIG
Polyhydramnios
  • Amniotic fluid over 2,000 mL, usually found between weeks 32 and 36
  • Linked to fetal anomalies such as GI obstruction, neural tube defects, trisomy 13 and 18, and impaired swallowing
Therapeutic amniocentesisRemoving amniotic fluid to relieve polyhydramnios.
Indomethacin
  • A drug that lowers amniotic fluid by decreasing fetal urine output
  • Used for polyhydramnios
Oligohydramnios
  • Amniotic fluid under 500 mL
  • Linked to maternal diabetes, IUGR, hypertension, and fetal urinary problems
Amnioinfusion
  • Fluid placed into the uterus through a catheter
  • Used for oligohydramnios, mainly to relieve cord compression
IUGR
  • Intrauterine growth restriction
  • The fetus is smaller than expected for gestational age
Multiple gestation
  • More than one fetus
  • Risks include anemia, excess weight gain, bleeding, hypertension, edema, and preterm birth
Uterus larger than expected for EDB
  • A key finding in multiple gestation
  • Confirmed by ultrasound
Monozygotic twins
  • Identical twins from one egg
  • They often share a placenta and chorion, so risk is higher
Dizygotic twins
  • Fraternal twins from two eggs
  • Each baby has its own placenta and sacs

🩸 Blood incompatibility

TopicABORh
WhoType O mother, fetus with type A or BRh-negative mother, Rh-positive fetus
SeverityLess severeMore severe, and worse with each later Rh-positive pregnancy

WhenWhy
28 weeksRoutine protection during pregnancy
Within 72 hours after birthIf the baby is Rh-positive
Ectopic pregnancyFetal blood may mix with hers
Abortion or maternal traumaSame reason
Amniocentesis, fetal surgery, or fetal demiseSame reason

  • ➕ Also know: IM injection (not IV)
  • It protects, and does not treat the baby
  • It works only if she has not already made antibodies
  • A negative indirect Coombs test on her blood shows she is unsensitized

📉 Her question: oligohydramnios in labor

Which deceleration is most expected? Variable deceleration.

  • Less fluid cushions the cord less
  • The cord gets compressed
  • Compressed cord gives variable decelerations
  • Amnioinfusion helps by adding fluid

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Twin typesDizygotic = fraternal, two placentas. Monozygotic = identical, shared placenta, higher risk.
⚠️ RhoGAM purposeRhoGAM protects the NEXT pregnancy. It does not treat the current baby.
⚠️ Which fluid problemVariable decelerations go with oligohydramnios (cord compression), not polyhydramnios.
⚠️ ABO vs RhRh is the more severe one. ABO is a type O mother with an A or B baby.
⚠️ Who gets RhoGAMOnly an Rh-negative mother. An Rh-positive mother never needs it.
⚠️ 72 hoursRhoGAM after birth is within 72 hours. It is also given at 28 weeks.
⚠️ Which fluid problemPolyhydramnios is too much fluid (over 2,000 mL). Oligohydramnios is too little (under 500 mL).
⚠️ Oligohydramnios decelerationsThe expected pattern is variable decelerations, not early and not late.
⚠️ IndomethacinIt treats polyhydramnios by lowering fetal urine output.
⚠️ Rh-negative mother, Rh-negative baby: RhoGAM after birth?No. The postpartum dose depends on the baby being Rh-positive. The 28 week dose is routine either way.

Oligohydramnios amount?
Under 500 mL.
Oligohydramnios in labor: expected deceleration and treatment?
Variable decelerations. Amnioinfusion.
How do you suspect twins on exam?
Uterus larger than expected for dates, severe nausea and vomiting, confirmed by ultrasound.
Multiple gestation postpartum worry?
Hemorrhage, so assess closely.
When is RhoGAM NOT needed after birth?
Rh-positive mother, or Rh-negative baby.

⏰ Preterm Labor, Birth, and PROM

Definitions first: preterm labor, preterm birth ranges, PROM, PPROM, and what to teach.

🧠 The big idea

  • Preterm means before 37 weeks
  • Rupture means infection risk the longer it goes.
    Regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks → Slow it, mature the lungs, treat infection → PROM over 24 hours risks chorioamnionitis → No unsterile vaginal exams until active labor

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 Preterm birth must be 20 0/7 to 36 6/7. If the pregnancy does not reach 20 weeks it is an abortion.
  2. 🎤 Preterm triggers: uterine distention (polyhydramnios, multiples), abruption or clotting disorder, stress or low oxygen (HPA axis), infection.
  3. 🎤 PPROM answer: A, D, E, F. Not B (nipple stimulation releases oxytocin). Not C (baths raise infection risk).
  4. 🎤 Confirm rupture with a nitrazine swab or fern test.
  5. Preterm labor: regular contractions that change the cervix before 37 weeks.
  6. Preterm birth is 20 0/7 to 36 6/7. Very preterm is under 32. Late preterm is 34 to 36.
  7. PROM is rupture before labor. PPROM is rupture before labor and before 37 weeks.
  8. Rupture over 24 hours: chorioamnionitis, endometritis, sepsis, neonatal infection.
  9. No unsterile digital cervical exams until active labor. Expectant management if fetal lungs are immature.
  10. Confirm rupture with the nitrazine test, fern test, and ultrasound.

🍬 Diabetes and Pregnancy

Definitions first: types of diabetes, effects on mother and baby, screening, targets, insulin, and care in labor.

🧠 The big idea

High maternal glucose crosses the placenta, the baby makes too much insulin, and everything that follows comes from that.
Hyperglycemia early → anomalies → Hyperglycemia late → macrosomia, birth trauma, cesarean → After birth the baby loses the sugar supply but still makes insulin → hypoglycemia

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 Two sets of numbers, two jobs. Screening GTT: fasting 95, 1 hour 140, 2 hours 120. Management targets: fasting 92, post-meal 180, 1 and 2 hour 153.
  2. 🎤 Diagnosis needs an abnormal 2-hour test AND an abnormal 3-hour test.
  3. 🎤 A1C at the first visit if high risk: a 3-month snapshot that shows diabetes before pregnancy.
  4. 🎤 Urine ketones check for DKA. Urine protein checks for preeclampsia, because diabetics are at higher risk.
  5. 🎤 Glyburide and metformin: not ideal and not well studied in pregnancy. Insulin is first line.
  6. Diabetes that starts in pregnancy is gestational diabetes, not type 2.
  7. GTT at 24 to 28 weeks: 75 g glucose, level at 2 hours. Abnormal leads to a 3-hour test.
  8. Insulin is first line. Glyburide and metformin are second line.
  9. First-trimester hyperglycemia causes congenital anomalies. Later hyperglycemia causes macrosomia and birth trauma.
  10. Neonate: polycythemia, hyperbilirubinemia, birth trauma, and risk of hypoglycemia.
  11. Labor: glucose every 1 to 2 hours, insulin drip, 50% dextrose at the bedside, monitor FHR and urine output.

📖 Diabetes and pregnancy (12 terms)

Glyburide and metforminSecond-line oral drugs for gestational diabetes.

❤️ Heart, Lungs, Blood, and Autoimmune Disease

Definitions first: cardiac disease, chronic hypertension, asthma, the anemias, and autoimmune disease.

🧠 The big idea

Pregnancy adds blood volume, so the sick heart, the sick lungs, and the sick blood all get pushed harder.
More volume → heart disease can fail → anemia gets worse → asthma flares → autoimmune disease can flare → The nurse protects rest, oxygen, and fluid balance

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 Heart disease symptoms mimic pregnancy: shortness of breath, fatigue, chest pain. Do not dismiss them.
  2. 🎤 Epidural for heart disease: pain raises BP and stress on the heart, so pain relief protects her.
  3. 🎤 ACE inhibitors and ARBs are teratogenic. Hemabate (carboprost) can trigger bronchospasm in asthma.
  4. 🎤 Ferrous sulfate: dark stools. Take with vitamin C.
  5. 🎤 Lupus, RA, MS: stable on the same medicines for 6 months before pregnancy.
  6. Class II heart disease: slight limitation, symptoms when she increases her activity.
  7. Cardiac nursing: vitals, apical rate, heart sounds, daily weights, edema, rest, prevent fluid overload, anticipate epidural.
  8. Chronic hypertension: before pregnancy or before 20 weeks, or lasting over 12 weeks after birth.
  9. Asthma: pregnancy worsens it for many women. Teach triggers and keep the medications.
  10. Iron-deficiency anemia: fatigue, pallor, tachycardia, more infections. Not pink membranes, not bradycardia.
  11. Sickle cell: preeclampsia, preterm labor, abruption, IUGR. Fluid overload can cause heart failure.
  12. Lupus is systemic. Hashimoto and Graves target the thyroid.
  13. ➕ Hashimoto = HYPOthyroid (low). Graves = HYPERthyroid (high). Both are localized to the thyroid.
  14. 📝 Thalassemia: alpha is the minor form, beta is the major form. Her notes say major usually means no pregnancy because of lifelong hemodialysis.

  • Pregnant clients are at higher risk for stroke, heart failure, and arrhythmias.

🎤 Autoimmune disease: what she added

  • Localized: Hashimoto and Graves affect the thyroid only. Systemic: lupus involves heart, joints, red blood cells, and more.
  • Lupus goal: control flares and prevent organ damage. Multiple sclerosis affects the CNS.
  • MS and RA: no known adverse effect on pregnancy or fertility. RA medications may be toxic to the fetus, so review the regimen.
  • Be stable on the current medication regimen for at least 6 months before getting pregnant (lupus, RA, MS).

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Heart symptomsShortness of breath and fatigue are normal in pregnancy, but they can also mean heart disease. Do not dismiss them.
⚠️ Epidural and the heartThe epidural is for pain relief. Pain stresses the heart.
⚠️ Asthma and HemabateCarboprost (Hemabate) is the postpartum drug that can worsen asthma.
⚠️ Iron teachingDark stools are expected. Take iron with vitamin C, not with milk.
⚠️ Class IIClass II is symptoms with increased activity. Class IV is symptoms at rest.
⚠️ Iron-deficiency findingsPale membranes and tachycardia, not pink and not bradycardia.
⚠️ Fluid overloadSickle cell and heart disease clients can go into heart failure from too much IV fluid.
⚠️ ThalassemiaMinor form has little effect on pregnancy. Major form usually means no pregnancy.
⚠️ Local vs systemicHashimoto and Graves are localized to the thyroid. Lupus is systemic.
⚠️ MS and RANo known adverse effects on pregnancy or fertility.
⚠️ Chronic hypertension timingOver 12 weeks after birth still counts as chronic.
⚠️ Hashimoto vs Graves: which is hypo and which is hyper?Hashimoto is hypothyroid (low). Graves is hyperthyroid (high).

🧪 Say it first: Heart, lungs, blood, and autoimmune

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

Pain raises BP and strains the heart.
Which BP drugs are teratogenic?
ACE inhibitors and ARBs.

Carboprost (Hemabate).

Dark stools. Take with vitamin C.

At least 6 months on the same medicines.

Slight limitation. Symptoms with increased activity.

Vitals, apical heart rate, heart sounds, daily weights, edema, fetal activity and heart rate.

Medications, rest, nutrition teaching, support, invasive monitoring in labor, prevent fluid overload, anticipate epidural.

Before pregnancy or before 20 weeks, or lasting over 12 weeks postpartum.

Worsens it for many women.

Fatigue, pallor, pale membranes, tachycardia, more infections.

Alpha is minor. Beta is major.

🦠 HIV, Group B Strep, and Infection Prevention

Definitions first: HIV treatment plan, GBS testing and antibiotics, and the hygiene guidelines.

🧠 The big idea

The goal is to keep the infection from reaching the baby.
HIV: treat the mother early, in labor, and the baby for 6 weeks, and avoid instrumentation → GBS: swab at 35 to 37 weeks, give penicillin G in labor, at least 2 doses before birth

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 GBS is a carried bacterium, not an STI, and is not reportable. Penicillin does not remove it. It prevents newborn infection.
  2. 🎤 Fewer than 2 antibiotic doses before birth: notify the physician. The baby may get antibiotics.
  3. 🎤 HIV: a low viral load can allow vaginal birth. Avoid episiotomy, forceps, vacuum, and scalp electrodes.
  4. 🎤 TORCH: Toxoplasmosis, Other, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes. All can cross the placenta.
  5. 🎤 Herpes with active lesions at birth: cesarean. Suppressive therapy at 36 weeks.
  6. HIV: oral antiretrovirals twice daily from 14 weeks until birth, IV in labor, oral syrup for the newborn for 6 weeks.
  7. Cesarean for HIV is recommended, but the method depends on viral load, how long membranes were ruptured, and labor progress.
  8. Reduce instrumentation in HIV: no episiotomy, no fetal scalp electrode.
  9. GBS: vagino-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks. Treatment of choice is penicillin G, at least 2 doses before birth.
  10. GBS prophylaxis also applies with unknown status and delivery under 37 weeks, rupture of 18 hours or more, or temp of 100.4 F or more.
  11. Hygiene: wash hands, do not share cups or utensils, do not put a child's pacifier in your mouth.
  12. 📝 GBS: swab at 35 to 37 weeks, penicillin G with at least 2 doses before birth, and give the baby antibiotics if necessary. TORCH infections cross the placenta.

🧼 Hygiene guidelines for pregnant women

  • Wash hands often with soap and water, and wear gloves after diaper changes, feeding, wiping a nose or drool, and handling toys
  • Do not share cups, plates, utensils, food, or toothbrushes
  • Do not share towels or washcloths
  • Do not put a child's pacifier in your mouth
  • Clean toys, counters, and surfaces touched by a child's urine or saliva
  • Practice safe sex: limit partners and use condoms every time

➕ These steps prevent cytomegalovirus (CMV), spread by children's urine and saliva.

🤝 Vulnerable Populations and Substance Use

Definitions first: adolescent pregnancy, advanced maternal age, obesity, harmful drugs, and substance abuse.

🧠 The big idea

Age, weight, drugs, and resources change the risk, and the nurse stays nonjudgmental so she keeps coming to care.
Teen: resources and education gaps → Over 35: chromosome, loss, hypertension, diabetes → BMI over 30: almost everything goes up → Drugs and alcohol: harm the fetus, so screen and support

⭐ Know these cold

  1. 🎤 Retinoids (Accutane) are absolutely contraindicated, even topical. Warfarin is avoided unless she has a mechanical valve.
  2. 🎤 NSAIDs: avoid, and must avoid from 30 weeks (can close the ductus arteriosus early).
  3. 🎤 No amount of alcohol is safe. Caffeine under 200 mg a day.
  4. 🎤 Positive newborn drug screen: call the state protective agency (CPS).
  5. 🎤 Teens: fewer resources and less support. How they cope depends on developmental level.
  6. Adolescent pregnancy: about 50% birth, 30% abortion, the rest miscarriage or stillbirth. Needs resources, education, and parenting support.
  7. Advanced maternal age is over 35: loss, chromosomal abnormalities, stillbirth, preeclampsia, GDM, preterm birth.
  8. Obesity is BMI over 30: GDM, preeclampsia, preterm labor, anomalies, macrosomia, stillbirth, maternal death, PPH.
  9. Drugs with adverse effects: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, androgens, some antiseizure drugs, some antidepressants, retinoids, warfarin, NSAIDs.
  10. Substance abuse care: history and physical, urine or serum toxicology, nonjudgmental approach, counseling, education.
  11. A positive newborn drug screen triggers a state protection agency investigation.
  12. 📝 Obesity raises the risk of preeclampsia, macrosomia, gestational diabetes, stillbirth, maternal mortality, congenital anomalies, and PPH.
