🌀 Dystocia, Induction, and Labor Interventions

Definitions first: dystocia types, ripening, induction, augmentation, oxytocin, tachysystole, version, and comfort measures.

🧠 The big idea

When labor is too slow, too fast, or stuck, find which P is the problem, then choose the least invasive fix.
Dystocia is the top reason for cesarean → Rest, hydration, and position fix many cases → Ripen, induce, or augment when needed → Oxytocin is a high-alert drug, so watch contractions and the FHR for tachysystole

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Dystocia (difficult labor, "failure to progress") is the leading cause of cesarean birth.
  2. Uterine dystocia: hypertonic or hypotonic dysfunction, uncoordinated activity. Hypertonic contractions are painful with little dilation and little relaxation. Rest and hydration usually fix it.
  3. Active phase disorder (cervix at 6 cm or more): 4 hours of adequate contractions with no cervical change, or more than 6 hours on oxytocin with no change.
  4. Second stage disorder (10 cm): no progress after at least 2 to 4 hours of active pushing. Precipitous labor: under 3 hours start to finish.
  5. Tachysystole is more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes.
  6. Oxytocin is a high-alert medication, titrated IV up and down by response. Cervidil (dinoprostone) and Cytotec (misoprostol) ripen the cervix.
  7. Induction criteria: 41 weeks or maternal or fetal distress. Contraindications: placenta previa, cord prolapse, transverse or breech presentation.
  8. 📝 Your notes: dystocia is the leading cause of cesarean birth. Hypertonic = painful contractions with no dilation. High stress can lead to dystocia. Precipitous labor = birth in under 3 hours.
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: hypertonic uterus contracts too much and does not relax (rupture and fetal distress risk). Do NOT give oxytocin for it. Oxytocin is for hypotonic.
  10. 🎤 Active phase disorder: cervix over 6 cm with adequate contractions and no change, or inadequate contractions with no change after oxytocin for over 6 hours. Pushing 2 to 4 hours counts as lack of progress.
  11. 🎤 Induction starts labor. Augmentation moves along labor that already started. She said expect NCLEX style questions on this.
  12. 🎤 AROM (amniotomy) is provider only, only in L&D, not ruptured over 24 hours. Cervidil has a string (pull it out for hyperstimulation). Cytotec has no string.
  13. 🎤 Stress can contribute to dystocia (true).

📖 Dystocia and labor interventions (12 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
Active phase disorder
  • Cervix over 6 cm with adequate contractions and no change, or no change after oxytocin for over 6 hours
  • A lack of progress that leads to cesarean
Dystocia
  • Difficult labor, also called failure to progress
  • It is the leading cause of cesarean birth
Uterine dystocia
  • Hypertonic or hypotonic uterine dysfunction or uncoordinated activity
  • Hypertonic contractions are painful with little dilation and little relaxation
Second stage disorderCervix is 10 cm and there is no progress after at least 2 to 4 hours of active pushing.
Precipitous laborExtremely rapid labor lasting fewer than 3 hours from start to finish.
Fetal dystociaThe fetus cannot move through the birth canal effectively.
Pelvic dystociaThe pelvic opening is inadequate for the size of the fetus.
Induction
  • Starting labor artificially
  • Criteria are 41 weeks or maternal or fetal distress
AugmentationStrengthening labor that has already started, using oxytocin or artificial rupture of membranes.
AmniotomyArtificial rupture of the membranes, also called AROM.
Dinoprostone (Cervidil)Prostaglandin E2 insert used for cervical ripening.
External cephalic version (ECV)Procedure that turns a breech fetus to a head-down position through the abdomen.

🌀 Types of dystocia

TypeWhat it isKey facts
Uterine dystociaHypertonic or hypotonic dysfunction, uncoordinated activity
  • Hypertonic: painful contractions, little dilation, little relaxation
  • Can cause FHR Category II or III
  • Rest and hydration usually resolve it
Active phase disorderCervix at 6 cm or more4 hours of adequate contractions with no cervical change, or inadequate contractions or no change on oxytocin for more than 6 hours
Second stage disorderCervix at 10 cmContinued lack of progress after at least 2 to 4 hours of active pushing
Precipitous laborExtremely fast laborUnder 3 hours from start to finish
Fetal dystociaFetus cannot move through the canal effectivelySize, position, or presentation of the fetus
Pelvic dystociaPelvic opening too small for the fetusSize mismatch between pelvis and fetus

  • ➕ Also know: hypotonic dysfunction is weak, infrequent contractions in the active phase and is treated with oxytocin or amniotomy
  • Hypertonic is a latent phase problem with painful, ineffective contractions
  • She says psychological stress can contribute to dystocia (true)

💊 Labor interventions at a glance

InterventionMethodsNotes
Cervical ripening
  • Mechanical: laminaria tents, balloons (Foley)
  • Pharmacological: oxytocin, Cervidil (dinoprostone), Cytotec (misoprostol)
  • Prepares the cervix
  • Prostaglandins (Cervidil, Cytotec) are the classic ripening drugs
InductionOxytocin, sweeping (stripping) the membranes, cervical ripeningStarts labor. Slide answer: all three are methods of induction
AugmentationOxytocin, artificial rupture of membranes (amniotomy)Strengthens labor that has already started
Sweeping or stripping the membranesProvider separates the membranes from the lower uterusReleases prostaglandins to stimulate labor
AmniotomyBreak the bag of watersDocument the color, odor, and amount of fluid and check the FHR right after

  • ➕ Also know: check for cord prolapse and take the FHR before and after amniotomy
  • Laminaria tents swell as they absorb fluid and open the cervix slowly
  • After rupture, the risk of infection rises with time

✅ Induction: criteria and contraindications

TopicKnow
Criteria41 weeks, maternal or fetal distress
IndicationsMaternal or fetal distress
ContraindicationsPlacenta previa, cord prolapse, transverse breech (transverse lie or breech presentation)
RiskTachysystole, uterine rupture, fetal distress, failed induction and cesarean (see slide: risk, then nursing care)
Nursing careContinuous FHR and contraction monitoring, assess cervix and membranes, titrate oxytocin to the lowest effective dose, document

💉 Oxytocin (Pitocin): the high-alert drug

TopicKnow
Class
  • Pharmacological method of induction and augmentation
  • High-alert medication
RouteIV by pump. Titrate UP and DOWN depending on response
Watch for
  • Tachysystole and uterine rupture (both on her slide)
  • Fetal heart rate changes
If tachysystole or Category II or III tracingStop or reduce the oxytocin, turn her left, give fluids and oxygen, and call the provider
➕ Also
  • Piggyback into the primary line
  • Terbutaline may be ordered to relax the uterus
  • Water intoxication is a risk with high doses over time

⚡ Tachysystole

FeatureKnow
DefinitionExcessive uterine activity, spontaneous or induced
CountMore than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes
Extra features
  • Contractions lasting 2 minutes or longer
  • Contractions of normal length occurring within 1 minute of each other
Why it matters
  • Little rest between contractions, so the placenta cannot refill
  • FHR falls

🔄 Presentation and external cephalic version (ECV)

ItemKnow
Presentations on her slideHead (cephalic), breech, transverse
Breech typesFrank breech, complete breech, complete footling, incomplete footling
FrankHips flexed, legs straight up, buttocks first (➕ the most common)
CompleteHips and knees flexed, the fetus sits cross-legged
FootlingOne or both feet come first (complete footling is both feet, incomplete is one)
ECVProvider turns the baby from breech to head-down through the abdomen

  • ➕ Also know: ECV is done around 36 to 37 weeks with ultrasound, a tocolytic, and continuous FHR monitoring
  • Avoid with placenta previa, multiples, ruptured membranes, or a nonreassuring FHR
  • Give RhoGAM if Rh-negative
  • Be ready for emergency cesarean

  • Breech is the bottom half first (frank, complete, footling)

🎤 Oct 21 lecture: induction and augmentation methods

MethodKnow
Laminaria tents
  • Dry sterilized seaweed insert
  • Rarely used now
  • Used for D&C or stillbirth when it is not urgent
Balloon (Foley)
  • Most seen mechanical method
  • Sits by the cervix, filled more to add pressure, falls out when the cervix opens
Oxytocin (Pitocin)
  • Used for hypotonic uterus
  • Titrated up and down by protocol
  • Watch for tachysystole and rupture, especially after a prior cesarean
Cervidil (dinoprostone)
  • Insert with a string like a tampon
  • Pull it out if hyperstimulation or the baby does not tolerate it
  • Costly, less used
Cytotec (misoprostol)Same idea, no string. Monitor for hyperstimulation
TachysystoleMore than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes
Amniotomy (AROM)
  • Provider only
  • Only in L&D where an emergency birth is possible
  • Slightly raises cesarean risk
  • Best in multiparas, dilated at least 2 cm
  • Not ruptured over 24 hours (infection)
  • Check the FHR after
Sweeping or stripping
  • Done by OB or midwife in the office
  • Separates the chorionic membrane from the wall to release prostaglandins and oxytocin
  • Want over 39 weeks or partly dilated
  • Fading practice
ECV
  • Elective
  • Done from the outside by OB or midwife
  • Only at term
  • Only in L&D
  • Ultrasound before and after
  • Slightly raises cesarean risk
  • If it does not turn, cesarean
Criteria and contraindications
  • Criteria: 41 weeks or maternal or fetal distress
  • Contraindicated with anything that blocks a vaginal birth: previa, cord prolapse, transverse or breech
Natural optionsYoga poses, birthing ball, dates, red raspberry leaf tea, acupuncture (certified and comfortable with pregnant clients), massage, sex (prostaglandins), breath work, meditation

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Induction vs augmentationInduction STARTS labor. Augmentation STRENGTHENS labor that has already started.
⚠️ Oxytocin and ripeningHer slide lists oxytocin under both ripening and augmentation. The prostaglandins Cervidil and Cytotec are the ripening drugs.
⚠️ 4 hours or 6 hoursActive phase disorder: 4 hours of adequate contractions with no change, or more than 6 hours on oxytocin.
⚠️ Precipitous laborUnder 3 hours start to finish. It is not defined by cervical dilation.
⚠️ Tachysystole countingMore than 5 in 10 minutes, averaged over 30 minutes. Not 5 or more.
⚠️ All of the aboveHer slide question on methods of induction has answer D: oxytocin, sweeping, and ripening are all methods.
⚠️ ContraindicationsPrevia, cord prolapse, and transverse or breech presentation block induction.
⚠️ Induction vs augmentationInduction starts labor. Augmentation speeds up labor that has already started.
⚠️ Hypertonic vs hypotonicHypertonic is painful and does not dilate. Hypotonic is weak and infrequent.
⚠️ Hypertonic and oxytocinOxytocin is for hypotonic dysfunction. In a hypertonic uterus it makes the problem worse.
⚠️ Cervidil vs CytotecCervidil has a string and can be pulled out. Cytotec has no string.
⚠️ Who breaks the waterThe provider does the amniotomy, in L&D only. The nurse monitors the baby afterward.

🚨 Assisted Birth, VBAC, and Obstetric Emergencies

Definitions first: vacuum, forceps, TOLAC and VBAC, post-term, meconium, stillbirth, Triple I, and the obstetric emergencies.

🧠 The big idea

Anything that helps the baby out also risks injuring the baby or the mother, and emergencies are won by speed and the right first move.
Vacuum and forceps help birth but injure the head or the canal → VBAC works for most but can rupture the scar → Complications raise risk (post-term, meconium, multiples, stillbirth, infection, obesity) → Know each emergency and its first action

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Vacuum risks to the baby: cephalhematoma, intracranial and retinal hemorrhage, asphyxia, jaundice. Mother: tears, cervix detachment, traumatic PPH.
  2. Forceps risks to the baby: facial injury, facial muscle paralysis, eye trauma, skull fracture, seizures. Mother: tears, incontinence, hemorrhage, bladder or urethra damage.
  3. VBAC: about 90% of women with a prior cesarean are eligible, with a 69 to 80% success rate. TOLAC is the trial. VBAC is the success.
  4. Post-term is beyond 41 6/7 weeks: neonatal death risk is greatly increased, the placenta ages out, macrosomia.
  5. Stillbirth (IUFD) is fetal death after 20 weeks. Risks: DIC and sepsis. Triple I is infection, inflammation, and fever of the fluid, placenta, membranes, or fetus.
  6. Obstetric emergencies: shoulder dystocia, prolapsed cord, vasa previa, uterine rupture, amniotic fluid embolism, DIC.
  7. Maternal red triggers: temperature under 35 or over 38, systolic under 90 or over 160, diastolic over 100, HR under 40 or over 120, RR under 10 or over 30, oxygen saturation under 95.
  8. 📝 Your notes: irregular uterine wall contour after TOLAC means the uterus ruptured. Vacuum: document the time from insertion to birth. Cord prolapse: keep the presenting part off the cord all the way to the OR.
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: vacuum needs an engaged head and a fully dilated cervix. 3-pull rule: after 3 good pulls with no baby, go to emergency cesarean. Document pulls, pop-offs, and time from insertion to birth.
  10. 🎤 Oct 21: shoulder dystocia is head out over 60 seconds without the body. McRoberts: push on the uterus (suprapubic) while another person pushes the legs back. Over 5 minutes stuck means high risk of brain injury.
  11. 🎤 Oct 21: cord prolapse: elevate the presenting part off the cord and go to the OR with that person still elevating. Occult (not seen or felt) vs frank (visible).
  12. 🎤 Oct 21: irregular uterine wall contour on a question means the uterus ruptured. Classic vertical incision can never have a vaginal birth.
  13. 🎤 Oct 21: Triple I needs only ONE: fever, maternal tachycardia, fetal tachycardia, or high WBC.
  14. 🎤 Oct 21: ACLS in pregnancy: push the uterus to the left. On magnesium: stop it and give calcium gluconate. AFE: massive transfusion. Deliver by 5 minutes if no pulse returns.
  15. ➕ VBAC candidate: one prior LOW TRANSVERSE cesarean, no other uterine scar, emergency surgery available. NOT a candidate: prior classical or T-shaped incision, prior uterine rupture, previa.

📖 Assisted birth and obstetric emergencies (19 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
3-pull rule
  • Vacuum rule: after 3 good pulls with no birth, go to emergency cesarean
  • Document pulls, pop-offs, and the time from insertion to birth
Pop-off
  • The vacuum cup detaching from the fetal head because of excess force
  • Each one is documented
McRoberts maneuver
  • Shoulder dystocia maneuver: legs pushed back toward the abdomen with suprapubic pressure
  • Never pull on the head
Occult cord prolapse
  • Cord below the presenting part that cannot be seen or felt on exam
  • Frank prolapse is visible
Vacuum-assisted delivery
  • A suction cup on the fetal head helps the birth
  • Risks include cephalhematoma and retinal hemorrhage
Forceps-assisted delivery
  • Curved instrument blades guide the fetal head
  • Risks include facial injury and facial muscle paralysis
Cephalhematoma
  • Collection of blood between the skull bone and its covering
  • It does not cross suture lines
TOLAC
  • Trial of labor after cesarean
  • A planned attempt to deliver vaginally after a previous cesarean, whatever the outcome
VBAC
  • Vaginal birth after cesarean
  • A successful trial of labor that ends in a vaginal birth
Post-term pregnancy
  • Pregnancy beyond 41 6/7 weeks
  • Neonatal death risk is greatly increased and the placenta ages out
Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)The fetus breathes meconium-stained amniotic fluid into the lungs.
Stillbirth (IUFD)
  • Intrauterine fetal demise: fetal death after 20 weeks with absent heart activity on visualization
  • Risk for DIC and sepsis
Intra-amniotic infection (Triple I)
  • Infection, inflammation, and fever involving amniotic fluid, placenta, fetus, membranes, or decidua
  • Also called chorioamnionitis
Shoulder dystociaObstetric emergency where the fetal shoulder is stuck behind the pubic bone after the head is born.
Prolapsed umbilical cordObstetric emergency where the cord slips ahead of or beside the presenting part.
Uterine rupture
  • Tearing of the uterus, often along a prior cesarean scar
  • Blood flows into the abdomen
Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE)
  • Anaphylactoid syndrome: amniotic fluid and fetal cells enter maternal circulation
  • Rare but fatal
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Widespread clotting then bleeding because clotting factors are used up
  • Obstetric emergency

🏥 Critical care in maternity

  • Preexisting conditions and complications raise the need for critical care
  • Assess high-risk situations continuously
  • Use the advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) algorithm
  • Care in special obstetrics and gynecology units or the ICU
  • ➕ In cardiac arrest, keep the uterus displaced left. Delivery within about 5 minutes can help resuscitation

Resolved by the Oct 21 lecture recording: the maneuver she named is McRoberts (your "Groggers" note). The "over 5 minutes" in your notes is how long the baby is stuck. Over 5 minutes means high risk of asphyxia and brain injury, and the goal is about 2.5 minutes. Shoulder dystocia itself is head out for over 60 seconds. ➕ Why classic is worse: it cuts through the upper, muscular part of the uterus that does the contracting, so the scar bears the pressure. The lower segment contracts far less.

Diabetes

  • Priority is glucose control in labor (high demand, not eating)

Triple I (chorioamnionitis)

🎤 Oct 21 lecture: emergencies in more detail

EmergencyKnow
Shoulder dystocia
  • Not predictable or preventable
  • Head is out but the shoulder is stuck behind the pubic symphysis
  • Over 60 seconds from head to body
McRoberts
  • One person presses on the uterus (suprapubic pressure)
  • Another pushes the legs back as far as possible
Shoulder dystocia risksMacrosomia over 4,500 g, maternal diabetes, prior shoulder dystocia, prolonged second stage, excessive weight gain
Shoulder dystocia outcomes
  • Baby: broken collarbone sometimes
  • Over 5 minutes stuck gives high risk of asphyxia and brain injury (aim for about 2.5 minutes).
  • Mother: lacerations, episiotomy, hemorrhage
Cord prolapse
  • Cord lies below the presenting part
  • Occult: cannot be seen or felt on exam
  • Frank: visible
  • Elevate the presenting part off the cord, and the person elevating rides to the OR
Vasa previa
  • Fetal vessels not protected by the placenta, over the cervical os
  • They can rupture as labor progresses
Uterine rupture
  • Catastrophic
  • Caused by hyperstimulation or a scar (TOLAC)
  • Excess bleeding
AFE (anaphylactoid syndrome)
  • Rare and life threatening
  • Sudden shortness of breath, then hypotension, cardiac arrest, respiratory failure
  • Now seen as a systemic inflammatory response, not just fluid in the lungs
  • Care: ACLS, ventilation, labs (CBC, platelets, coagulation, type and screen), massive transfusion, ICU
DIC
  • Clotting runs faster than the body can make clots
  • Bleeding from IVs, orifices, eyes
  • Causes: AFE, stillbirth, HELLP, sepsis, preeclampsia

StepKnow
Position
  • Push or pull the uterus to the left (left uterine displacement)
  • Prevents inferior vena cava compression
  • The patient stays flat for compressions
On magnesiumStop the magnesium and give calcium gluconate
AFE suspectedMassive transfusion protocol
Time goal
  • Deliver within 5 minutes if no return of circulation (perimortem cesarean)
  • It can save both
Where
  • ICU or a women's ICU
  • If she goes to a general ICU, the postpartum nurse goes to assess and teach the ICU nurses

➕ VBAC: candidate vs not a candidate

Good candidateNOT a candidate
Prior uterine scarOne low transverse (low segment) cesareanClassical (vertical) or T-shaped incision, or extensive uterine surgery
HistoryNo prior rupturePrior uterine rupture
This pregnancyHead down, no previaPlacenta previa or transverse lie
SettingHospital that can do an emergency cesarean right awayNo immediate surgical or anesthesia team
ChoiceClient informed and agreesClient declines a trial of labor (repeat cesarean)
VBACRepeat cesarean
UpsideShorter recovery, less blood loss, lower infection and clot riskPlanned, no risk of scar rupture in labor
DownsideUterine rupture (rare, an emergency)Surgical risks: bleeding, infection, clots, longer recovery, risks in later pregnancies

➕ Added from standard OB sources. Her slides give the 90% eligible and 69 to 80% success numbers.

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ TOLAC vs VBACTOLAC is the planned trial. VBAC is a trial that ends in a vaginal birth. A failed trial is still a TOLAC.
⚠️ Vacuum vs forceps injuriesFacial paralysis and facial injury are forceps. Cephalhematoma and retinal hemorrhage are vacuum.
⚠️ Post-term cutoffBeyond 41 6/7 weeks. The placenta ages out.
⚠️ Stillbirth cutoffAfter 20 weeks. Before 20 weeks it is a miscarriage.
⚠️ Triple IIt is intra-amniotic infection, another name for chorioamnionitis. Fever is part of the definition.
⚠️ AFE findingLook for sudden respiratory distress. Hypotension (not hypertension) and coagulopathy follow.
⚠️ Vasa previaThe fetal vessels, not the maternal ones, cross the os. That is why rupture can kill the fetus fast.
⚠️ Irregular uterine contourAfter a trial of labor, an irregular uterine wall contour means the uterus ruptured.
⚠️ Vacuum documentationDocument the time from vacuum insertion to birth, not only the birth time.
⚠️ Vacuum documentationPulls, pop-offs, and the time from insertion to birth. Not just the birth time.
⚠️ Shoulder dystocia clock60 seconds defines it. 5 minutes is when brain injury risk becomes high.
⚠️ AFE vs PEAFE is sudden shortness of breath with collapse and a bleeding problem (DIC). The answer on her slide quiz was respiratory distress.
⚠️ Classic vs low transverseClassic vertical: never vaginal birth after. Low transverse: standard and lower risk.
⚠️ Triple IOne finding is enough to diagnose it.
⚠️ Who is NOT a VBAC candidate?Prior classical or T-shaped incision, prior uterine rupture, previa, or no emergency surgery team.

🏥 Cesarean Birth and Maternal Early Warning

Definitions first: cesarean classes, ERAS, MEWC, STS, SUPC, and postoperative care.

🧠 The big idea

A cesarean is major abdominal surgery, so the care is surgical care plus bonding.
Know why it is done and how urgent it is → Know how to lower the rate → Prevent infection, hemorrhage, and clots → Use early warning criteria and protect bonding

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Cesarean classes: scheduled, emergent (cord prolapse, rupture, abnormal FHR), urgent (malpresentation, previa with mild bleeding and Category I), non-urgent (failure to progress or descend with Category I).
  2. Indications: previous cesarean, arrest of labor, placental or uterine abnormalities, cephalopelvic disproportion, maternal risk factors, malpresentation, Category II and III FHR.
  3. Ways to lower the rate: induce only for medical reasons, let the second stage proceed, consider vacuum or forceps, avoid unneeded costs and risks. All of the above is the answer.
  4. Perioperative: teaching, labs, catheter, NPO, anesthesia, prophylactic antibiotics, and sequential compression devices before surgery.
  5. Intraoperative risks: hemorrhage, bladder, ureter and bowel trauma, respiratory depression, hypotension (raises fetal acidemia), anesthetic injected into the bloodstream.
  6. Postoperative: infection, hemorrhage, and thromboembolism are the main complications. Hospital about 3 days, recovery 6 weeks or more.
  7. MEWC: systolic under 90 or over 160, diastolic over 100, HR under 50 or over 120, RR under 10 or over 30, oxygen saturation under 95%, urine under 30 mL/hr for 2 hours, agitation, confusion, unresponsiveness, hypertension with persistent headache or shortness of breath.
  8. 🎤 Oct 21: any hospital with L&D must do an emergency cesarean within 30 minutes of the decision. Length of stay: vaginal 24 to 48 hours, cesarean 3 to 4 days (72 to 96 hours).
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: after cesarean: bed rest about 12 hours, then Foley out and first walk with the nurse. Baby goes back in the bassinet if mom gets drowsy.
  10. 🎤 Oct 21: always a time-out, even in an emergency. Platelets matter for the spinal. Antibiotic about 1 hour before. NPO preferred.

📖 Cesarean birth (13 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
Classic vertical incision
  • Older up-and-down uterine incision
  • Very high rupture risk, so no vaginal birth afterward
Lower transverse incision
  • Today's standard uterine incision
  • Much lower rupture risk and the one that allows TOLAC
Perimortem cesarean
  • Delivery within 5 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest when circulation does not return
  • Can save mother and baby
Cesarean indicationsPrevious cesarean, arrest of labor, placental or uterine abnormalities, cephalopelvic disproportion, maternal risk factors, malpresentation, Category II or III FHR.
Emergent cesareanImmediate need to deliver the fetus, such as cord prolapse, uterine rupture, or abnormal FHR patterns.
Urgent cesareanNeed for rapid delivery, such as malpresentation after labor starts or previa with mild bleeding and a Category I FHR.
Non-urgent cesareanFailure to progress or failure to descend with a Category I FHR.
Scheduled cesareanPlanned (elective or medically indicated) cesarean birth.
Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)Bundle of steps that speed recovery: early oral intake, warmth, early catheter removal, early ambulation, non-opioid analgesia, thromboprophylaxis.
Maternal Early Warning Criteria (MEWC)Vital sign and symptom triggers that prompt bedside evaluation of a postpartum or surgical client.
Sudden Unexpected Postnatal Collapse (SUPC)Infant born at 35 weeks or later with a 5-minute Apgar of 7 or more who collapses and dies suddenly in the first week.
Skin-to-skin contact (STS)Newborn placed on the mother chest right after birth to support bonding and transition.
DehiscenceSeparation of the edges of a surgical incision.

Preoperative

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Emergent vs urgentEmergent is immediate (cord prolapse, rupture, abnormal FHR). Urgent is rapid but not immediate (malpresentation, previa with mild bleeding and Category I).
⚠️ Non-urgentFailure to progress or descend with a Category I tracing. The FHR category is what keeps it non-urgent.
⚠️ All of the aboveQuestions on lowering the cesarean rate and on postoperative complications both have answer D.
⚠️ Sequential compression devicesApplied BEFORE surgery, not after.
⚠️ HypotensionMaternal hypotension from anesthesia raises the risk of FETAL acidemia.
⚠️ Heart rate cutoffMEWC says under 50 or over 120. The red trigger table says under 40. Know which tool the question names.
⚠️ SUPCThe baby looked healthy (Apgar 7 or more at 5 minutes) and collapses in the first week. Keep the airway open and watch the position.
⚠️ Time-outThe time-out is done even in an emergency.
⚠️ Length of stayCesarean is 3 to 4 days (72 to 96 hours), not the 24 to 48 hours of a vaginal birth.
⚠️ Drowsy motherIf she is drowsy, the baby goes back in the bassinet or to dad. Do not leave the baby in her arms.

💓 FHR Patterns and Categories

Every pattern, its cause, its category, and your first action. Exam 3 has more FHR questions, so this tab is the full set.

🧠 The big idea

Read every strip in the same order, name the pattern, name the cause, then act on the cause.
Baseline and variability tell you the baby oxygen reserve → Decelerations tell you the cause (VEAL CHOP) → Category I, II, or III tells you how fast to act → First move is almost always reposition, stop oxytocin, fluids, oxygen, and call

📖 FHR patterns (15 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
FHR baseline
  • Average fetal heart rate over a 10 minute window, rounded to 5 bpm, excluding accelerations and decelerations
  • Normal is 110 to 160 bpm
Fetal tachycardia
  • Baseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more
  • Causes include fever, infection, dehydration, anxiety, anemia, cocaine, and terbutaline
Fetal bradycardia
  • Baseline below 110 bpm for 10 minutes or more
  • Causes include supine hypotension, abruption, cord occlusion, and cardiac problems
Variability
  • Fluctuation in the baseline
  • Absent is undetectable, minimal is 5 bpm or less, moderate is 6 to 25 bpm, marked is over 25 bpm
Acceleration
  • Abrupt rise of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds or more (10 bpm for 10 seconds under 32 weeks)
  • Reassuring
Early deceleration
  • Gradual drop that mirrors the contraction
  • Caused by fetal head compression
  • Benign, so just watch
Late deceleration
  • Gradual drop that starts after the contraction begins, with the low point after the peak
  • Caused by uteroplacental insufficiency
Variable deceleration
  • Abrupt drop of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds to under 2 minutes, with changing shape and timing
  • Caused by cord compression
Prolonged decelerationDrop of 15 bpm or more lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes.
Sinusoidal pattern
  • Smooth, wave-like baseline that is very ominous
  • It is Category III and needs urgent action
Category I tracing
  • Normal: baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations
  • Early decelerations and accelerations may be present or absent
Category II tracing
  • Indeterminate: anything that is not Category I or III
  • Needs evaluation, continued surveillance, and often resuscitation measures
Category III tracing
  • Abnormal: absent variability with recurrent late or variable decelerations or bradycardia, or a sinusoidal pattern
  • Always abnormal
Intrauterine resuscitationSteps to restore fetal oxygen: reposition, stop oxytocin, IV bolus for maternal hypotension, oxygen only if SpO2 is under 95%, check for prolapse, check vitals, notify the provider.
Reactive nonstress test
  • At least two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes
  • This is the normal result

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Baseline 110 to 160 bpm, judged over 10 minutes. Tachycardia is above 160, bradycardia is below 110, each for 10 minutes or more.
  2. Moderate variability (6 to 25 bpm) is the reassuring finding. Absent, minimal, and marked are the concerning ones.
  3. VEAL CHOP: Variable = Cord, Early = Head, Acceleration = OK, Late = Placental insufficiency.
  4. Early decelerations need no action. Late and variable decelerations get repositioning, fluids, oxygen, stop oxytocin, and a call to the provider.
  5. Category I is normal, Category II is indeterminate (needs evaluation), Category III is abnormal and urgent.
  6. Intrauterine resuscitation: reposition, stop oxytocin, IV bolus, oxygen, check for prolapse, check vitals, notify, prepare for birth.

⚖️ Why this matters

  • The fetal heart rate is how you see fetal oxygenation
  • Misreading or not acting on a tracing delays care, which leads to injury to the baby and claims against nurses and providers
  • Nurses are legally responsible for fetal monitoring and assessment, and FHR monitoring is a highly litigated area

  • AWHONN (Association of Women's Health, Obstetric and Neonatal Nurses) sets the recommendations.
    • Goal of EFM: interpret and continually assess fetal condition, and start appropriate interventions
  • Use standard NICHD terms so everyone describes the tracing the same way
  • Clinical judgment: recognize the cue, analyze it, prioritize, act, and evaluate.
    • Then report with SBAR and use the chain of command if no one responds
  • Evidence-based practice sets how often you assess and what you do for each pattern

🩺 Methods of monitoring

MethodDetails
Intermittent auscultation
How
  • Fetoscope or handheld Doppler over the fetal back
  • Listen for 30 to 60 seconds after a contraction
Notes
  • Used for low-risk labor, and common at home and birth center births
  • Count the rate, note rhythm, and the response to a contraction
  • Frequency depends on stage and risk
External electronic
How
Two transducers held by belts: an ultrasound (Doppler) over the fetal back (find it with Leopold maneuvers) and a tocodynamometer ("toco") over the fundus
Notes
  • Noninvasive
  • The toco shows frequency and duration of contractions, not intensity
  • A baseline strip is 20 minutes
  • If the tracing is erratic, reposition the transducers first
Internal electronic
How
Fetal scalp electrode screwed into the fetal head for FHR, and an intrauterine pressure catheter (IUPC) for contractions in mm Hg
Notes
  • Used when external monitoring is inadequate
  • Needs ruptured membranes, at least 2 cm dilation, and an accessible presenting part
  • More accurate
  • Invasive
  • Avoid with placenta previa, herpes, HIV
Multiples
How
Each fetus is monitored separately
Notes
  • Before membranes rupture, two external transducers (baby A and baby B)
  • After rupture, one external and one internal

Frequency, duration, intensity, and resting tone are explained in your Week 2 guide (Labor Basics). The monitoring points that matter here are in the uterine activity card below.

🔎 Reading the strip

PartWhat to know
Layout
  • Top tracing is the FHR
  • Bottom is the contractions
  • Big boxes are 1 minute and small boxes are 10 seconds
What affects the FHR
  • The placental unit
  • Parasympathetic (vagus) slows it
  • Sympathetic speeds it and gives variability, and is stimulated by hypoxia
  • Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors in the aortic arch
  • The central nervous system
  • Hormones (epinephrine, norepinephrine, vasopressin)
Uterine activity: tachysystole
  • More than 5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes
  • Can cause fetal hypoxia
  • Treat the cause regardless of fetal status: stop oxytocin, remove a cervical ripener such as misoprostol, or give a tocolytic (terbutaline stops contractions)
What skews the contraction tracing
  • Breathing, pushing, vomiting, and fetal movement (sharp spikes)
  • Baseline shifts with position changes
  • Reposition the transducer if the tracing is obscure or inverted
Preterm fetus
  • Tolerates stress poorly
  • Baseline a bit higher but still normal
  • Variable decelerations are the most common, even without contractions
  • Late and prolonged decelerations are still concerning
  • Magnesium sulfate lowers variability (CNS depression)
  • Terbutaline or tachysystole can cause tachycardia in mother and fetus

✅ Step by step: monitoring properly

  1. Explain the procedure, wash hands, and get consent.
    • Place her in a comfortable position, not flat on her back (left side, semi-Fowler, or sitting)
  2. Do Leopold maneuvers to find the fetal back.
    • Heart tones are loudest over the fetal back (for a vertex baby, the lower quadrant of the abdomen)
  3. Place the Doppler over the fetal back and the toco at the fundus. Secure the belts and recheck often
  4. Check the maternal pulse to be sure you are recording the baby and not the mother (a rate of 70 to 90 may be maternal)
  5. Assess contractions: frequency, duration, resting tone, and intensity
  6. Look at a 10 minute window. Identify baseline, variability, accelerations, and decelerations and how they relate to contractions
  7. Label it as Category I, II, or III
  8. Act on the category. Start intrauterine resuscitation for a nonreassuring pattern and call with SBAR
  9. Document on time, in standard terms, with what you did and who you told

⏱️ How often to assess

RiskActive first stageSecond stage (pushing)
Low riskEvery 30 minutesEvery 15 minutes
High risk or oxytocinEvery 15 minutesEvery 5 minutes

These are the commonly taught intervals (ACOG and AWHONN). Always follow your facility protocol and your instructor's version for exams. Reassess after any change: rupture of membranes, medication, epidural, change in contractions, or a change in her condition.

📏 Terms and normal values (NICHD)

TermDefinition and what it means
Baseline
  • Average rate over a 10 minute window, rounded to 5 bpm, a consistent reading for at least 2 minutes, not counting accelerations or decelerations
  • Normal 110 to 160 bpm
Tachycardia
  • Baseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more
  • Causes: fever, infection, dehydration, anxiety, anemia, drugs such as cocaine, compensation for hypoxia, cardiac problems
Bradycardia
  • Baseline below 110 bpm for 10 minutes or more
  • Causes: mother on her back, hypotension, dehydration, placental abruption, electrolyte imbalance, cord occlusion, cardiac problems
  • Usually not a good sign
Variability
  • Fluctuation in the baseline
  • Absent: flat line, undetectable, not a good sign
  • Minimal: 5 bpm or less, the baby may be sleeping, so stimulate or reposition
  • Moderate: 6 to 25 bpm, ideal
  • Marked: more than 25 bpm, the baby is irritated and something may be wrong
Acceleration
  • Abrupt rise of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds or more (under 32 weeks: 10 bpm for 10 seconds)
  • Reassuring
Prolonged acceleration2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes
Prolonged decelerationDrop of 15 bpm or more lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes
Sinusoidal pattern
  • Smooth wave-like pattern
  • Very ominous
  • Needs a cesarean right away
Episodic vs periodicEpisodic: not tied to contractions. Periodic: tied to contractions

📉 Decelerations: cause and nursing action

🧠 Memory hook
VEAL CHOP MINE
VEAL is the pattern, CHOP is the cause, MINE is the management. Variable = Cord compression = Maternal repositioning. Early = Head compression = Identify labor progress. Acceleration = Okay = No interventions. Late = Placental insufficiency = Execute interventions.
PatternDetails
Early
What it looks like
  • Gradual drop and return
  • A mirror image of the contraction
  • Lowest point matches the peak of the contraction
Cause
Fetal head compression
Nursing action
  • Benign
  • Continue to monitor
  • No intervention needed
Variable
What it looks like
  • Abrupt drop (under 30 seconds to the low point) of 15 bpm or more, lasting 15 seconds to under 2 minutes
  • Shape and timing vary (V, U, or W)
Cause
Umbilical cord compression
Nursing action
  • Change maternal position (side to side), stop oxytocin, check for cord prolapse by vaginal exam, give oxygen and IV fluid, notify provider
  • Amnioinfusion may be ordered
Late
What it looks like
  • Gradual drop that begins after the contraction starts, and the lowest point comes after the peak
  • Returns after the contraction ends
Cause
Uteroplacental insufficiency (poor oxygen to the fetus)
Nursing action
  • Turn her to the left side, give IV fluid and oxygen, stop oxytocin, check her BP, notify provider now, prepare for possible urgent birth (cesarean if prolonged)
  • Recurrent late decelerations are ominous
Prolonged
What it looks like
Drop lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes
Cause
Cord prolapse, uterine hyperstimulation, maternal hypotension (supine or after an epidural), rapid descent, maternal seizure
Nursing action
  • Find and fix the cause
  • Reposition, fluids, oxygen, stop oxytocin, check for prolapse, notify provider
Acceleration
What it looks like
Abrupt rise of 15 bpm or more for 15 seconds or more
Cause
Fetal movement or stimulation. A sign of a well-oxygenated fetus
Nursing action
  • Reassuring
  • Document it
  • No intervention
Minimal or absent variability
What it looks like
Flat line pattern
Cause
Fetal sleep (usually under 40 minutes), opioids, magnesium sulfate, acidemia
Nursing action
  • Look for the cause
  • Stimulate the fetus
  • Absent variability with decelerations is serious

🚦 NICHD three-tier system

CategoryDetails
I (normal)
Findings
  • Baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations
  • Early decelerations and accelerations may be present or absent
Meaning and action
Normal acid-base status. Routine care and routine monitoring
II (indeterminate)
Findings
  • Everything that is not Category I or III
  • Examples: tachycardia, bradycardia without absent variability, minimal or marked variability, recurrent variable decelerations, prolonged decelerations (over 2 minutes and under 10), or no accelerations after stimulation
Meaning and action
  • Needs evaluation, continued surveillance, and often resuscitation measures
  • Could be fine, could be bad
  • Notify provider
III (abnormal)
Findings
Absent variability with recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia, OR a sinusoidal pattern
Meaning and action
  • Always abnormal
  • Abnormal acid-base status
  • Immediate action: resuscitation measures, notify provider, prepare for prompt birth

  • Her tip: learn Category I and Category III cold
  • Everything else falls in the middle
  • Category III is always bad

🩹 Intrauterine resuscitation (for a nonreassuring pattern)

  • Do these together, quickly, and tell the provider
  • Follow your facility protocol
  • Goals: maximum uterine blood flow, umbilical circulation, and maternal-fetal oxygenation

  • Reposition her to the left side (or right, hands and knees) to improve blood flow and free the cord
  • Stop or reduce oxytocin if infusing, especially with tachysystole
  • Give an IV isotonic fluid bolus of at least 500 mL lactated Ringer's
  • Give oxygen by nonrebreather mask at about 10 L/min as protocol directs
  • Do a vaginal exam to rule out cord prolapse and check dilation
  • Check her vital signs and treat hypotension
  • Notify the provider with SBAR.
    • The provider may order a tocolytic (terbutaline, relaxes the uterus) for tachysystole or amnioinfusion for variable decelerations
  • Prepare for operative or assisted birth if the tracing does not improve

📞 SBAR for an abnormal tracing

PartExample
Situation
  • "This is the nurse for Ms
  • J in room 4, 39 weeks, in active labor
  • She has recurrent late decelerations for the last 20 minutes."
Background"G2 P1, oxytocin at 12 milliunits per minute, epidural placed an hour ago, no allergies."
Assessment
  • "Baseline 150 with minimal variability
  • Late decelerations with every contraction
  • BP 92/50, contractions every 2 minutes
  • I turned her left, started a fluid bolus, gave oxygen, and stopped the oxytocin."
Recommendation
  • "I need you to come to the bedside now and evaluate for birth
  • Do you want me to prepare for a cesarean?"

📝 Documentation and legal protection

  • Chart the baseline, variability, accelerations, type of decelerations, contraction pattern, category, interventions, her and the baby's response, who you notified, the time, and the provider's response
  • Use standard terms. Do not write "reassuring" or "nonreassuring" alone. Describe what you see
  • Label and keep the strip. Never alter or erase an entry. Late entries are labeled as late
  • If the provider does not respond to a concerning tracing, use the chain of command (charge nurse, then supervisor, then chair) and document that you did
  • Patient safety comes before convenience

🧪 Before labor: NST and biophysical profile

  • Nonstress test (NST): from 32 weeks for high-risk pregnancies.
    • She eats first and lies on her left side
    • External monitor, event marker for movements, 20 to 30 minutes
    • Reactive: at least two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes
    • Nonreactive: not met after 40 minutes
    • More than half are false positives, so repeat, use vibroacoustic stimulation, or do a BPP
BPP component2 points if
Body movements3 or more
Fetal tone1 or more flexion and extension
Fetal breathing1 or more lasting over 30 seconds
Amniotic fluid1 pocket over 2 cm
NSTReactive

  • Score 8 to 10 normal, 4 to 5 abnormal, under 2 chronic (the worst)
  • Amniocentesis, CVS, and the other antepartum tests are in your Week 1 guide

🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Baseline vs variabilityBaseline is the average rate over 10 minutes. Variability is the wiggle around it. A baseline of 140 can still have absent variability, and that combination is the bad one.
⚠️ Early vs lateLook at timing against the peak of the contraction. Early mirrors the contraction (head compression, no action). Late starts after the peak and recovers after it ends (placental insufficiency, act now).
⚠️ Category II is not "fine"Category II is indeterminate. It needs evaluation and continued surveillance, and the nurse still acts on what is causing it. Category III is the emergency.
⚠️ Absent variability aloneCategory III needs absent variability WITH recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia, or a sinusoidal pattern.
⚠️ Whose heart rate is it?A rate of 70 to 90 may be the mother. Check her pulse before you call the fetus bradycardic.
⚠️ The 10 minute ruleTachycardia and bradycardia are baseline changes that last 10 minutes or more. A short dip is a deceleration, not bradycardia.
⚠️ First nursing actionFor late or variable decelerations the first move is to reposition her (usually to the left side) and stop oxytocin, before you chart or wait for the provider.
⚠️ Reactive NSTReactive means at least 2 accelerations of 15 bpm lasting 15 seconds within 20 minutes. Reactive is the normal result.

🧪 Say it first: FHR monitoring

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

Normal baseline? Tachycardia and bradycardia?
110 to 160 bpm. Above 160 and below 110 for 10 minutes or more.
Four variability levels and ranges?
Absent (undetectable), minimal (5 or less), moderate (6 to 25), marked (over 25).
Which variability is normal and reassuring?
Moderate, 6 to 25 bpm.
VEAL CHOP: which cause goes with each pattern?
Variable = cord. Early = head. Acceleration = OK. Late = placental insufficiency.
Early deceleration: action?
None. It is benign head compression.
Late deceleration: actions?
Turn her left, IV fluid, oxygen, stop oxytocin, check BP, notify the provider now.
Variable deceleration: actions?
Change position, stop oxytocin, check for cord prolapse, oxygen and fluids, notify. Amnioinfusion may be ordered.
Category I, II, III in one line each?
I: normal. II: indeterminate, everything else. III: absent variability with recurrent lates, variables, or bradycardia, or sinusoidal.
Which category is always bad?
Category III.
Name the intrauterine resuscitation steps.
Reposition, stop or reduce oxytocin, IV bolus (500 mL or more), oxygen 10 L/min, check for prolapse, check vitals, notify, prepare for birth.
Why check the maternal pulse?
To be sure the monitor is recording the baby and not the mother (70 to 90 may be hers).
What does the toco measure? The IUPC?
Toco: frequency and duration. IUPC: strength in mmHg and resting tone.
What is needed for an internal scalp electrode or IUPC?
Ruptured membranes, at least 2 cm dilation, accessible presenting part. Avoid with previa, herpes, HIV.
What lowers variability?
Fetal sleep (under 40 minutes), opioids, magnesium sulfate, acidemia.
Preterm fetus: most common deceleration?
Variable decelerations.
Chain of command if the provider does not respond?
Charge nurse, then supervisor, then chair. Document it.
Reactive NST?
At least two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes.
BPP scoring?
Five parts at 2 points each. 8 to 10 normal, 4 to 5 abnormal, under 2 chronic (worst).

➕ Extra detail that can decide a Category question

TermKnow
RecurrentDecelerations that occur with at least half of the contractions in any 20 minute period
IntermittentDecelerations with fewer than half of the contractions
SinusoidalSmooth sine wave, regular, about 3 to 5 cycles per minute, lasting 20 minutes or more
Pseudosinusoidal
  • Short sine-like wave after opioids
  • It has normal accelerations and does not last
Worrying variable featuresOvershoot after the drop, slow return to baseline, loss of variability inside the drop, a W shape, drop below 70 bpm lasting over 60 seconds
Prolonged vs bradycardia
  • 2 to under 10 minutes is a prolonged deceleration
  • 10 minutes or more is a baseline change (bradycardia)

Her slides do not define these. They come from the NICHD and ACOG definitions.

🧪 Sim: fetal tracing matrix and intrauterine resuscitation (Defending the Dyad)

CategoryTracingAction
I (Normal)Moderate variability, accelerations present, no late or variable decelerationsRoutine continuous EFM
II (Indeterminate)Tachycardia or bradycardia, minimal variability, or recurrent variable decelerationsHeightened vigilance and start nursing interventions
III (Abnormal)Absent variability WITH recurrent lates, recurrent variables, or a sinusoidal pattern
  • Notify provider immediately
  • Prepare for possible emergency delivery
  • No vaginal exams unless ordered
Resuscitation stepSim rule
1. RepositionLeft lateral right away. Relieves vena cava compression
2. FluidsLactated Ringer's 250 mL bolus over 20 to 30 minutes, specifically for documented maternal hypotension
3. Oxygen
  • Nasal cannula 2 to 4 L/min ONLY if maternal SpO2 is under 95%
  • Titrate to keep SpO2 over 95%
  • No routine oxygen (avoids toxicity)
4. DiscontinueStop any running oxytocin

⚠️ Conflicts resolved: older teaching says routine oxygen at about 10 L/min and a 500 mL or larger bolus. The sim says oxygen only if SpO2 is under 95% and a 250 mL bolus for hypotension, so use the sim. Standard teaching also lists a vaginal exam to rule out cord prolapse. The sim says no vaginal exams unless ordered in Category III. Know both: a vaginal exam is a resuscitation step in general lists, but not one the nurse does on her own in this sim.

🔍 Look-alikes: how to tell them apart

PairHow to tell
Early vs late
  • Early is a mirror: the low point matches the peak
  • Late starts after the contraction starts and the low point is after the peak
Late vs variable
  • Late is gradual and uniform and repeats the same way
  • Variable is abrupt, with changing shape and timing
Variable vs prolonged
  • Variable lasts under 2 minutes
  • Prolonged lasts 2 minutes or more but under 10
Prolonged vs bradycardia
  • Prolonged is an episode
  • Bradycardia is a new baseline lasting 10 minutes or more
Minimal vs absent variabilityMinimal is 5 bpm or less but visible. Absent is undetectable (flat)
Marked vs moderate variabilityModerate is 6 to 25. Marked is over 25
Category II vs III
  • Category III needs absent variability with recurrent lates, variables, or bradycardia, or sinusoidal
  • Everything else abnormal is II
Her pulse vs baby pulseA rate of 70 to 90 may be hers. Check her pulse first

🪤 More ways she could trap you on FHR

⚠️ Absent variability aloneOn its own it is Category II. It becomes Category III only with recurrent lates, recurrent variables, or bradycardia.
⚠️ Tachycardia aloneCategory II. It is not Category III. Look for fever and infection first.
⚠️ Early decelerations in Category IEarly decelerations may be present in Category I. They do not change the category.
⚠️ Magnesium and minimal variabilityMagnesium lowers variability. It is an expected finding, but still look for other signs.
⚠️ Recurrent means halfRecurrent decelerations occur with at least half of contractions in 20 minutes.
⚠️ Epidural dropIf the fetus has a prolonged deceleration after an epidural, check her blood pressure first.
⚠️ TerbutalineIt treats tachysystole but causes tachycardia in mother and fetus. Do not read the new tachycardia as fetal distress alone.
⚠️ Charting wordsDo not chart only reassuring or nonreassuring. Describe baseline, variability, decelerations, interventions, and notifications.

🧪 More say-it-first: FHR patterns

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

DR C BRAVADO stands for?
Determine Risk, Contractions, Baseline Rate, Variability, Accelerations, Decelerations, Overall assessment.
Which pattern is always Category III?
Sinusoidal.
When is absent variability Category III?
With recurrent late decelerations, recurrent variable decelerations, or bradycardia.
What does recurrent mean?
Decelerations with at least half of contractions in 20 minutes.
Prolonged deceleration vs bradycardia?
Prolonged is 2 minutes to under 10. Bradycardia is 10 minutes or more.
What drug lowers variability and is expected?
Magnesium sulfate (also opioids).
Epidural, low BP, prolonged deceleration: first move?
Turn left, fluids, check BP.
Oxytocin plus tachysystole plus late decelerations: first move?
Stop or reduce the oxytocin, turn her left, oxygen, fluids, call.
What causes sinusoidal patterns?
Severe fetal anemia or severe hypoxia.
Which FHR categories can occur with hypertonic uterine dysfunction?
Category II or III.

🩸 Postpartum Hemorrhage

Definitions first: PPH, atony, the four Ts, uterotonics, and the signs of hypovolemic shock.

🧠 The big idea

PPH is a race against blood loss, so find the cause (the four Ts) while you resuscitate.
Blood loss over 1,000 mL → Uterine atony is the top cause (Tone) → Massage, uterotonics, fluids, blood → Watch the shock signs and use the red and yellow triggers

⭐ Know these cold

  1. PPH is blood loss over 1,000 mL regardless of type of delivery.
  2. Most common cause: uterine atony. Lacerations are second. Treatment of choice for primary PPH: oxytocin.
  3. Four Ts: Tone, Tissue, Trauma, Thrombin. Atony is a boggy uterus. Trauma is a firm uterus with steady bright red bleeding.
  4. Two-pronged approach: resuscitate and treat shock, and find and treat the cause.
  5. Resuscitation: fluids, blood transfusion, bimanual compression, fundal massage, iron, uterotonics.
  6. Uterotonics: oxytocin, methylergonovine (Methergine), misoprostol (Cytotec), carboprost (Hemabate).
  7. Shock: mild about 20% loss, moderate 20 to 40%, severe over 40%. Signs: tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, oxygen under 95%, oliguria, pallor, dizziness, altered mental status.
  8. 🎤 Oct 21: oxytocin is FIRST line. Methergine, Hemabate, and misoprostol are all SECOND line. Methergine: avoid with uncontrolled hypertension. Hemabate: avoid with asthma. Misoprostol: option when Methergine cannot be used.
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: firm fundus with a steady trickle of bright red blood means laceration. Boggy fundus: massage until firm like a baseball.
  10. 🎤 Oct 21: she said PPH is likely on the exam and the med quiz covers PPH drugs and their contraindications.
  11. ➕ Methergine avoided in hypertension, so use oxytocin, Hemabate, or Cytotec. Hemabate avoided in asthma, so use oxytocin, Methergine, or Cytotec.

📖 Postpartum hemorrhage (11 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)Blood loss over 1,000 mL regardless of type of delivery.
Uterine atony
  • Failure of the uterus to contract firmly after birth
  • The most common cause of PPH
Primary PPH causesUterine atony, lacerations, hematomas.
Secondary PPH causesHematomas, subinvolution, retained placental tissue.
The four TsTone (atony), Tissue (retained placenta), Trauma (lacerations, hematoma), Thrombin (clotting disorders).
Subinvolution
  • Uterus fails to return to its normal size and position
  • Cause of late bleeding
UterotonicMedication that makes the uterus contract: oxytocin, methylergonovine, misoprostol, carboprost.
Methylergonovine (Methergine)
  • Ergot uterotonic for PPH
  • Avoid in hypertension and preeclampsia
Carboprost (Hemabate)
  • Prostaglandin F2 alpha uterotonic for PPH
  • Avoid in asthma
Bimanual compressionOne hand inside the vagina and one on the abdomen compress the uterus to stop bleeding.
Hypovolemic shockShock from blood loss: tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, low oxygen saturation, oliguria, pallor, altered mental status.

📏 Definition and causes

TopicKnow
DefinitionBlood loss over 1,000 mL regardless of type of delivery
Primary causesUterine atony, lacerations, hematomas
Secondary causesHematomas, subinvolution, retained placental tissue
Most commonUterine atony
Second most common (primary)Lacerations

  • ➕ Also know: primary PPH is within the first 24 hours
  • Secondary is from 24 hours up to 12 weeks
  • Risk factors for atony: large baby, high parity, rapid or prolonged labor, fever, fibroids, magnesium sulfate, oxytocin use

4️⃣ The four Ts: signs and nursing actions

TDetails
Tone (uterine atony)
Medical factors
Large baby, high parity, rapid labor, fever, fibroids
Signs
  • Bleeding slow and steady or profuse
  • Large, boggy uterus
  • Clots
Nursing actions
  • Massage the uterus or give medications
  • Monitor bleeding: weigh pads and Chux (1 g = 1 mL)
  • Maintain fluids (second IV, Foley)
  • Monitor vitals and labs
  • Oxygen 10 to 12 L by face mask
  • Keep her warm
Tissue
Medical factors
Retained or abnormal placenta
Signs
  • Same as above, plus uterus does not respond to interventions
  • Uterus stays larger than normal
  • Strings of tissue in the blood
Nursing actions
  • Call the provider (D&C may be needed)
  • Monitor for shock
  • Oxygen if indicated
Trauma: laceration
Medical factors
Lacerations
Signs
  • FIRM uterus with continued bleeding
  • Steady trickle of unclotted, bright red blood
Nursing actions
  • Call the provider to evaluate, locate, repair
  • Monitor vitals and lochia
  • Weigh pads and Chux
Trauma: hematoma
Medical factors
Hematoma (vulvar, vaginal, cervical, retroperitoneal)
Signs
  • Firm uterus
  • Sudden painful perineal pressure
  • Bulging area under the skin
  • Difficulty voiding or sitting
Nursing actions
  • Assess for visible hematoma
  • Call provider
  • Anticipate excision and ligation if over 3 cm
  • Consider indwelling catheter
  • Ice and pain management
Thrombin
Medical factors
Preeclampsia, stillbirth
Signs
  • DIC
  • Oozing from IV sites, nosebleeds, petechiae, bleeding gums, hypotension and shock
  • Abnormal clotting labs
Nursing actions
  • Early recognition saves lives
  • Confirm accurate blood loss
  • Monitor labs, vitals, intake and output
  • Volume replacement, platelets IV, oxygen by mask at 10 L/min

💊 Uterotonics and other medications for PPH

DrugRole➕ Dose and cautions
Oxytocin (Pitocin)Treatment of choice for primary PPH
  • 10 to 40 units in 500 to 1,000 mL IV, or 10 units IM
  • Do not give undiluted IV push (hypotension)
Methylergonovine (Methergine)Ergot. Strong uterine contraction
  • 0.2 mg IM, may repeat every 2 to 4 hours.
  • AVOID with hypertension or preeclampsia
Carboprost (Hemabate)Prostaglandin F2 alpha250 mcg IM every 15 to 90 minutes, up to 8 doses. AVOID with asthma
Misoprostol (Cytotec)Prostaglandin E1800 to 1,000 mcg rectally, once. Can cause fever and chills
Other medicationsHer slide lists "other medications"➕ Tranexamic acid (TXA) 1 g IV over 10 minutes, antibiotics, blood products, iron

Her slide shows "Staging, Box 14-2, stage 1, 2, 3, 4" with no content. ➕ Common obstetric hemorrhage staging: Stage 1 blood loss over 500 mL vaginal or over 1,000 mL cesarean, Stage 2 continued bleeding to 1,500 mL, Stage 3 over 1,500 mL or unstable vitals or DIC, Stage 4 cardiovascular collapse.

📉 Clinical manifestations of shock from blood loss

Degree of shockBlood lossSigns and symptoms
MildAbout 20%Diaphoresis, increased capillary refill time, cool extremities, maternal anxiety
Moderate20 to 40%Tachycardia, postural hypotension, oliguria
SevereOver 40%Hypotension, agitation or confusion, hemodynamic instability

🧍 What it looks like at the bedside

  • Boggy uterus, heavy lochia, drop in hematocrit and hemoglobin
  • Hypotension (BP 90/60), tachycardia (HR 110), decreased urine output (under 50 mL in 4 hours), increased lochia
  • Capillary refill over 3 seconds, cold hands and feet, pale and clammy skin
  • Acute pain with fundal massage. Anxiety, fatigue, delay in mother-infant attachment
  • Impaired gas exchange: hemoglobin 9 g/dL, dyspnea, hypoxia, restlessness

🚦 Postpartum hemorrhage threshold parameters

ParameterRed triggerYellow trigger
TemperatureUnder 35 or over 38 C35 to 36 C
Systolic BPUnder 90 or over 160150 to 160 or 90 to 100
Diastolic BPOver 10090 to 100
Heart rateUnder 40 or over 120100 to 120 or 40 to 50
Respiratory rateUnder 10 or over 3021 to 30
Oxygen saturationUnder 95%

🧭 Priority actions for PPH

OrderAction
1Call for help and stay with her. Massage the fundus
2Empty the bladder (full bladder blocks contraction)
3Start or open the second large-bore IV, give oxytocin as ordered
4Oxygen, warmth, lay flat, legs raised as appropriate
5Quantify the blood loss, check vitals, notify provider with SBAR
6Give second-line uterotonics and blood products as ordered, prepare for the OR if needed

➕ Standard nursing order of response. Her slides list the interventions without a ranked order.

🎤 Oct 21 lecture: fundal massage and the causes

TopicKnow
Fundal massage
  • Check fundal height
  • Support the lower uterus just above the symphysis
  • Press down on the top
  • A boggy uterus firms up like a baseball
  • Keep massaging until it does
Atony risks
  • Precipitous labor under 3 hours
  • Polyhydramnios (overdistended uterus)
Laceration
  • Firm fundus with a constant trickle
  • Risks: macrosomia, forceps or vacuum, precipitous labor
  • Second most common cause of primary PPH
Hematoma
  • Visible or concealed
  • Mark the size
  • Sudden pain and pressure means it is growing
  • Small: provider watches
  • Large: provider opens it and removes it
Subinvolution
  • Uterus stays larger and higher than expected
  • May have back pain
  • Causes: retained placenta, endometritis, fibroids
Retained placenta
  • A piece stays behind (the placenta looked incomplete, "dirty" rough side instead of the shiny side)
  • Bleeding and infection (fever, uterine tenderness)
  • Treatment: D&C or manual removal, IV antibiotics
  • Prevention: check that the whole placenta is intact at birth
The four Ts
  • Tone (atony, most common)
  • Tissue (retained placenta)
  • Trauma (lacerations, hematomas)
  • Thrombin (clotting disorders such as DIC)

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

Define PPH.
Blood loss over 1,000 mL regardless of type of delivery.
Most common cause of PPH?
Uterine atony.
Primary and secondary causes?
Primary: atony, lacerations, hematomas. Secondary: hematomas, subinvolution, retained placental tissue.
Four Ts?
Tone, Tissue, Trauma, Thrombin.
Treatment of choice for primary PPH?
Oxytocin.
Name the uterotonics.
Oxytocin, methylergonovine (Methergine), misoprostol (Cytotec), carboprost (Hemabate).
Which uterotonic is avoided in hypertension?
Methylergonovine (Methergine).
Which uterotonic is avoided in asthma?
Carboprost (Hemabate).
Two-pronged approach?
Resuscitate and treat shock, and find and treat the cause.
What does resuscitation include?
Fluids, blood, bimanual compression, fundal massage, iron, uterotonics.
Shock stages by blood loss?
Mild about 20%, moderate 20 to 40%, severe over 40%.
Signs of hypovolemia?
Tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, oxygen under 95%, oliguria, pallor, dizziness, altered mental status.
How do you quantify blood loss?
Weigh pads and Chux. 1 gram equals 1 mL.
Which PPH drug is first line?
Oxytocin.
Which PPH drugs are second line?
Methergine, Hemabate, misoprostol.
Contraindications for Methergine and Hemabate?
Methergine: hypertension. Hemabate: asthma.
Fundal massage steps?
Check height, support above the symphysis, massage the top until firm.
Subinvolution signs and causes?
Larger and higher uterus, back pain. Retained placenta, endometritis, fibroids.
Hypertensive client with atony: which drug is out?
Methergine. Use oxytocin, Hemabate, or Cytotec.

🦠 Clots, Embolism, Infection, and Birth Trauma

Definitions first: DIC, AFE, VTE, endometritis, wound infection, UTI, mastitis, lacerations, and hematomas.

🧠 The big idea

After birth, the big three threats are clots, infection, and hidden bleeding.
Pregnancy makes blood clot more → DVT, then pulmonary embolism → Cesarean, long labor, and procedures raise infection risk → Unexplained perineal pain means hematoma

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Coagulation disorders on her slide: DIC, anaphylactoid syndrome (AFE), and VTE.
  2. AFE: rare but fatal, during pregnancy, labor, or up to 24 hours postpartum. Hypoxia, lung injury, pulmonary hypertension, hypotension, cardiac arrest, coagulopathy.
  3. Thrombosis causes: venous stasis, injury to the vessel lining, hypercoagulation. Types: superficial (saphenous vein), deep vein thrombosis (can cause PE).
  4. Postpartum DVT: the drug is heparin (not ibuprofen, amoxicillin, or acetaminophen).
  5. Endometritis: cesarean is the primary cause. Temp over 100.4 F, uterine tenderness, subinvolution, foul lochia. Treat with antibiotics.
  6. Mastitis: continue breastfeeding and give antibiotics. Wound infection: antibiotics. UTI risk: epidural, overdistended bladder.
  7. Lacerations are the second most common cause of primary PPH. Hematomas: very painful, unexplained pain, sometimes not visible.
  8. 🎤 Oct 21: mastitis is one breast with fever and hardness. Engorgement is both breasts. Keep breastfeeding with mastitis. Antibiotics help in 24 to 48 hours. Abscess in about 10%.
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: endometritis is the most common cause of postpartum fever, starts at the placental site, and is treated with IV antibiotics.
  10. 🎤 Oct 21: AFE: sudden shortness of breath, then hypotension and arrest. Old name amniotic fluid embolism, new name anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancy (a systemic inflammatory response).

🧠 Postpartum Mood Disorders and Follow-Up

Definitions first: blues, depression, psychosis, severe hypertension, diabetes after birth, follow-up, and POST-BIRTH warning signs.

🧠 The big idea

After birth, mood and blood pressure problems can hide behind "normal" tiredness, so screen and teach the warning signs.
Blues are brief and mild → Depression is severe and needs treatment → Psychosis is rare and most severe → Teach the POST-BIRTH signs so she calls early

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Blues: within the first 2 weeks, from hormones, stress, and fatigue. Resolve without treatment. She can safely care for herself and the baby.
  2. Postpartum depression: within the first 12 months, about 11.5% of women. Needs psychiatric intervention. She may be unable to safely care for herself and the baby.
  3. PPD risk factors: history of depression, inadequate social support, complications of pregnancy, labor, or birth, history of sexual abuse.
  4. Psychosis: rare, rapid onset, as early as 2 to 3 days postpartum. Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior. The most severe form.
  5. Severe postpartum hypertension: systolic 160 or more or diastolic 110 or more. Both need urgent antihypertensive therapy.
  6. Pregestational diabetes after birth: insulin needs DECREASE, higher infection risk, most return to normal glucose tolerance, follow-up essential.
  7. Follow-up within 6 weeks. Contraception on board. A chance to ask about labor, birth, and complications.
  8. 🎤 Oct 21: severe postpartum hypertension is 160 systolic or 110 diastolic or higher. Labetalol IV first, then hydralazine IV. Oral nifedipine if there is no IV access.
  9. 🎤 Oct 21: POST-BIRTH: call 911 for chest pain, obstructed breathing, seizures, or thoughts of harming herself or the baby. Call the provider for heavy bleeding, bad incision, red swollen leg, fever of 100.4 or higher, headache that does not get better, vision changes.
  10. 🎤 Oct 21: blues under 2 weeks and she can care for the baby. Depression 6 to 12 months and she cannot safely care for the baby. Psychosis can start at 2 to 3 days and happen up to a year.

💊 Medications: Weeks 1 to 3

Definitions first, then the at-a-glance table, every drug from the slides by week, the head-to-heads, and a full card for every drug on your ATI templates.

🧠 The big idea

For every drug, answer five things: why it works, what it is used for, what to watch for, who must NOT get it, and what the nurse does.
Class tells you the action → The action explains the side effect → The side effect explains the contraindication → The contraindication tells you what to give instead.

⭐ Know these cold

  1. Oxytocin is HIGH ALERT: dilute IV on a pump, titrated up and down. First line for PPH. Watch for tachysystole and uterine rupture.
  2. PPH second line: Methergine (AVOID in hypertension), Hemabate (AVOID in asthma), Cytotec (rectal, sublingual, or buccal).
  3. Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures, not BP. Reflexes go first in toxicity. Antidote: calcium gluconate. Therapeutic level 4 to 7 mEq/L.
  4. Cervidil and Cytotec ripen the cervix. Neither with a prior cesarean scar. Wait 30 minutes after Cervidil removal before oxytocin.
  5. Terbutaline: hold if maternal HR is over 120. Nifedipine: watch BP, severe hypotension with magnesium.
  6. Combined pill (estrogen): avoid with smoking over 35, clots, migraine with aura, hypertension, liver disease, and while breastfeeding. Progestin-only pill is safe.
  7. Depo-Provera: bone loss boxed warning, every 11 to 13 weeks. Plan B within 72 hours, less effective with BMI over 30. Premarin: boxed warning for cancer, stroke, MI, clots.

📖 Medications (10 terms)

Her questions are definition based. Read each meaning once.

TermMeaning
Tocolytic
  • A drug that slows or stops uterine contractions
  • Magnesium sulfate, terbutaline, nifedipine
Uterotonic (oxytocic)
  • A drug that makes the uterus contract
  • Oxytocin, Methergine, Hemabate, Cytotec
Cervical ripening
  • Softening and thinning the cervix before induction
  • Cervidil, Cytotec, balloon, laminaria
Tachysystole
  • More than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, or contractions lasting over 90 seconds
  • Seen with oxytocin and prostaglandins
High alert medication
  • A drug where an error can cause serious harm
  • Oxytocin and magnesium sulfate are examples
Boxed warning
  • The strongest FDA warning on a label
  • Depo-Provera (bone loss), Premarin (cancer, stroke, MI, clots), terbutaline (prolonged tocolysis)
Teratogenic
  • Able to cause birth defects
  • Danazol, Cytotec (category X), retinoids, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs
Antidote
  • The drug that reverses another drug
  • Calcium gluconate for magnesium
  • Protamine sulfate for heparin
Onset, peak, durationHow fast a drug starts, when it works best, and how long it lasts.
Diffusion hypoxia
  • Low oxygen after nitrous oxide stops
  • Give oxygen afterward
