🎯 Med quiz sheet: what it is, why, who can NOT have it, what to watch

Drug and classDetails
Medroxyprogesterone (DepoProvera)
Progestin; hormonal contraceptive
Why we use it
  • Contraception
  • Endometriosis pain, abnormal uterine bleeding, secondary amenorrhea, prevents endometrial hyperplasia with estrogen therapy
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, breast cancer, liver disease, history of thromboembolism or stroke
Watch for
  • Bone mineral density loss (boxed warning, risk rises with use over 2 years)
  • Irregular bleeding or spotting early, then amenorrhea
Danazol
Synthetic androgen; gonadotropin inhibitor
Why we use it
Endometriosis; Fibrocystic breast disease
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy (category X), breastfeeding, undiagnosed genital bleeding, liver, kidney, or heart disease, thromboembolic disease, porphyria
Watch for
  • Androgenic effects: acne, oily skin, hirsutism, deepened voice (may be permanent), decreased breast size
  • Weight gain, edema, hot flashes, amenorrhea or irregular menses
Levonorgestrel (Plan B)
Progestin; emergency contraceptive
Why we use it
Emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure
Who can NOT have it
Known pregnancy, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, hypersensitivity
Watch for
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness
  • Irregular bleeding
  • next period early or late
Conjugated estrogens (Premarin)
Estrogen; hormone replacement
Why we use it
  • Menopause hot flashes, vulvovaginal atrophy
  • Hypoestrogenism (ovarian failure), prevention of osteoporosis, abnormal uterine bleeding
Who can NOT have it
Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, breast or endometrial cancer, history of DVT, PE, stroke, MI, liver disease, pregnancy
Watch for
  • Boxed warning: endometrial cancer (unopposed), stroke, MI, DVT, PE, breast cancer, probable dementia
  • Nausea, headache, breast tenderness, fluid retention, hypertension
Magnesium sulfate
Anticonvulsant; CNS depressant; electrolyte; tocolytic
Why we use it
  • Prevent and treat seizures in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia
  • Short-term tocolysis in preterm labor, fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks, hypomagnesemia
Who can NOT have it
Heart block, myocardial damage, myasthenia gravis, hypermagnesemia, hypersensitivity
Watch for
  • Toxicity: loss of deep tendon reflexes (first sign, about 10 mEq/L), RR under 12 (resp. depression 12 to 15), urine output under 30 mL/hr, hypotension, bradycardia, pulmonary edema, cardiac arrest (about 30)
  • Therapeutic level 4 to 7 mEq/L (4.8 to 8.4 mg/dL)
Terbutaline
Beta2 adrenergic agonist; bronchodilator; tocolytic
Why we use it
  • Short-term tocolysis in preterm labor (off label, not over 48 to 72 hr)
  • Uterine tachysystole with fetal distress
  • asthma and bronchospasm
Who can NOT have it
Tachydysrhythmias, heart disease, chorioamnionitis, severe preeclampsia, hemorrhage, hypersensitivity
Watch for
  • Maternal tachycardia (HR over 120), palpitations, chest pain, dysrhythmias, tremor, nervousness, hypotension
  • Hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, pulmonary edema
Methylergonovine maleate (Methergine)
Ergot alkaloid; uterotonic
Why we use it
Prevent and treat postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony or subinvolution (after placenta delivery)
Who can NOT have it
Hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, cardiovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, sepsis, hypersensitivity, before placenta delivery
Watch for
Hypertension (can be severe), headache, nausea, vomiting, cramping; Chest pain, bradycardia, tinnitus, dizziness
Nitrous oxide
Inhaled analgesic and anxiolytic gas
Why we use it
Pain and anxiety relief in labor; Perineal repair and minor procedures
Who can NOT have it
Impaired consciousness, pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, middle ear disease, vitamin B12 deficiency
Watch for
Dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, disorientation, euphoria; Diffusion hypoxia if oxygen not given after use
Oxytocin (Pitocin)
Oxytocic hormone; uterotonic
Why we use it
Induce or augment labor; Control postpartum hemorrhage after placenta delivery
Who can NOT have it
Cephalopelvic disproportion, placenta previa, vasa previa, prior classical uterine incision, active genital herpes, cord prolapse, nonreassuring FHR, malpresentation
Watch for
  • Tachysystole (over 5 contractions in 10 min or lasting over 90 sec), uterine rupture, abruptio placentae
  • Nonreassuring FHR, fetal bradycardia
Cervidil (Dinoprostone)
Prostaglandin E2; cervical ripening agent
Why we use it
Cervical ripening before labor induction at or near term
Who can NOT have it
Fetal distress, unexplained vaginal bleeding, placenta previa, prior cesarean or uterine surgery, cephalopelvic disproportion, active herpes, hypersensitivity, already on oxytocin
Watch for
Uterine tachysystole and hyperstimulation; Nonreassuring FHR, uterine rupture
Bupivacaine
Amide local anesthetic
Why we use it
Epidural and spinal anesthesia for labor and cesarean; Local infiltration for perineal repair
Who can NOT have it
Allergy to amide anesthetics, infection at site, coagulopathy or platelets under 100,000, hypovolemia, sepsis, increased ICP
Watch for
  • Maternal hypotension (most common), bradycardia, urinary retention
  • Spinal headache, fever, itching, nausea, prolonged second stage
Carboprost tromethamine (Hemabate)
Prostaglandin F2 alpha analog; uterotonic
Why we use it
Postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony not controlled by oxytocin or methylergonovine; Second trimester abortion
Who can NOT have it
Asthma, active heart, lung, kidney, or liver disease, acute pelvic inflammatory disease, hypersensitivity
Watch for
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chills, flushing, headache; Bronchospasm and wheezing
Cytotec (Misoprostol)
Prostaglandin E1 analog
Why we use it
  • Off label: cervical ripening and induction, postpartum hemorrhage, miscarriage or abortion
  • Approved: prevent NSAID gastric ulcers
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy when used for ulcers, prior cesarean or uterine scar, fetal distress, placenta previa, unexplained bleeding, cephalopelvic disproportion, hypersensitivity
Watch for
  • Tachysystole, hyperstimulation, uterine rupture, abnormal FHR
  • Fever, chills, shivering, diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache
Nifedipine (Procardia)
Calcium channel blocker; tocolytic; antihypertensive
Why we use it
Short-term tocolysis in preterm labor (off label); Hypertension including severe hypertension in pregnancy
Who can NOT have it
Hypotension, cardiogenic shock, aortic stenosis, hypersensitivity
Watch for
Hypotension, reflex tachycardia, headache, flushing, dizziness, palpitations; Peripheral edema, nausea, constipation
Calcium gluconate
Antidote
Why we use it
Reverses magnesium sulfate toxicity
Who can NOT have it
Caution with digoxin (➕)
Watch for
Give slowly IV. Keep at the bedside
Labetalol (Trandate)
Alpha and beta blocker
Why we use it
Severe hypertension (160 systolic or 110 diastolic or higher)
Who can NOT have it
Asthma, heart block, bradycardia (➕)
Watch for
Low heart rate and BP. Check both before each dose
Hydralazine (Apresoline)
Vasodilator
Why we use it
Severe hypertension, IV
Who can NOT have it
Coronary artery disease (➕)
Watch for
Hypotension, reflex tachycardia, headache (➕)
Betamethasone (Celestone)
Corticosteroid
Why we use it
Fetal lung maturity before preterm birth, 2 IM doses 24 hours apart
Who can NOT have it
Use caution with maternal infection (➕)
Watch for
Maternal hyperglycemia, so check glucose in diabetes (➕)
RhoGAM
Rho(D) immune globulin
Why we use it
Prevent Rh sensitization in an Rh-negative mother
Who can NOT have it
  • Rh-positive mother
  • Rh-negative baby
  • Already sensitized (positive Coombs)
Watch for
IM only. Injection site soreness (➕)
Methotrexate
Antimetabolite
Why we use it
Unruptured ectopic pregnancy
Who can NOT have it
  • Folic acid (blocks it), alcohol, sun
  • Not with a ruptured or unstable ectopic (➕)
Watch for
Hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity, nausea. Avoid pregnancy 3 months
Ursodiol (UDCA)
Bile acid
Why we use it
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
Who can NOT have it
Complete biliary obstruction (➕)
Watch for
  • Check bile acids and liver function
  • Postpartum liver check about 6 weeks
Insulin
Why we use it
First line for gestational and pregestational diabetes
Who can NOT have it
Hypoglycemia is the risk
Watch for
Hypoglycemia. Glyburide and metformin are second line
Penicillin G
Antibiotic
Why we use it
Group B strep prophylaxis, at least 2 doses before birth
Who can NOT have it
  • Penicillin allergy
  • Then cefazolin, clindamycin, or vancomycin by reaction
Watch for
Allergic reaction, anaphylaxis
Heparin
Anticoagulant
Why we use it
Postpartum DVT
Who can NOT have it
Active bleeding, low platelets (➕)
Watch for
Bleeding, low platelets. Antidote protamine sulfate (➕)
Warfarin
Anticoagulant
Why we use it
Clots, mechanical heart valves
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy, unless she has a mechanical valve
Watch for
Teratogenic (nasal and bone defects), bleeding. Safe in breastfeeding
Tranexamic acid (TXA)
Why we use it
PPH adjunct, 1 g IV over 10 minutes (➕)
Who can NOT have it
Active clotting disease (➕)
Watch for
Clots, nausea (➕)
Ibuprofen (Motrin, Advil)
NSAID
Why we use it
First line postpartum pain and cramps
Who can NOT have it
NSAID allergy, GI bleeding, kidney disease (➕)
Watch for
Stomach upset. Give with food (➕)
Acetaminophen (Tylenol)
Why we use it
First line postpartum pain and fever
Who can NOT have it
Severe liver disease (➕)
Watch for
Liver injury if the daily limit is exceeded (➕)
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco)
Opioid combination
Why we use it
Severe laceration, hemorrhoid, or cesarean pain
Who can NOT have it
Respiratory depression risk. Use caution with sedatives (➕)
Watch for
Sedation, constipation, respiratory depression (➕)
Morphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, fentanyl
Opioids
Why we use it
Labor pain, early labor only
Who can NOT have it
Close to birth, because they cross the placenta
Watch for
Respiratory depression in mother and newborn. Naloxone ready
Naloxone (Narcan)
Opioid reversal
Why we use it
Reverse opioid respiratory depression
Who can NOT have it
Opioid dependence can trigger withdrawal (➕)
Watch for
Effects can wear off before the opioid does, so watch again (➕)
Lidocaine
Local anesthetic
Why we use it
Numb tissue for episiotomy and laceration repair
Who can NOT have it
Allergy to amide anesthetics (➕)
Watch for
Toxicity if absorbed into the blood (➕)
Combined oral contraceptive (the pill)
Estrogen plus progestin
Why we use it
Prevent pregnancy, regulate periods
Who can NOT have it
Smoking over 35, clots, migraine with aura, hypertension, breast cancer, liver disease, BREASTFEEDING
Watch for
Clots (ACHES warning signs). Lower milk supply
Progestin-only pill (minipill)
Why we use it
Prevent pregnancy, safe while breastfeeding
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy, breast cancer, undiagnosed bleeding (➕)
Watch for
Irregular bleeding. Take at the same time every day
Folic acid
Why we use it
Prevent neural tube defects, start before conception
Who can NOT have it
None for the standard dose. Methotrexate is blocked by it
Watch for
Prior neural tube defect needs a higher dose
Clomiphene (Clomid)
Why we use it
Ovulation induction for infertility
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy, liver disease (➕)
Watch for
Hot flashes, multiple births
Isotretinoin (Accutane), ACE inhibitors, ARBs
Why we use it
Acne, hypertension
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy. iPLEDGE needs two forms of birth control for isotretinoin
Watch for
Teratogenic
MMR and varicella vaccines
Live vaccines
Why we use it
Immunity to measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella
Who can NOT have it
Pregnancy. Give before conception or after birth
Watch for
Avoid pregnancy 4 weeks after MMR
Tdap, influenza (inactivated)
Why we use it
Protect mother and baby
Who can NOT have it
Safe in pregnancy
Watch for
Tdap with each pregnancy

The four things she asks: what the drug is, why we use it, who cannot use it, and what the nurse watches for. Items marked ➕ are added from standard sources.

💊 Week 1: contraception, drug by drug (your slides plus ATI Ch 1)

MethodDetails
Combined oral contraceptive (the pill)
Brands
Yaz, Yasmin, Ortho Tri-Cyclen, Loestrin, Lo Loestrin Fe, Seasonique, Seasonale
Generic
Ethinyl estradiol plus a progestin (norethindrone, levonorgestrel, norgestimate, drospirenone)
Use and key points
  • 1 tablet daily, usually 21 active plus 7 placebo
  • Avoid with smoking over 35, clots, migraine with aura, hypertension, breast cancer, liver disease, and while BREASTFEEDING (estrogen can lower milk supply)
  • ACHES: Abdominal pain, Chest pain, Headache, Eye problems, Severe leg pain
Progestin-only pill (minipill)
Brands
Camila, Errin, Heather, Ortho Micronor, Slynd
Generic
Norethindrone 0.35 mg or drospirenone 4 mg
Use and key points
  • Same time every day
  • Norethindrone within 3 hours, Slynd within 24 hours
  • The pill to use while breastfeeding (no estrogen)
Patch
Brands
Xulane, Twirla
Generic
Norelgestromin plus ethinyl estradiol, or levonorgestrel plus ethinyl estradiol
Use and key points
  • Weekly for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week
  • Estrogen, so avoid while breastfeeding
  • Less effective at higher weight
Vaginal ring
Brands
NuvaRing, Annovera
Generic
Etonogestrel plus ethinyl estradiol, or segesterone acetate plus ethinyl estradiol
Use and key points
  • In 3 weeks, out 1
  • Estrogen, so avoid while breastfeeding
  • Annovera is reused for 1 year
Injection (the shot)
Brands
Depo-Provera CI, depo-subQ provera 104
Generic
Medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA)
Use and key points
  • Every 11 to 13 weeks (subQ every 12 to 14)
  • Bone loss so calcium and vitamin D
  • Delayed return of fertility
Implant
Brands
Nexplanon (replaced Implanon)
Generic
Etonogestrel 68 mg rod
Use and key points
Upper inner arm, lasts 3 years. Irregular bleeding is common
Hormonal IUD
Brands
Mirena, Liletta (up to 8 years), Kyleena (5 years)
Generic
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system
Use and key points
  • PAINS: Period late, Abdominal pain, Infection signs, Not feeling well, String problems
  • Lighter periods
Copper IUD
Brands
ParaGard
Generic
Copper T 380A, no hormone
Use and key points
  • Up to 10 years
  • Heavier cramping and bleeding
  • Most effective emergency contraception (within 5 days)

💊 Week 1: pregnancy drugs, vitamins, vaccines, and teratogens

DrugKnow
Folic acid (vitamin B9)
  • 400 to 800 mcg daily, starting BEFORE conception
  • Prevents neural tube defects
  • Prior neural tube defect needs a higher dose
Iron
  • 27 mg ferrous iron daily
  • Take with vitamin C
  • Constipation and dark stool are common
Vitamin D
  • 600 IU
  • Low levels link to preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, and newborn rickets
High-dose vitamin ATeratogenic (thymic and cardiac anomalies)
TdapWith EACH pregnancy (passes pertussis protection to the baby)
Influenza (inactivated)Yes in pregnancy
MMR and varicella (live vaccines)
  • NOT in pregnancy
  • Give MMR at least 1 month and varicella at least 3 months before conception, or after birth
Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM)28 weeks if Rh-negative, and after amniocentesis, CVS, or PUBS
Hepatitis B vaccine and immune globulin
  • Newborn gets the vaccine
  • Immune globulin too if the mother is positive
Betamethasone (antenatal corticosteroid)Speeds fetal surfactant production when early birth is expected
Indomethacin
  • Can close a patent ductus arteriosus
  • Prostaglandin E1 keeps it open in some heart defects
Ampicillin (IV)Treats listeriosis
Vitamin B6, ginger
  • Natural remedies for early nausea
  • Natural does not mean safe, so tell the provider
Vitamin E, garlic, aspirinAll have anticoagulant effects together
TeratogensAlcohol, ACE inhibitors, anticonvulsants, cocaine, warfarin (nasal and bone defects, bleeding), lithium (heart defects), isotretinoin, high-dose vitamin A, and the TORCH infections

🤱 Birth control while breastfeeding: estrogen free or nonhormonal only

ChoiceMethodsWhy
OK: estrogen free hormonalDepo-Provera shot, implant (Nexplanon), progestin-only pill (minipill), hormonal IUDProgestin only. No estrogen, so milk supply is protected
OK: nonhormonalCopper IUD (ParaGard), condoms, diaphragm, cap, sponge, spermicide, lactational amenorrhea methodNo hormones at all
AVOID: contains estrogenCombined oral contraceptive, patch, vaginal ringEstrogen can lower milk supply

Quick rule: while breastfeeding, pick estrogen free or nonhormonal. The shot, implant, and minipill are the three to know.

💊 Week 2: labor pain relief drugs

Drug or typeKnow
Opioids: morphine, butorphanol (Stadol), nalbuphine (Nubain), fentanyl (Sublimaze)
  • IM or IV, EARLY labor only
  • Too close to birth causes neonatal respiratory depression because they cross the placenta
  • Opioid use disorder may need higher doses
Naloxone (Narcan)Opioid reversal drug. Keep it available for the newborn
Nitrous oxideInhaled gas the client self-administers by mask during contractions (full card below)
Epidural: fentanyl or sufentanil with local anesthetic
  • Epidural space with a catheter and repeat doses, usually around 5 cm
  • Hypotension and respiratory depression are the big concerns
  • Avoid supine
  • Can lengthen the second stage
Spinal blockSubarachnoid space, single fast dose, mainly cesarean
Pudendal blockTransvaginal injection that numbs the perineum for the second stage and birth
Lidocaine (local)Episiotomy and laceration repair
General anesthesiaEmergency cesarean when there is no time for a spinal
Contraindications to regional anesthesiaSpinal surgery or abnormalities, coagulation defects, hypovolemia

💊 Week 2: postpartum medications and comfort products

Drug or productKnow
Oxytocin (Pitocin)First line for PPH (full card below)
Methergine, Hemabate, CytotecSecond line uterotonics (full cards below)
Ibuprofen (Motrin, Advil)First-line postpartum pain medicine, also helps cramps
Acetaminophen (Tylenol)First-line postpartum pain medicine
Hydrocodone and acetaminophen (Norco)
  • Stronger
  • For severe lacerations, hemorrhoids, or cesarean
  • Cesarean may also get morphine
Dermoplast sprayTopical pain spray for the perineum
Tucks pads, witch hazelPerineal and hemorrhoid comfort. Also sitz baths
Stool softeners, fiber, fluidsFor constipation and fear of a bowel movement after lacerations or hemorrhoids
Lanolin cream
  • Cracked, sore nipples
  • Also check the latch and air dry expressed milk
Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM)
  • Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive baby, Coombs negative
  • Usually within 72 hours
  • A client who is Rh-positive does not need it
MMRIf not rubella immune. Avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks afterward
Tdap, flu, COVIDKeep current to protect the baby. Tdap is mainly for pertussis
Prenatal vitamins and iron
  • Prenatal vitamins at least 6 weeks postpartum
  • Iron may be needed after blood loss

⚖️ Look-alikes and head-to-heads

PairThe difference
Magnesium sulfate vs calcium gluconate
  • Magnesium prevents seizures
  • Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity
Methergine vs Hemabate
  • Methergine: avoid in hypertension
  • Hemabate: avoid in asthma
  • Both are second line
  • Oxytocin is first line
Cervidil vs Cytotec
  • Both ripen the cervix
  • Cervidil is a vaginal insert with a string (E2)
  • Cytotec is a tablet (E1) that also treats PPH and miscarriage
  • Neither with a prior cesarean scar
Terbutaline vs nifedipine
  • Both are tocolytics
  • Terbutaline raises maternal HR (hold above 120)
  • Nifedipine drops BP (careful with magnesium)
Oxytocin vs Cervidil
  • Never together
  • Wait 30 minutes after removing Cervidil before starting oxytocin
Hemabate vs terbutaline
  • Hemabate can cause bronchospasm
  • Terbutaline relaxes the bronchi and the uterus
Depo-Provera vs Plan B
  • Depo is an ongoing injection every 11 to 13 weeks
  • Plan B is a one time pill within 72 hours
  • Neither protects against STIs
Premarin vs Depo-Provera
  • Premarin is an estrogen with a boxed warning for cancer, stroke, MI, and clots
  • Depo is a progestin with a boxed warning for bone loss
Epidural vs nitrous oxide
  • Bupivacaine epidural: needs anesthesia provider and fluid preload, hypotension is the problem
  • Nitrous: client holds the mask herself, no IV needed

🚫 Avoid it, and what to give instead

Client hasAVOIDSafer choices
Hypertension or preeclampsiaMethylergonovine (Methergine)Oxytocin (Pitocin), carboprost (Hemabate), misoprostol (Cytotec)
AsthmaCarboprost (Hemabate)Oxytocin (Pitocin), methylergonovine (Methergine), misoprostol (Cytotec)
Prior cesarean or uterine scarCervidil, Cytotec for ripeningMechanical ripening such as a balloon, or repeat cesarean as ordered
Already on oxytocinCervidilStop and wait 30 minutes after any Cervidil removal before oxytocin
Heart block or myasthenia gravisMagnesium sulfateAnother anticonvulsant as ordered by the provider
Tachydysrhythmia or heart diseaseTerbutalineNifedipine or another tocolytic as ordered
Low blood pressureNifedipineAnother tocolytic as ordered

The avoid side is from the cards. The safer choices are ➕ added so both sides are on the page.

💊 Medroxyprogesterone (DepoProvera) (Week 1)

TopicKnow
ClassProgestin; hormonal contraceptive
Why it works
  • Suppresses ovulation by inhibiting FSH and LH
  • Thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium so implantation is unlikely
Used for
  • Contraception
  • Endometriosis pain, abnormal uterine bleeding, secondary amenorrhea, prevents endometrial hyperplasia with estrogen therapy
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • 150 mg IM every 11 to 13 weeks (deltoid or gluteal); subQ form every 12 to 14 weeks
  • Do not massage site
  • Give in first 5 days of cycle after negative pregnancy test
  • Onset: within 24 hr if given in first 5 days of cycle
  • Peak: about 3 weeks
  • Duration: 3 months
Watch for
  • Bone mineral density loss (boxed warning, risk rises with use over 2 years)
  • Irregular bleeding or spotting early, then amenorrhea
  • Weight gain, headache, depression, breast tenderness, injection site reaction
  • Thromboembolism (DVT, PE, stroke); delayed return of fertility (up to 10 months)
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: pregnancy, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, breast cancer, liver disease, history of thromboembolism or stroke
  • Precautions: osteoporosis risk, depression, diabetes, hypertension, smoking
  • Does not protect against STIs
Interactions
  • CYP450 inducers decrease effectiveness: rifampin, St. John's wort, carbamazepine, phenytoin, some HIV drugs
  • Aminoglutethimide decreases levels
  • Use backup contraception with these drugs
Nurse does
  • Confirm negative pregnancy test before first dose
  • Obtain BP, weight, history of clots
  • Give deep IM, do not massage
  • Document date, schedule next dose
  • Assess calcium intake, mood, bleeding pattern
Teach
  • Return every 11 to 13 weeks
  • Use condoms for STI protection
  • Calcium, vitamin D, weight bearing exercise
  • Irregular bleeding is common at first
  • Report chest pain, leg swelling, severe headache, severe abdominal pain, depression
  • Do not smoke
It is working when
  • Pregnancy is prevented
  • Pain and bleeding decrease when used for endometriosis or abnormal bleeding
  • Client keeps injection schedule
  • No adverse effects; bone health monitored
➕ Added
  • Your slides say every 11 to 13 weeks (subQ form every 12 to 14)
  • The ATI card says 12 to 13
  • Use 11 to 13

💊 Danazol (Week 1)

TopicKnow
ClassSynthetic androgen; gonadotropin inhibitor
Why it works
  • Suppresses pituitary release of FSH and LH, lowering estrogen
  • Causes atrophy of endometrial tissue; has androgenic effects
Used for
  • Endometriosis
  • Fibrocystic breast disease
  • Hereditary angioedema
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • Oral capsule, 100 to 800 mg daily in 2 divided doses
  • Start during menses
  • Endometriosis course is 3 to 6 months
  • Onset: gradual, weeks
  • Peak: 2 to 8 hr after dose
  • Duration: given daily
Watch for
  • Androgenic effects: acne, oily skin, hirsutism, deepened voice (may be permanent), decreased breast size
  • Weight gain, edema, hot flashes, amenorrhea or irregular menses
  • Hepatotoxicity (jaundice), thromboembolism (boxed warning), intracranial hypertension
  • Teratogenic: virilization of a female fetus
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: pregnancy (category X), breastfeeding, undiagnosed genital bleeding, liver, kidney, or heart disease, thromboembolic disease, porphyria
  • Precautions: migraine, epilepsy, diabetes
  • Not for use with hormonal contraceptives
Interactions
  • Warfarin: increased bleeding risk, monitor INR
  • Carbamazepine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus: levels increase
  • Statins: myopathy risk
  • Insulin and oral hypoglycemics: glucose needs change
Nurse does
  • Confirm negative pregnancy test before starting
  • Monitor liver function, BP, weight, edema, glucose
  • Assess for DVT (calf pain, swelling)
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin
  • Assess for virilizing effects
Teach
  • Use nonhormonal contraception (condoms)
  • Report jaundice, dark urine, severe headache, vision changes, calf pain
  • Voice changes may be permanent
  • Expect missed periods
  • Report acne, hair growth
It is working when
  • Decreased pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea
  • Smaller endometrial implants
  • Fewer angioedema attacks
  • Decreased breast pain and nodularity
  • Liver function normal

💊 Levonorgestrel (Plan B) (Week 1)

TopicKnow
ClassProgestin; emergency contraceptive
Why it works
  • Prevents or delays ovulation, thickens cervical mucus, blocks sperm transport
  • Does not end an existing pregnancy
Used for
  • Emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • 1.5 mg PO single dose as soon as possible, within 72 hr (3 days); may work up to 120 hr with less effect
  • With or without food
  • Onset: within hours
  • Peak: about 2 hr
  • Duration: single dose covers that episode only
Watch for
  • Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, dizziness, breast tenderness
  • Irregular bleeding; next period early or late
  • Ectopic pregnancy risk if it fails
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: known pregnancy, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, hypersensitivity
  • Precautions: less effective with BMI over 30, history of ectopic pregnancy
  • Does not protect against STIs
Interactions
  • Rifampin, St. John's wort, barbiturates, carbamazepine, phenytoin, some HIV drugs lower effectiveness
  • Ulipristal: do not combine
Nurse does
  • Ask date of last period and time of intercourse
  • Pregnancy test if indicated
  • Assess history of ectopic pregnancy
  • If vomiting within 2 hr, notify provider (repeat dose)
  • Screen for STIs, assault; give nonjudgmental care
Teach
  • Take as soon as possible
  • Not an abortion pill; not for regular birth control
  • Use condoms for STI protection
  • Period may come early or late
  • Test if period is over 1 week late
  • Severe lower abdominal pain 3 to 5 weeks later: seek care
It is working when
  • Menses returns on time or within 1 week
  • Negative pregnancy test
  • Client plans ongoing contraception

💊 Conjugated estrogens (Premarin) (Week 1)

TopicKnow
ClassEstrogen; hormone replacement
Why it works
  • Replaces estrogen; relieves vasomotor symptoms and vaginal atrophy
  • Decreases bone resorption
Used for
  • Menopause hot flashes, vulvovaginal atrophy
  • Hypoestrogenism (ovarian failure), prevention of osteoporosis, abnormal uterine bleeding
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • PO 0.3 to 1.25 mg daily (often 3 weeks on, 1 week off)
  • IV or IM 25 mg for abnormal uterine bleeding
  • Lowest dose for shortest time; add progestin if uterus intact
  • Onset: PO relief takes weeks
  • Peak: PO 4 to 10 hr
  • Duration: daily dosing
Watch for
  • Boxed warning: endometrial cancer (unopposed), stroke, MI, DVT, PE, breast cancer, probable dementia
  • Nausea, headache, breast tenderness, fluid retention, hypertension
  • Gallbladder disease, hypercalcemia, breakthrough bleeding
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, breast or endometrial cancer, history of DVT, PE, stroke, MI, liver disease, pregnancy
  • Precautions: hypertension, gallbladder disease, migraine, smoking, diabetes
Interactions
  • Warfarin: decreased effect, monitor INR
  • Rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort lower estrogen effect
  • Grapefruit juice raises levels
  • May raise levothyroxine needs
Nurse does
  • Baseline BP, weight, breast exam, mammogram, Pap
  • Assess clot history
  • Monitor liver function, lipids, glucose, calcium
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin
  • Hold before major surgery per provider
Teach
  • Do not smoke
  • Report abnormal bleeding, calf pain, chest pain, SOB, severe headache, vision changes, breast lumps
  • Monthly breast self-exam, yearly mammogram
  • Calcium, vitamin D, exercise
  • Take at same time daily
It is working when
  • Fewer and milder hot flashes
  • Vaginal dryness relieved
  • Bone density maintained
  • Abnormal bleeding controlled
  • No adverse effects

💊 Magnesium sulfate (Week 2)

TopicKnow
ClassAnticonvulsant; CNS depressant; electrolyte; tocolytic
🎤 Her emphasis
  • Prevents seizures
  • It is a CNS depressant and does NOT lower the BP
  • Flushing and sweating are expected
  • Lethargy, slow breathing, absent reflexes, and dysrhythmias mean toxicity
  • Antidote: calcium gluconate at the bedside
Why it works
  • CNS depressant that decreases acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
  • Relaxes smooth muscle and raises seizure threshold
Used for
  • Prevent and treat seizures in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia
  • Short-term tocolysis in preterm labor, fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks, hypomagnesemia
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • IV loading dose 4 to 6 g over 15 to 30 min, then 1 to 2 g/hr by pump
  • Give as secondary (piggyback) infusion
  • Onset: IV immediate; IM 1 hr
  • Peak: end of IV infusion
  • Duration: IV about 30 min; IM 3 to 4 hr
Watch for
  • Toxicity: loss of deep tendon reflexes (first sign, about 10 mEq/L), RR under 12 (resp. depression 12 to 15), urine output under 30 mL/hr, hypotension, bradycardia, pulmonary edema, cardiac arrest (about 30)
  • Therapeutic level 4 to 7 mEq/L (4.8 to 8.4 mg/dL)
  • Flushing, sweating, drowsiness, blurred vision; newborn hypotonia and respiratory depression
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: heart block, myocardial damage, myasthenia gravis, hypermagnesemia, hypersensitivity
  • Precautions: renal impairment (excreted by kidneys), imminent delivery, hypocalcemia
Interactions
  • Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine): hypotension, neuromuscular blockade
  • Opioids, barbiturates, anesthetics: added CNS depression
  • Neuromuscular blockers, aminoglycosides, digoxin
  • Antidote: calcium gluconate
Nurse does
  • Check DTRs, RR, urine output (hourly), BP, HR, LOC, lung sounds
  • Foley catheter, monitor intake and output
  • Keep calcium gluconate at bedside
  • Seizure precautions; continuous fetal monitoring
  • Check magnesium level
Teach
  • Warmth, flushing, sweating, drowsiness, blurred vision, nausea are expected
  • Stay in bed, side rails up
  • Frequent checks are needed
  • Report SOB, chest pain, weakness
  • Often continued 24 hr after birth
It is working when
  • No seizures
  • BP lower, no hyperreflexia or clonus
  • Magnesium level therapeutic
  • Contractions stop in preterm labor
  • No signs of toxicity
➕ Added
  • Check reflexes, respirations (12 or more), and urine output (30 mL/hr or more) before and during the infusion
  • Continue about 24 hours after birth

💊 Terbutaline (Week 2)

TopicKnow
ClassBeta2 adrenergic agonist; bronchodilator; tocolytic
Why it works
  • Stimulates beta2 receptors, relaxing uterine and bronchial smooth muscle
  • Decreases uterine contractions
Used for
  • Short-term tocolysis in preterm labor (off label, not over 48 to 72 hr)
  • Uterine tachysystole with fetal distress; asthma and bronchospasm
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • SubQ 0.25 mg, may repeat in 15 to 30 min, max 0.5 mg in 4 hr
  • Hold and notify if maternal HR over 120
  • Onset: subQ 5 to 15 min
  • Peak: 30 to 60 min
  • Duration: 1.5 to 4 hr
Watch for
  • Maternal tachycardia (HR over 120), palpitations, chest pain, dysrhythmias, tremor, nervousness, hypotension
  • Hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, pulmonary edema
  • Fetal tachycardia, neonatal hypoglycemia
  • Boxed warning: prolonged tocolysis can cause maternal death
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: tachydysrhythmias, heart disease, chorioamnionitis, severe preeclampsia, hemorrhage, hypersensitivity
  • Precautions: diabetes, hypertension, hyperthyroidism, hypokalemia, seizure disorders
Interactions
  • Beta blockers block the effect
  • MAOIs, tricyclics, other sympathomimetics: more cardiac effects
  • Diuretics, corticosteroids: hypokalemia
  • Corticosteroids with tocolytics: pulmonary edema
  • Digoxin
Nurse does
  • Monitor maternal HR, BP, RR, lung sounds, chest pain
  • Monitor glucose and potassium
  • Continuous fetal monitoring and contractions
  • Keep left side lying
  • Track intake and output
Teach
  • Tremor, nervousness, palpitations, headache are expected
  • Report chest pain, SOB, racing heart
  • Rest on left side
  • Report contractions or leaking fluid
It is working when
  • Contractions decrease or stop
  • Preterm birth delayed so steroids can work
  • HR under 120
  • No maternal or fetal adverse effects
  • Bronchospasm relieved
➕ Added
  • Also the drug given for tachysystole with a nonreassuring tracing
  • Check maternal HR first and hold above 120

💊 Methylergonovine maleate (Methergine) (Week 2)

TopicKnow
ClassErgot alkaloid; uterotonic
🎤 Her emphasis
  • Second line for PPH
  • Big contraindication: uncontrolled hypertension (and preeclampsia)
Why it works
  • Directly stimulates uterine smooth muscle for strong, sustained contractions
  • Constricts uterine vessels, reducing bleeding
Used for
  • Prevent and treat postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony or subinvolution (after placenta delivery)
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • IM 0.2 mg every 2 to 4 hr, up to 5 doses
  • IV 0.2 mg slowly over 60 sec, emergency only
  • PO 0.2 mg 3 to 4 times daily, up to 7 days
  • Onset: IM 2 to 5 min; IV immediate; PO 5 to 10 min
  • Peak: PO 1 to 3 hr
  • Duration: IM 3 hr; IV 45 min; PO 3 hr
  • Store refrigerated, protect from light
Watch for
  • Hypertension (can be severe), headache, nausea, vomiting, cramping
  • Chest pain, bradycardia, tinnitus, dizziness
  • Vasospasm, stroke, seizures
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: hypertension, preeclampsia, eclampsia, cardiovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, sepsis, hypersensitivity, before placenta delivery
  • Not for labor induction
  • Precautions: liver or kidney disease
Interactions
  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (protease inhibitors, macrolides, azole antifungals): vasospasm
  • Triptans, other ergots, vasopressors, epinephrine
  • Smoking increases vasoconstriction
Nurse does
  • Check BP and HR before each dose; hold and notify if hypertensive
  • Assess fundus (firm, midline), lochia amount
  • Massage a boggy fundus
  • Check Hgb and Hct
  • Assess pain and cramping
Teach
  • Cramping is expected
  • Report severe headache, chest pain, SOB, vision changes, cold or numb extremities, heavy bleeding
  • Do not smoke
  • Take as scheduled
It is working when
  • Fundus firm at midline
  • Lochia decreases
  • BP and HR stable
  • No hemorrhage
  • Hgb stable

💊 Nitrous oxide (Week 2)

TopicKnow
ClassInhaled analgesic and anxiolytic gas
Why it works
  • Inhaled CNS depressant that produces analgesia, anxiety relief, and mild sedation
  • Usually mixed 50% nitrous oxide with 50% oxygen
Used for
  • Pain and anxiety relief in labor
  • Perineal repair and minor procedures
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • Client self-administers by holding the mask or mouthpiece
  • Start inhaling 30 sec before contraction, stop between contractions
  • Use scavenging system
  • Onset: 30 to 60 sec
  • Peak: about 5 min
  • Duration: wears off within 5 min of stopping
Watch for
  • Dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, disorientation, euphoria
  • Diffusion hypoxia if oxygen not given after use
  • Long term exposure: vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Does not slow labor progress
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: impaired consciousness, pneumothorax, bowel obstruction, middle ear disease, vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Precautions: COPD, head injury, claustrophobia
  • Client must be able to hold the mask
Interactions
  • Opioids and sedatives: more CNS and respiratory depression
  • Methotrexate: increased toxicity
  • Other inhaled anesthetics
Nurse does
  • Stay with client, monitor sedation, SpO2, RR, BP
  • Client holds mask herself
  • Fall precautions
  • Ensure room ventilation
  • Continuous fetal monitoring
Teach
  • Breathe deeply 30 sec before the contraction
  • Hold the mask yourself; stop if drowsy
  • May feel dizzy, tingly, nauseated
  • Lowers pain, does not remove it
  • Stay in bed, call for help
It is working when
  • Pain score lower
  • Anxiety decreased
  • Client alert and cooperative
  • SpO2 stable
  • No adverse effects
➕ AddedNeeds no IV, does not slow labor, and the client controls it herself.

💊 Oxytocin (Pitocin) (Week 2)

TopicKnow
ClassOxytocic hormone; uterotonic
🎤 Her emphasis
  • High alert medication, IV, titrated up and down by response
  • First line for PPH
  • Watch for tachysystole and uterine rupture
Why it works
  • Stimulates rhythmic uterine contractions
  • Triggers milk let-down
Used for
  • Induce or augment labor
  • Control postpartum hemorrhage after placenta delivery
  • Complete an incomplete abortion
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • Dilute IV, secondary infusion by pump, titrate per protocol
  • Labor: start 0.5 to 2 mU/min, increase 1 to 2 mU/min every 30 to 60 min
  • Postpartum: 10 to 40 units IV in 1000 mL or 10 units IM
  • Onset: IV within 1 min; IM 3 to 5 min
  • Peak: steady state about 40 min
  • Duration: IV 1 hr; IM 2 to 3 hr
Watch for
  • Tachysystole (over 5 contractions in 10 min or lasting over 90 sec), uterine rupture, abruptio placentae
  • Nonreassuring FHR, fetal bradycardia
  • Water intoxication (headache, confusion, seizures)
  • Hypotension with rapid IV push; PPH from atony after birth
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: cephalopelvic disproportion, placenta previa, vasa previa, prior classical uterine incision, active genital herpes, cord prolapse, nonreassuring FHR, malpresentation
  • Precautions: grand multiparity, history of PPH
Interactions
  • Other prostaglandins or oxytocics: hyperstimulation
  • Vasopressors: severe hypertension
  • Wait 30 min after Cervidil removal, 4 hr after misoprostol
Nurse does
  • Continuous fetal and uterine monitoring
  • For tachysystole or nonreassuring FHR: stop infusion, side lying, O2, IV fluid, notify provider
  • Monitor BP, HR, intake and output
  • Watch for water intoxication
  • After birth, check fundus and lochia
Teach
  • Contractions will be strong and monitored continuously
  • Bed rest with monitoring
  • Discuss pain relief
  • Report constant pain without relaxation, SOB, severe headache
  • Afterbirth cramping is expected
It is working when
  • Contractions every 2 to 3 min lasting 40 to 60 sec
  • Cervix dilates and effaces
  • FHR reassuring
  • Fundus firm, bleeding controlled
  • No tachysystole or water intoxication

💊 Cervidil (Dinoprostone) (Week 3)

TopicKnow
ClassProstaglandin E2; cervical ripening agent
🎤 Her emphasis
  • Ripening drug with a retrieval string
  • Cervidil and Cytotec are the classic ripening drugs
Why it works
  • Softens and dilates the cervix by breaking down collagen
  • Stimulates uterine contractions
Used for
  • Cervical ripening before labor induction at or near term
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • 10 mg vaginal insert placed transversely in posterior fornix, releases 0.3 mg/hr
  • Keep frozen; remove with retrieval string at 12 hr or onset of active labor
  • Client stays lying down 2 hr
  • Onset: within hours
  • Peak: not clearly defined
  • Duration: 12 hr
Watch for
  • Uterine tachysystole and hyperstimulation
  • Nonreassuring FHR, uterine rupture
  • Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, back pain, abdominal pain
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: fetal distress, unexplained vaginal bleeding, placenta previa, prior cesarean or uterine surgery, cephalopelvic disproportion, active herpes, hypersensitivity, already on oxytocin
  • Precautions: asthma, glaucoma, heart, kidney, or liver disease, more than 6 term births
Interactions
  • Oxytocin: wait 30 min after Cervidil removal
  • Other oxytocics and misoprostol: hyperstimulation
  • NSAIDs may lessen effect
Nurse does
  • Verify gestational age, presentation, Bishop score
  • Continuous fetal and contraction monitoring
  • Remove insert for tachysystole or nonreassuring FHR; give terbutaline per order
  • Wear gloves, check for allergy
Teach
  • Lie down for 2 hr after insertion
  • Do not remove the insert yourself
  • Cramping is expected
  • Report severe pain, bleeding, leaking fluid, decreased fetal movement
It is working when
  • Cervix softer, thinner, more open (Bishop score rises)
  • Labor starts
  • FHR reassuring
  • No tachysystole

💊 Bupivacaine (Week 3)

TopicKnow
ClassAmide local anesthetic
Why it works
  • Blocks sodium channels in nerve membranes
  • Stops nerve impulse conduction, causing loss of sensation (motor loss with higher doses)
Used for
  • Epidural and spinal anesthesia for labor and cesarean
  • Local infiltration for perineal repair
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • Epidural by anesthesia provider after test dose, bolus then continuous infusion
  • IV fluid preload first
  • Onset: epidural 10 to 20 min
  • Peak: 20 to 30 min
  • Duration: 2 to 4 hr
Watch for
  • Maternal hypotension (most common), bradycardia, urinary retention
  • Spinal headache, fever, itching, nausea, prolonged second stage
  • Local anesthetic toxicity: metallic taste, tinnitus, circumoral numbness, seizures, cardiac arrest
  • High spinal block with respiratory depression; fetal bradycardia
  • 0.75% not for obstetric use (boxed warning)
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: allergy to amide anesthetics, infection at site, coagulopathy or platelets under 100,000, hypovolemia, sepsis, increased ICP
  • Precautions: heart or liver disease, preeclampsia
Interactions
  • Opioids: added respiratory depression
  • Beta blockers, antiarrhythmics: added cardiac depression
  • Anticoagulants: epidural hematoma risk
  • Magnesium sulfate: added hypotension
Nurse does
  • Check consent, IV access, baseline vitals and FHR
  • BP every 1 to 2 min at first, then every 5 to 15 min
  • Left lateral position
  • Assess block level, pain, bladder
  • Keep O2, ephedrine, and lipid emulsion ready
Teach
  • Numbness and heaviness in legs expected
  • Stay in bed, call for help
  • May need urinary catheter
  • Report ringing in ears, metallic taste, numb mouth, SOB
  • Headache: lie flat, fluids
It is working when
  • Pain 0 to 3 on scale
  • BP and FHR stable
  • Block level adequate (T10 vaginal, T4 cesarean)
  • No adverse effects
➕ Added
  • Preload IV fluids and watch for maternal hypotension
  • Keep the client on her left side
  • A drop in BP can drop the fetal heart rate

💊 Carboprost tromethamine (Hemabate) (Week 3)

TopicKnow
ClassProstaglandin F2 alpha analog; uterotonic
🎤 Her emphasis
  • Second line for PPH
  • Big contraindication: asthma (bronchospasm)
Why it works
  • Stimulates strong uterine contractions
  • Reduces uterine blood loss
Used for
  • Postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony not controlled by oxytocin or methylergonovine
  • Second trimester abortion
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • 250 mcg deep IM, repeat every 15 to 90 min, max 8 doses (2 mg)
  • Refrigerate
  • Onset: rapid, within minutes
  • Peak: 30 min
  • Duration: about 2 hr
Watch for
  • Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chills, flushing, headache
  • Bronchospasm and wheezing
  • Hypertension, tachycardia, uterine cramping
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: asthma, active heart, lung, kidney, or liver disease, acute pelvic inflammatory disease, hypersensitivity
  • Precautions: hypertension, glaucoma, seizures
Interactions
  • Oxytocin and other oxytocics: increased effect
  • Other prostaglandins
Nurse does
  • Assess fundus, lochia, BP, HR, temperature
  • Listen to lung sounds, watch for wheezing
  • Give antiemetic and antidiarrheal per order
  • Massage fundus, track Hgb and Hct
  • Notify provider if bleeding continues
Teach
  • Nausea, diarrhea, fever, chills, cramping are temporary
  • Report SOB, wheezing, chest pain, heavy bleeding
  • Stay hydrated, rest
It is working when
  • Fundus firm
  • Bleeding decreases
  • Vitals stable
  • Hgb and Hct stable
  • No breathing problems

💊 Cytotec (Misoprostol) (Week 3)

TopicKnow
ClassProstaglandin E1 analog
🎤 Her emphasis
  • Second line for PPH (rectal, sublingual, or buccal)
  • Good choice when Methergine is not allowed because of hypertension
  • Also a ripening drug and the usual drug for a missed or incomplete miscarriage
Why it works
  • Softens and dilates the cervix and stimulates uterine contractions
  • Also decreases stomach acid and protects gastric lining
Used for
  • Off label: cervical ripening and induction, postpartum hemorrhage, miscarriage or abortion
  • Approved: prevent NSAID gastric ulcers
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • Ripening: 25 mcg vaginally every 3 to 6 hr
  • PPH: 600 to 1000 mcg rectal, SL, or PO once
  • Onset: oral within minutes; vaginal gradual
  • Peak: oral 12 min; vaginal 1 to 2 hr
  • Duration: about 3 to 4 hr
Watch for
  • Tachysystole, hyperstimulation, uterine rupture, abnormal FHR
  • Fever, chills, shivering, diarrhea, cramps, nausea, vomiting, headache
  • Vaginal bleeding
  • Teratogenic (category X)
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: pregnancy when used for ulcers, prior cesarean or uterine scar, fetal distress, placenta previa, unexplained bleeding, cephalopelvic disproportion, hypersensitivity
  • Precaution: heart disease
Interactions
  • Oxytocin: wait 4 hr after last dose
  • Other oxytocics, prostaglandins
  • Magnesium antacids: diarrhea
Nurse does
  • Verify no uterine scar, gestational age, Bishop score
  • Continuous fetal and contraction monitoring
  • Stop for tachysystole or nonreassuring FHR; terbutaline per order
  • Wait 4 hr before oxytocin
  • Check temperature, fundus, bleeding
Teach
  • Cramping and contractions expected
  • Lie down after dose
  • Report severe pain, heavy bleeding, fever, decreased fetal movement
  • Never take if pregnant when used for ulcers
It is working when
  • Bishop score rises
  • Labor begins, contractions every 2 to 5 min
  • FHR reassuring
  • PPH: fundus firm, bleeding decreased
➕ Added
  • Postpartum dose: 600 to 1,000 mcg once (rectal dose is usually 800 to 1,000 mcg)
  • Her Week 2 slide: oral, sublingual, buccal, or rectal
  • NOT vaginal during a hemorrhage because she is already bleeding

💊 Nifedipine (Procardia) (Week 3)

TopicKnow
ClassCalcium channel blocker; tocolytic; antihypertensive
🎤 Her emphasis➕ In pregnancy it treats severe hypertension (BP 160 systolic or 110 diastolic or higher) and works as a tocolytic.
Why it works
  • Blocks calcium entry into smooth muscle cells
  • Relaxes uterine and vascular smooth muscle, lowering contractions and BP
Used for
  • Short-term tocolysis in preterm labor (off label)
  • Hypertension including severe hypertension in pregnancy
  • Angina
How to give it (onset, peak, duration)
  • PO immediate release; typical load 20 to 30 mg, then 10 to 20 mg every 4 to 6 hr
  • Swallow whole; do not crush extended release; no sublingual use
  • Onset: IR 20 min
  • Peak: 30 to 60 min
  • Duration: 4 to 8 hr
Watch for
  • Hypotension, reflex tachycardia, headache, flushing, dizziness, palpitations
  • Peripheral edema, nausea, constipation
  • Syncope; decreased placental perfusion
  • Severe hypotension with magnesium
Do NOT give / use caution
  • Contraindicated: hypotension, cardiogenic shock, aortic stenosis, hypersensitivity
  • Precautions: heart failure, liver disease, volume depletion, concurrent magnesium sulfate
Interactions
  • Magnesium sulfate: hypotension, neuromuscular blockade
  • Other antihypertensives, beta blockers
  • Grapefruit juice and CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels
  • Rifampin, phenytoin lower levels; digoxin
Nurse does
  • Check BP and HR before and after each dose; hold if hypotensive
  • Monitor contractions and FHR
  • Assess edema, headache
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Use caution with magnesium
Teach
  • Change positions slowly
  • Avoid grapefruit juice
  • Report dizziness, fainting, palpitations, chest pain, ankle swelling
  • Report contractions or leaking fluid
  • Swallow capsule whole
It is working when
  • Contractions slow or stop
  • Birth delayed at least 48 hr for steroids
  • BP and HR stable
  • No adverse effects

💉 Other drugs from this week (not on a template)

DrugUsed forKnow
Calcium gluconateMagnesium toxicity🎤 Antidote. Keep it at the bedside whenever magnesium is running
Labetalol (Trandate)Severe hypertension
  • Common first choice for BP 160 systolic or 110 diastolic or higher
  • Sim ladder: 20, 40, 80 mg IV, max 220 mg
Hydralazine (Apresoline)Severe hypertensionIV. Used when labetalol is not an option
Betamethasone (Celestone)Fetal lung maturityIM, two doses 24 hours apart before preterm birth
IndomethacinTocolysis (ATI question)➕ Contraindicated after 32 weeks. Do not use at 35 weeks
RhoGAM (Rh immune globulin)Prevent Rh sensitization
  • 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth if baby is Rh-positive, and after ectopic, abortion, trauma, amniocentesis
  • Protects FUTURE pregnancies
MethotrexateEctopic pregnancy
  • Single IM dose
  • No folic acid, no alcohol, no sun, give an antiemetic, avoid pregnancy 3 months
  • Hepatotoxic
Ursodiol (UDCA)Intrahepatic cholestasisLowers bile acids and itching. Menthol creams help the itch too
InsulinGestational diabetesFirst line. Glyburide and metformin are second line
Penicillin GGBS prophylaxis
  • Drug of choice
  • At least 2 doses before birth
  • Allergy: cefazolin, then clindamycin, then vancomycin by reaction and susceptibility
AntiretroviralsHIV in pregnancyOral twice daily from 14 weeks until birth, IV in labor, newborn syrup for 6 weeks
HeparinPostpartum DVT
  • Watch aPTT, bleeding, platelets
  • Antidote protamine sulfate (➕)
  • Warfarin and enoxaparin are safe in breastfeeding
Tranexamic acid (TXA)PPH adjunct➕ 1 g IV over 10 minutes with the other PPH measures
Retinoids (isotretinoin, Accutane)AcneAbsolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. iPLEDGE needs two forms of birth control
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, androgens, warfarin, NSAIDsVarious
  • Adverse effects in pregnancy
  • Warfarin only with a mechanical valve
  • Some antiseizure drugs and antidepressants need a risk-benefit talk
SSRIs and SNRIsDepression
  • Generally considered safe
  • TCAs are not preferred and bupropion is not the best option
