🪤 How she could trap you

⚠️ Magnesium lowers BPNo. It prevents seizures. A different drug (labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine) lowers the BP.
⚠️ Methergine vs HemabateMethergine goes with hypertension. Hemabate goes with asthma. The wrong drug to the wrong client is the question.
⚠️ Oxytocin as the ripening drugHer slide lists oxytocin under ripening and augmentation. Cervidil and Cytotec are the classic ripening drugs.
⚠️ Terbutaline for tachysystoleIt slows the uterus. But hold it if the maternal HR is over 120.
⚠️ Cervidil then oxytocinNot at the same time. Wait 30 minutes after removing the insert.
⚠️ Plan B or Depo protects from STIsNeither does. Teach condoms.
⚠️ Combined pill while breastfeedingAvoid it. Estrogen can lower milk supply. Use estrogen free or nonhormonal methods: the shot, implant, minipill, IUD, or condoms.
⚠️ Bupivacaine and low BPHypotension is the most common problem. Give the IV fluid preload and position left.
⚠️ Which antidoteMagnesium: calcium gluconate. Heparin: protamine sulfate.

🧪 Say it first: Medications

Say the answer out loud first. Then tap the question to check yourself.

Which PPH drug is first line?
Oxytocin.
Which PPH drug is out with asthma?
Carboprost (Hemabate).
Which PPH drug is out with hypertension?
Methylergonovine (Methergine).
Magnesium antidote and first sign of toxicity?
Calcium gluconate. Loss of deep tendon reflexes.
Therapeutic magnesium level?
4 to 7 mEq/L.
Terbutaline hold parameter?
Maternal heart rate over 120.
How long after Cervidil removal before oxytocin?
30 minutes.
Plan B window?
As soon as possible, within 72 hours (3 days). Less effect up to 120 hours.
Depo-Provera boxed warning and schedule?
Bone mineral density loss. Every 11 to 13 weeks.
Which birth control pill is avoided while breastfeeding?
The combined oral contraceptive (estrogen). The progestin-only pill is safe.
Birth control choices while breastfeeding?
Estrogen free or nonhormonal only: Depo shot, implant (Nexplanon), minipill, IUD, condoms. Not the combined pill, patch, or ring.
Which drugs ripen the cervix?
Cervidil (dinoprostone), Cytotec (misoprostol), oxytocin, and mechanical methods.
Which tocolytics are on the cards?
Magnesium sulfate, terbutaline, nifedipine.
Which local anesthetic is the epidural drug?
Bupivacaine. Hypotension is the most common problem.

➕ marks a fact added from standard OB nursing sources because her slides do not say it. Her lecture and slides win if they differ.

📖 Vocabulary by chapter

238 terms. Tap a chapter to filter, then drill them in the Flash Study Game or Match Games.

Bleeding in Pregnancy (34)

TermMeaning
High-risk pregnancyA pregnancy that puts the mother, the fetus, or both in jeopardy. It comes from the pregnancy itself or from a condition that was there before it, and it carries higher morbidity and mortality.
Risk assessmentDone at the first prenatal visit and repeated through the pregnancy to find high-risk factors early.
Spontaneous abortionLoss of the fetus before 20 weeks. It is the most common complication of early pregnancy. Also called: miscarriage.
Induced abortionTermination caused by a procedure or a medication.
Elective abortionTermination before viability at the request of the woman.
Therapeutic abortionTermination for serious maternal medical indications or fetal anomalies.
D&C (dilation and curettage)Procedure that empties the uterus. Used when products of conception are not all expelled on their own.
Threatened abortionBleeding with a closed cervix. The pregnancy may continue. (added)
Inevitable abortionBleeding and cramping with a dilated cervix. The loss cannot be stopped. (added)
Incomplete abortionSome products of conception are passed and some are retained. (added)
Complete abortionAll products of conception are passed. (added)
Missed abortionThe embryo or fetus has died but nothing has been expelled. (added)
Ectopic pregnancyThe ovum implants outside the uterus: fallopian tube, cervix, ovary, or abdominal cavity. It happens in about 1 in 50 pregnancies and is the leading cause of death in the first trimester.
Classic triad of ectopic pregnancyAbdominal pain, amenorrhea, and vaginal bleeding. Most women do not have all three.
Hallmark sign of ectopic pregnancyAbdominal pain and spotting within 6 to 8 weeks after a missed period.
SalpingostomySurgery that opens the fallopian tube to remove an ectopic pregnancy.
MethotrexateSingle-dose IM drug for ectopic pregnancy. Teach: no folic acid, it is hepatotoxic, take an antiemetic, no alcohol, avoid pregnancy for at least 3 months, and it causes photosensitivity.
Gestational trophoblastic diseaseAbnormal growth of placental tissue. The two types are hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma. The pregnancy is not viable.
Hydatidiform moleA benign neoplasm of the placenta. It can be complete or partial. Also called: molar pregnancy.
ChoriocarcinomaA cancer that can follow a complete molar pregnancy. It can occur during pregnancy, after childbirth, or years later. Remission rate is about 90%.
Cervical insufficiencyPainless premature dilation of the cervix without contractions. Cause is unknown. Possible causes are cervical damage, less elastin or collagen, and more relaxin. Also called: incompetent cervix.
CerclageA stitch placed around the cervix to hold it closed in cervical insufficiency.
Placenta previaThe placenta is inserted in the lower uterine segment and partly or completely covers the internal os. Painless bright red bleeding in the last two trimesters.
Placental abruptionEarly separation of the placenta, which compromises the fetal blood supply. Dark red bleeding, knifelike pain, and a firm to rigid uterus.
Placenta accretaThe placenta attaches too deeply into the uterine wall. Postpartum hemorrhage is likely and a hysterectomy may be needed.
Concealed hemorrhageBleeding that stays trapped behind the placenta. It can happen with abruption, so the outside blood loss can understate how much she has lost.
Maternal-fetal medicine (MFM)Specialists a high-risk client may be referred to after risk assessment at the first prenatal visit.
Early pregnancy lossAnother name for spontaneous abortion or miscarriage: loss before 20 weeks.
Misoprostol (Cytotec)Medication that can end an early pregnancy. Bleeding is heavier than a normal period.
Uterine aspirationProcedure that removes the products of conception after an early pregnancy loss.
Vasa previaFetal vessels cross the cervical opening. Third trimester bleeding cause with risk to the baby.
Placenta incretaAbout 15% of accreta cases. The placenta invades the uterine muscle.
Placenta percretaAbout 5% of accreta cases. The placenta goes through the uterus into other organs such as the bladder.
Placenta accreta spectrumAccreta (about 80%), increta (15%), percreta (5%). Ranked by depth of invasion. Prior cesarean is a risk.

Hyperemesis, Liver, and Hypertensive Disorders (25)

TermMeaning
Hyperemesis gravidarumSevere nausea and vomiting of pregnancy with weight loss over 5% of pre-pregnancy weight, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance. It usually resolves by about week 20.
Gut restNPO to rest the GI tract. It is the priority for hyperemesis, along with IV fluids and antiemetics.
TPNTotal parenteral nutrition. IV nutrition used when a client with hyperemesis cannot take anything by mouth.
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancyPregnancy-specific liver disease where bile acids build up. Main finding is severe itching (pruritus). Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid.
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)The drug used to treat intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
Gestational hypertensionNew-onset BP above 140/90 after 20 weeks of gestation, without proteinuria. It raises the risk of preeclampsia.
Chronic hypertensionBP above 140/90 before pregnancy or before 20 weeks. About 25% of these women develop preeclampsia.
PreeclampsiaNew-onset hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria.
Preeclampsia with severe featuresPreeclampsia plus signs of organ involvement: liver (epigastric pain, high liver enzymes), brain (headache, blurred vision), kidneys (oliguria, abnormal kidney tests).
EclampsiaNew-onset seizure activity in a woman with preeclampsia. Client safety is the primary concern.
HELLP syndromeHemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets. A severe form of preeclampsia.
Superimposed preeclampsiaPreeclampsia that develops in a woman who already has chronic hypertension.
ProteinuriaProtein in the urine. 24-hour urine of 300 mg or more, or a protein to creatinine ratio of 0.3 or more, is a lab value of concern.
OliguriaLow urine output. A sign of kidney involvement in severe preeclampsia.
Magnesium sulfateThe drug that prevents and treats seizures in preeclampsia and eclampsia. Antidote: calcium gluconate. (added)
Calcium gluconateThe antidote for magnesium sulfate toxicity. Keep it at the bedside. (added)
Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs)Checked before and during magnesium sulfate. Losing the patellar reflex is the first sign of magnesium toxicity. (added)
UrsodiolMedication used for itching and bile acid buildup in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
Severe feature cutoffsBP 160/110, platelets under 100,000, creatinine over 1.1 or doubled, liver enzymes twice normal, brain or vision change, epigastric pain.
Mag WatchSim name for the magnesium sulfate check every 4 hours and PRN: DTRs 2+ with no clonus, RR 12 or more, urine 30 mL/hr or more, alert and oriented (GCS 15).
ClonusRhythmic muscle jerks after a reflex test. It is absent in the safe Mag Watch finding and can signal hyperreflexia.
HypermagnesemiaMagnesium toxicity. Cascade: absent DTRs, lethargy and slurred speech, respiratory depression, cardiac arrest. Stop the infusion, call for help, give calcium gluconate.
Protein to creatinine ratio (UPCR)Urine test for proteinuria. 0.3 or more is abnormal in preeclampsia. Sim client had 0.38.
Labetalol IV ladderSevere BP (160/110 sustained 15 min): 20 mg, 40 mg, 80 mg IV, each over 2 minutes, recheck BP 10 minutes after each. Max 220 mg. Notify the provider if severe BP persists after 80 mg.
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP)Also called PUPPP. Itchy red bumps and plaques that start in the stretch marks in late pregnancy. Normal labs, no risk to the baby. Topical steroids and antihistamines. (added)

Blood Incompatibility, Fluid, and Multiples (14)

TermMeaning
ABO incompatibilityType O mother with a fetus who has type A or B blood. Less severe than Rh incompatibility.
Rh incompatibilityAn Rh-negative mother is exposed to Rh-positive fetal blood, which makes her form antibodies (sensitization). The risk rises with each later Rh-positive fetus.
SensitizationThe mother makes antibodies against Rh-positive blood after exposure to it.
RhoGAMRh immune globulin. Given to an Rh-negative mother at 28 weeks, within 72 hours after birth, and after events such as ectopic pregnancy, abortion, trauma, amniocentesis, or fetal demise. Also called: Rh immune globulin, RhIG.
PolyhydramniosAmniotic fluid over 2,000 mL, usually found between weeks 32 and 36. Linked to fetal anomalies such as GI obstruction, neural tube defects, trisomy 13 and 18, and impaired swallowing.
Therapeutic amniocentesisRemoving amniotic fluid to relieve polyhydramnios.
IndomethacinA drug that lowers amniotic fluid by decreasing fetal urine output. Used for polyhydramnios.
OligohydramniosAmniotic fluid under 500 mL. Linked to maternal diabetes, IUGR, hypertension, and fetal urinary problems.
AmnioinfusionFluid placed into the uterus through a catheter. Used for oligohydramnios, mainly to relieve cord compression.
IUGRIntrauterine growth restriction. The fetus is smaller than expected for gestational age.
Multiple gestationMore than one fetus. Risks include anemia, excess weight gain, bleeding, hypertension, edema, and preterm birth.
Uterus larger than expected for EDBA key finding in multiple gestation. Confirmed by ultrasound.
Monozygotic twinsIdentical twins from one egg. They often share a placenta and chorion, so risk is higher.
Dizygotic twinsFraternal twins from two eggs. Each baby has its own placenta and sacs.

Preterm Labor, Birth, and PROM (13)

TermMeaning
Preterm laborRegular contractions that change the cervix before 37 weeks of gestation.
Preterm birthBirth between 20 0/7 and 36 6/7 weeks. Preterm is under 37 weeks, very preterm is under 32, and late preterm is 34 to 36.
Very pretermBirth before 32 weeks.
Late pretermBirth at 34 to 36 weeks.
PROMPremature (prelabor) rupture of membranes. The water breaks before labor starts.
PPROMPreterm premature rupture of membranes. The water breaks before labor and before 37 weeks.
ChorioamnionitisInfection of the membranes and amniotic fluid. A risk when rupture lasts more than 24 hours.
EndometritisInfection of the uterine lining. A risk of prolonged rupture of membranes.
Nitrazine testPaper that turns blue with amniotic fluid. Used with the fern test and ultrasound to confirm rupture.
Fern testDried amniotic fluid on a slide shows a fern pattern under the microscope.
Expectant managementWatching closely and waiting. Used for PPROM when the fetal lungs are immature.
Antenatal corticosteroidsBetamethasone given to the mother before preterm birth to mature fetal lungs. (added)
TocolyticA drug that slows or stops preterm contractions, such as nifedipine or terbutaline. (added)

Diabetes and Pregnancy (12)

TermMeaning
Pregestational diabetesType 1 or type 2 diabetes that was present before pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)Diabetes that develops during pregnancy. It is not type 2 diabetes.
Glucose tolerance test (GTT)Done at 24 to 28 weeks. The woman drinks 75 g of glucose and a level is drawn 2 hours later. An abnormal result leads to a 3-hour test.
HbA1cBlood test of average glucose over about 3 months. Ordered at the first visit if the client is high risk.
MacrosomiaA very large baby from fetal hyperglycemia. Leads to birth trauma and cesarean birth.
PolycythemiaToo many red blood cells. A neonatal complication of maternal diabetes.
HyperbilirubinemiaHigh bilirubin. A neonatal complication of maternal diabetes.
GlucosuriaSugar in the urine. It raises the risk of urinary tract infections in diabetic pregnancy.
InsulinFirst-line therapy for diabetes in pregnancy.
Glyburide and metforminSecond-line oral drugs for gestational diabetes.
50% dextroseKept at the bedside in labor for a diabetic mother in case of hypoglycemia.
PostprandialAfter a meal. Postprandial glucose is checked 1 or 2 hours after eating.

Heart, Lungs, Blood, and Autoimmune Disease (14)

TermMeaning
Class II heart diseaseSlight limitation of activity. She is comfortable at rest and has symptoms when she increases her activity.
Peripartum cardiomyopathyHeart failure that develops late in pregnancy or soon after birth. An acquired cardiac disorder.
Congenital heart disordersTetralogy of Fallot, atrial septal defect (ASD), ventricular septal defect (VSD), and patent ductus arteriosus.
Acquired heart disordersMitral valve prolapse, mitral valve stenosis, aortic stenosis, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and myocardial infarction.
Invasive hemodynamic monitoringUsed in labor for a client with heart disease to watch cardiac function and fluid status closely.
Iron-deficiency anemiaAnemia from not enough iron, usually from inadequate dietary intake. Findings include fatigue, pallor, tachycardia, and more infections.
ThalassemiaInherited anemia. Alpha is the minor form and beta is the major form. The minor form has little effect on pregnancy.
Sickle cell anemiaInherited anemia with sickling of red cells. Raises the risk of preeclampsia, preterm labor, abruption, IUGR, and maternal death.
AsthmaPregnancy worsens it for many women. Teach trigger avoidance and keep medications going.
Autoimmune diseaseThe immune system attacks the body. It can be localized, such as the thyroid, or systemic, such as lupus.
Hashimoto thyroiditis and Graves diseaseLocalized autoimmune diseases that target the thyroid gland.
Systemic lupus erythematosusSystemic autoimmune disease of the lung, heart, joints, kidneys, brain, and red blood cells. Raises the risk of flares, preeclampsia, loss, IUGR, and preterm birth.
Multiple sclerosisAutoimmune disease of the central nervous system. No known adverse effect of pregnancy or fertility.
Rheumatoid arthritisAutoimmune joint inflammation. No known adverse effect on pregnancy. Avoid medications that are toxic to the fetus.

HIV, Group B Strep, and Infection Prevention (12)

TermMeaning
HIVVirus that attacks the immune system. Threatens the mother, fetus, and newborn.
Antiretroviral therapyOral drugs twice daily from 14 weeks until birth, IV during labor, and oral syrup for the newborn for the first 6 weeks.
Viral loadThe amount of HIV in the blood. Helps decide the method of birth.
Group B streptococcus (GBS)Bacteria found by a vagino-rectal swab at 35 to 37 weeks. About 1 in 100 to 200 newborns of carriers develop disease.
Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxisAntibiotics given in labor to prevent GBS in the newborn. At least 2 doses are needed before birth.
Penicillin GThe treatment of choice for GBS. 5 million units IV, then 2.5 million units every 4 hours until delivery.
Early-onset GBS diseaseGBS illness in the newborn in the first days of life. A previous infant with it is a reason to give prophylaxis.
Vagino-rectal swabThe specimen used to test for GBS.
Cytomegalovirus (CMV)Common virus spread by a child's urine and saliva. The hygiene guidelines on her slide are the prevention steps. (added)
TORCHToxoplasmosis, Other, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex. Infections that can cross the placenta and cause fetal anomalies.
ToxoplasmosisTORCH infection from raw or undercooked meat and cat feces.
Herpes simplex virus (HSV)TORCH infection. Cesarean birth if active lesions are present at labor. Suppressive therapy at 36 weeks.

Vulnerable Populations and Substance Use (13)

TermMeaning
Adolescent pregnancyAbout 50% end in birth and 30% in abortion. The rest end in miscarriage or stillbirth.
Advanced maternal ageOver age 35. Raises the risk of loss, chromosomal abnormalities, stillbirth, preeclampsia, gestational diabetes, and preterm birth.
ObesityBMI over 30. Raises the risk of GDM, preeclampsia, preterm labor, anomalies, macrosomia, stillbirth, maternal death, and postpartum hemorrhage.
TeratogenA drug or substance that can cause fetal harm.
RetinoidsActive forms of vitamin A. They are on her list of drugs with adverse pregnancy effects.
WarfarinAn anticoagulant on her list of drugs with adverse effects in pregnancy. (Coumadin)
ACE inhibitors and ARBsBlood pressure drugs on her list of drugs with adverse effects in pregnancy.
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD)Lifelong physical, behavioral, and learning problems from alcohol exposure before birth.
Substance abuseCommon substances: alcohol, caffeine, nicotine, cocaine, marijuana, opiates and narcotics, sedatives, and methamphetamines.
Nonjudgmental approachThe nursing approach for a client who uses substances. It builds trust so she keeps coming to care.
TeratogenicAble to cause birth defects when the fetus is exposed. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, retinoids, and androgens are examples.
Isotretinoin (Accutane) and iPLEDGERetinoid that is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. iPLEDGE requires two forms of birth control.
Amotivational syndromeMarijuana effect listed in lecture, along with fetal growth restriction.

Dystocia, Induction, and Labor Interventions (12)

TermMeaning
Active phase disorderCervix over 6 cm with adequate contractions and no change, or no change after oxytocin for over 6 hours. A lack of progress that leads to cesarean.
DystociaDifficult labor, also called failure to progress. It is the leading cause of cesarean birth.
Uterine dystociaHypertonic or hypotonic uterine dysfunction or uncoordinated activity. Hypertonic contractions are painful with little dilation and little relaxation.
Second stage disorderCervix is 10 cm and there is no progress after at least 2 to 4 hours of active pushing.
Precipitous laborExtremely rapid labor lasting fewer than 3 hours from start to finish.
Fetal dystociaThe fetus cannot move through the birth canal effectively.
Pelvic dystociaThe pelvic opening is inadequate for the size of the fetus.
InductionStarting labor artificially. Criteria are 41 weeks or maternal or fetal distress.
AugmentationStrengthening labor that has already started, using oxytocin or artificial rupture of membranes.
AmniotomyArtificial rupture of the membranes, also called AROM.
Dinoprostone (Cervidil)Prostaglandin E2 insert used for cervical ripening.
External cephalic version (ECV)Procedure that turns a breech fetus to a head-down position through the abdomen.

Assisted Birth, VBAC, and Obstetric Emergencies (19)

TermMeaning
3-pull ruleVacuum rule: after 3 good pulls with no birth, go to emergency cesarean. Document pulls, pop-offs, and the time from insertion to birth.
Pop-offThe vacuum cup detaching from the fetal head because of excess force. Each one is documented.
McRoberts maneuverShoulder dystocia maneuver: legs pushed back toward the abdomen with suprapubic pressure. Never pull on the head.
Occult cord prolapseCord below the presenting part that cannot be seen or felt on exam. Frank prolapse is visible.
Vacuum-assisted deliveryA suction cup on the fetal head helps the birth. Risks include cephalhematoma and retinal hemorrhage.
Forceps-assisted deliveryCurved instrument blades guide the fetal head. Risks include facial injury and facial muscle paralysis.
CephalhematomaCollection of blood between the skull bone and its covering. It does not cross suture lines.
TOLACTrial of labor after cesarean. A planned attempt to deliver vaginally after a previous cesarean, whatever the outcome.
VBACVaginal birth after cesarean. A successful trial of labor that ends in a vaginal birth.
Post-term pregnancyPregnancy beyond 41 6/7 weeks. Neonatal death risk is greatly increased and the placenta ages out.
Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)The fetus breathes meconium-stained amniotic fluid into the lungs.
Stillbirth (IUFD)Intrauterine fetal demise: fetal death after 20 weeks with absent heart activity on visualization. Risk for DIC and sepsis.
Intra-amniotic infection (Triple I)Infection, inflammation, and fever involving amniotic fluid, placenta, fetus, membranes, or decidua. Also called chorioamnionitis.
Shoulder dystociaObstetric emergency where the fetal shoulder is stuck behind the pubic bone after the head is born.
Prolapsed umbilical cordObstetric emergency where the cord slips ahead of or beside the presenting part.
Uterine ruptureTearing of the uterus, often along a prior cesarean scar. Blood flows into the abdomen.
Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE)Anaphylactoid syndrome: amniotic fluid and fetal cells enter maternal circulation. Rare but fatal.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)Widespread clotting then bleeding because clotting factors are used up. Obstetric emergency.
Maternal trigger parametersRed and yellow vital sign limits that tell the nurse to escalate care.

Cesarean Birth and Maternal Early Warning (13)

TermMeaning
Classic vertical incisionOlder up-and-down uterine incision. Very high rupture risk, so no vaginal birth afterward.
Lower transverse incisionToday's standard uterine incision. Much lower rupture risk and the one that allows TOLAC.
Perimortem cesareanDelivery within 5 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest when circulation does not return. Can save mother and baby.
Cesarean indicationsPrevious cesarean, arrest of labor, placental or uterine abnormalities, cephalopelvic disproportion, maternal risk factors, malpresentation, Category II or III FHR.
Emergent cesareanImmediate need to deliver the fetus, such as cord prolapse, uterine rupture, or abnormal FHR patterns.
Urgent cesareanNeed for rapid delivery, such as malpresentation after labor starts or previa with mild bleeding and a Category I FHR.
Non-urgent cesareanFailure to progress or failure to descend with a Category I FHR.
Scheduled cesareanPlanned (elective or medically indicated) cesarean birth.
Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS)Bundle of steps that speed recovery: early oral intake, warmth, early catheter removal, early ambulation, non-opioid analgesia, thromboprophylaxis.
Maternal Early Warning Criteria (MEWC)Vital sign and symptom triggers that prompt bedside evaluation of a postpartum or surgical client.
Sudden Unexpected Postnatal Collapse (SUPC)Infant born at 35 weeks or later with a 5-minute Apgar of 7 or more who collapses and dies suddenly in the first week.
Skin-to-skin contact (STS)Newborn placed on the mother chest right after birth to support bonding and transition.
DehiscenceSeparation of the edges of a surgical incision.

FHR Patterns and Categories (15)

TermMeaning
FHR baselineAverage fetal heart rate over a 10 minute window, rounded to 5 bpm, excluding accelerations and decelerations. Normal is 110 to 160 bpm.
Fetal tachycardiaBaseline above 160 bpm for 10 minutes or more. Causes include fever, infection, dehydration, anxiety, anemia, cocaine, and terbutaline.
Fetal bradycardiaBaseline below 110 bpm for 10 minutes or more. Causes include supine hypotension, abruption, cord occlusion, and cardiac problems.
VariabilityFluctuation in the baseline. Absent is undetectable, minimal is 5 bpm or less, moderate is 6 to 25 bpm, marked is over 25 bpm.
AccelerationAbrupt rise of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds or more (10 bpm for 10 seconds under 32 weeks). Reassuring.
Early decelerationGradual drop that mirrors the contraction. Caused by fetal head compression. Benign, so just watch.
Late decelerationGradual drop that starts after the contraction begins, with the low point after the peak. Caused by uteroplacental insufficiency.
Variable decelerationAbrupt drop of 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds to under 2 minutes, with changing shape and timing. Caused by cord compression.
Prolonged decelerationDrop of 15 bpm or more lasting 2 minutes or more but under 10 minutes.
Sinusoidal patternSmooth, wave-like baseline that is very ominous. It is Category III and needs urgent action.
Category I tracingNormal: baseline 110 to 160, moderate variability, no late or variable decelerations. Early decelerations and accelerations may be present or absent.
Category II tracingIndeterminate: anything that is not Category I or III. Needs evaluation, continued surveillance, and often resuscitation measures.
Category III tracingAbnormal: absent variability with recurrent late or variable decelerations or bradycardia, or a sinusoidal pattern. Always abnormal.
Intrauterine resuscitationSteps to restore fetal oxygen: reposition, stop oxytocin, IV bolus for maternal hypotension, oxygen only if SpO2 is under 95%, check for prolapse, check vitals, notify the provider.
Reactive nonstress testAt least two accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes. This is the normal result.

Postpartum Hemorrhage (11)

TermMeaning
Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH)Blood loss over 1,000 mL regardless of type of delivery.
Uterine atonyFailure of the uterus to contract firmly after birth. The most common cause of PPH.
Primary PPH causesUterine atony, lacerations, hematomas.
Secondary PPH causesHematomas, subinvolution, retained placental tissue.
The four TsTone (atony), Tissue (retained placenta), Trauma (lacerations, hematoma), Thrombin (clotting disorders).
SubinvolutionUterus fails to return to its normal size and position. Cause of late bleeding.
UterotonicMedication that makes the uterus contract: oxytocin, methylergonovine, misoprostol, carboprost.
Methylergonovine (Methergine)Ergot uterotonic for PPH. Avoid in hypertension and preeclampsia.
Carboprost (Hemabate)Prostaglandin F2 alpha uterotonic for PPH. Avoid in asthma.
Bimanual compressionOne hand inside the vagina and one on the abdomen compress the uterus to stop bleeding.
Hypovolemic shockShock from blood loss: tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, low oxygen saturation, oliguria, pallor, altered mental status.

Clots, Embolism, Infection, and Birth Trauma (12)

TermMeaning
ThrombophlebitisInflammation of the vein lining with a clot. Superficial (saphenous) or deep (DVT).
Anaphylactoid syndrome of pregnancyAnother name for amniotic fluid embolism. Rare but fatal, up to 24 hours postpartum.
Venous thromboembolism (VTE)Blood clot in a vein: superficial thrombosis or deep vein thrombosis (DVT) that can travel as a pulmonary embolism.
Virchow triadVenous stasis, injury to the vessel lining, and hypercoagulation. The three causes of thrombosis.
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)Clot in a deep vein, usually the leg. One-sided pain, swelling, warmth, redness. It can travel to the lungs.
Pulmonary embolism (PE)Clot in the lung arteries. Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, tachycardia, low oxygen saturation. Emergency.
Superficial thrombosisClot in a surface vein, usually the saphenous vein of the lower leg.
HeparinAnticoagulant used for postpartum DVT. Antidote is protamine sulfate.
Wound infectionErythema, swelling, tenderness, and purulent drainage at an incision or laceration.
MastitisBreast infection: tender, swollen, hard breast with fever. Continue breastfeeding and give antibiotics.
Hematoma (postpartum)Blood collects in the connective tissue of the vagina or perineum. Very painful.
LacerationTear of the birth canal. Second most common cause of primary PPH.

Postpartum Mood Disorders and Follow-Up (9)

TermMeaning
Postpartum bluesMild mood changes in the first 2 weeks from hormones, stress, and fatigue. Resolves without treatment.
Postpartum depression (PPD)Severe mood disorder within the first 12 months. Needs psychiatric intervention.
Postpartum psychosisRare, rapid onset, as early as 2 to 3 days postpartum. Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech or behavior. Most severe.
Perinatal mood and anxiety disorders (PMADs)Group of mood and anxiety disorders around pregnancy and the postpartum period.
POST-BIRTH warning signsAWHONN list of danger signs the mother must report: chest pain, trouble breathing, seizures, thoughts of harm, heavy bleeding, bad incision, painful leg, fever, headache.
Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)Common screening questionnaire for postpartum depression. Any answer about thoughts of self-harm needs immediate action.
Postpartum follow-up visitVisit within 6 weeks of birth. Contraception is started and she can ask questions about labor, birth, and complications.
Pregestational diabetes after birthInsulin requirements decrease. Higher infection risk. Most return to normal glucose tolerance, and follow-up is essential.
Severe postpartum hypertensionSystolic 160 or more or diastolic 110 or more. Needs urgent antihypertensive treatment.

Medications: Weeks 1 to 3 (10)

TermMeaning
TocolyticA drug that slows or stops uterine contractions. Magnesium sulfate, terbutaline, nifedipine.
Uterotonic (oxytocic)A drug that makes the uterus contract. Oxytocin, Methergine, Hemabate, Cytotec.
Cervical ripeningSoftening and thinning the cervix before induction. Cervidil, Cytotec, balloon, laminaria.
TachysystoleMore than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, or contractions lasting over 90 seconds. Seen with oxytocin and prostaglandins.
High alert medicationA drug where an error can cause serious harm. Oxytocin and magnesium sulfate are examples.
Boxed warningThe strongest FDA warning on a label. Depo-Provera (bone loss), Premarin (cancer, stroke, MI, clots), terbutaline (prolonged tocolysis).
TeratogenicAble to cause birth defects. Danazol, Cytotec (category X), retinoids, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs.
AntidoteThe drug that reverses another drug. Calcium gluconate for magnesium. Protamine sulfate for heparin.
Onset, peak, durationHow fast a drug starts, when it works best, and how long it lasts.
Diffusion hypoxiaLow oxygen after nitrous oxide stops. Give oxygen afterward.

🚦 Priority Decoder

Four clients, one nurse. This is the table that ranks them.

The ranking rule

Rank by how fast it can hurt the mother or the fetus, not by how abnormal it sounds. Airway, breathing, and circulation come first. Bleeding with fetal distress, seizure risk, and toxicity beat stable abnormal findings. A new, acute change beats a long-standing one. Teaching and routine labs come last.

  • Minutes: abruption with fetal distress, heavy bleeding, previa that bleeds, magnesium toxicity, eclampsia, heart failure signs, low glucose with symptoms.
  • Hours: fever after prolonged rupture, severe preeclampsia signs, preterm labor, missed GBS prophylaxis, DKA.
  • Days to weeks: stable anemia, routine screening, vitamins, teaching.

Added for Ch 21, Ch 22 and FHR

  • Minutes: Category III tracing, cord prolapse, uterine rupture, amniotic fluid embolism, postpartum hemorrhage with shock signs, PE, postpartum psychosis with thoughts of harm.
  • Hours: Category II tracing, tachysystole on oxytocin, severe postpartum hypertension (treat within the hour), endometritis, hematoma.
  • Routine: early decelerations, blues, mild mastitis, expected incisional pain.

Always fix the cause that starves the baby of oxygen or drains the mother of blood first, then notify.
